Android can now securely migrate your logins between password managers

Ars Technica September 10, 2026

App support is slim right now, but Google says more are coming.

As longer, more complex passwords have become a necessity, remembering all those strings of numbers, letters, and special characters has become nearly impossible. Password managers can solve that problem, but what happens when you want to move to a different login organizer? Sure, you could manually type all your logins into a new app, but now Android can do that for you without the tedium.

Google designed the new login transfer process to happen entirely on your phone, so you need the corresponding apps installed with your credentials synced. To start the move, you’ll have to find the import option in the app you want to use. The location of that feature will vary, but in Google Password Manager (built into Android), it’s near the top under the settings tab.

The import option in Google Password Manager will plug in to the new migration system, while export still just creates an unencrypted CSV with your passwords that can be dumped into any app. It will be similar in other apps, so make sure to start the process in the app you want to use. Currently, this works in Google’s app, 1Password, Bitwarden, and Dashlane.

Once you trigger the migration, the Android system will verify your identity and ask you to confirm the move in your new password manager. Android can move both passwords and passkeys without creating any risky text files. Even if you’ve got a lot of passwords, the process should wrap up quickly.

This feature doesn’t require an OS update or new app downloads beyond grabbing the password manager you want to use. It’s integrated with Google Play Services and works on all devices running Android 8.0 Oreo or higher. Play Services support currently only goes back to 7.0 Nougat, so password migration should work on virtually every operational Google-certified Android device in the world.

If you want to use a password manager that isn’t on the list, you’re currently stuck doing a manual import or an unencrypted CSV. This feature relies on the Credential Transfer API, which the previously mentioned apps have all implemented. Google says more password managers will add support for transfers via this API eventually but does not offer a timeline.

Panic builds over bankrupt Spirit’s looming data sale to Google

Ars Technica September 10, 2026

“Bankruptcy cannot become the new land grab for AI.”

Doug Kreuzkamp was shocked when news outlets reported that Google won an auction to buy a huge amount of operational data as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy proceedings.

Kreuzkamp founded a startup called Springshot in 2011, which created a widely used proprietary platform that helps humans and AI systems improve airline efficiency and quickly solve logistics problems so flights can stay on time and airlines can operate as smoothly as possible. Hundreds of airports use it globally.

Springshot powered Spirit’s technology stack for the last three years, right up to the “very last flight,” Kreuzkamp told Ars. Yet his company got no notice when Spirit prepared to auction off a massive dataset that he thinks likely improperly includes a substantial amount of data and intellectual property (IP) that Springshot owns—not Spirit.

In a limited objection filed last month, Springshot argued that Spirit’s sale agreement does not make it clear what data is being sold. It only vaguely references categories of data that would possibly rope in Springshot data, including “productivity and collaboration data,” “core business systems and business application data,” and “workflow and process data.”

“This expansive definition does nothing to differentiate between Springshot’s intellectual property that exists within Spirit’s data repositories and systems, but Spirit does not own, and Spirit data that it actually owns and has the capacity to sell,” Springshot argued.

Springshot urged the court to pause Spirit’s data sale until a transparent forensic process establishes that none of the data Google is grabbing is actually owned by third parties.

If the bankruptcy court does not “pump the brakes,” it risks sanctioning an “unauthorized acquisition and use of trade secrets” that could doom startups, Springshot alleged. In an email to Ars, Springshot summarized its fears as the court possibly creating “a precedent where startups see massive amounts of IP transferred to the world’s richest and most monopolistic companies via bankruptcy courts.”

“Bankruptcy cannot become the new land grab for AI,” Kreuzkamp told Ars. “The possession of IP is not ownership.”

Asked for comment, Google’s spokesperson declined to discuss mounting objections and repeated a prior statement provided to Ars that did not address any of the concerns raised.

“We acquired part of an enterprise dataset from Spirit Airlines, which can be helpful in improving our products and AI models,” Google’s spokesperson said. “We will not receive any personal information from this dataset.”

It seems likely that a wide range of Spirit vendors could be in the same spot as Springshot, Kreuzkamp suspects, and his firm is not the only one complaining.

Citing Springshot’s concerns in a separate objection, the International Aero Engines LLC and the IAE International Aero Engines AG alleged that the dataset might also include its proprietary commercial information, technical data, and financial data. Both vendors cited confidentiality provisions in Spirit agreements that appear to have been completely ignored in the push to get the data sale approved.

Top concerns are that proprietary data could be transferred to Google without consent, giving firms no chance to guard against Google—or a third party later gaining access to the data—infringing ownership rights and exposing trade secrets. Both vendors said they risked irreparable harm through the sale to Google and then again through possible resales to future third parties.

For Springshot, it also seems possible that Google could use its valuable IP to create a rival product. In August, just a week before the controversial Spirit auction, Europe’s largest airline, Ryanair, announced a five-year partnership with Google. Under the deal, Ryanair will share operational data to improve Gemini Enterprise tools. That “is precisely the function Springshot served for Spirit,” the startup said in a footnote in its objection, while alleging that “Springshot’s data may be among the most AI-relevant assets to be purchased.” As Springshot argued:

“Should the sale proceed without such safeguards, and should Google obtain Springshot’s intellectual property and ingest that data, Springshot would forfeit the value of its technology it has spent 15 years developing. That existential threat is only amplified by the fact that Google has recently announced its desire to operationalize its own AI platform for airline operations, placing it in direct competition with Springshot.”

Adam Schwartz, a privacy litigation director for a digital rights nonprofit called the Electronic Frontier Foundation, told Ars that allowing Google to buy this dataset via bankruptcy proceedings is unusual.

“This is the first time I am aware of so public a bankruptcy proceeding regarding whether a bankrupt company may sell off the personal data it has amassed as an asset in bankruptcy,” Schwartz said. “It is also the first time I am aware of a company seeking to sell its employees’ data (as opposed to its customers’ data) as an asset in bankruptcy.”

Kreuzkamp is worried that because bankruptcy courts have not deeply considered this issue before, the system is just not set up to protect vendors like his company. In the past, it was straightforward to determine who owned an asset. Consider how Spirit is selling airplanes, which bills of sale clearly demonstrate that it owns, he said. His experience suggests that when it comes to digital assets, courts don’t have the proper notice provisions that are necessary to ensure vendors can advocate for IP to be segregated from sales, should purchases like Google’s become the norm.

“Our main concern with everything is if you want startups to continue building, you need to protect what they built,” Kreuzkamp told Ars. “If they spent 15 years building IP, that IP should not be misappropriated because their customer went bankrupt.”

Springshot and the IAE objectors both want the court to require Spirit to segregate any proprietary vendor data before approving the sale to Google. Springshot argued that it should include any data or information generated by its service or software, including data “likely commingled with much of Spirit’s own operational data (like its employees’ emails, chat histories, etc.).”

“To ensure Springshot’s intellectual property is not among the data acquired by Google (or any other potential buyer) a forensic process is necessary to first identify, and then segregate, Springshot’s intellectual property from that actually owned by Spirit,” Springshot argued.

Kreuzkamp told Ars that Springshot engaged with Spirit every day before it shut down.

“We were very tightly coupled with them, did a lot of great work helping that airline,” he said. “And so, I know there are tens of thousands of emails and documents that I’m sure are in their servers.”

If Spirit is forced to segregate a large chunk of data, the value of the dataset may substantially depreciate for Google. In its sale agreement, Google stipulated that Spirit ensure that “no portion of the Assets has been deleted, modified, or removed,” other than through planned processes like the deidentification of customers’ personal data and “de minimis” removals preserving privileged materials.

Kreuzkamp told Ars that prior to reading the Spirit-Google sale agreement, he assumed that if one of the companies he partnered with became insolvent, that either vendor data would be destroyed or that agreements would be honored to prevent transfers to third parties.

On September 16, there will be a hearing where the court will mull objections to the sale. Along with vendors, unions and groups representing many former Spirit employees have joined flight attendants who quickly opposed the sale out of fears that Google or a third party could possibly link them to scrubbed data.

Troublingly, the sale agreement only required de-identification of customer personal data, and former Spirit workers worried that Google’s AI system may combine confidential worker data in ways that may expose information that they might not want public. As groups representing machinists, aerospace workers, and transport workers noted, workers aren’t even aware of all the risks, since “the proposed sale raises novel technological and legal concerns on very short notice.” Seemingly, not even Spirit knows the “ultimate uses” to which the data “may be put after it is sold and processed through artificial intelligence,” they warned.

Schwartz told Ars that Spirit should have gotten consent from workers before selling 80,000 email accounts, 100 million emails, 20 million SharePoint documents, and 500 million Teams messages.

“My top concern is that data privacy is a fundamental human right, enjoyed for example by employees in relation to their employers,” Schwartz said. “This includes the norm that data collected from a person for one reason should not be used or disclosed for another reason without first getting their opt-in consent. Therefore, it is the Spirit Airline employees themselves who should be making the decision whether they want to bear the risk to their privacy of their emails being turned into AI training data.”

Some former workers are alarmed that the data sale could possibly harm the public.

Most ominously, the Air Line Pilots Association, International warned that if Google’s AI system re-identifies pilots in the data set, airways could become more dangerous.

Flight safety programs depend on pilots feeling comfortable sharing in-depth incident reports without fear that confidential information may become public, the Federal Aviation Administration has found. Therefore, any “disclosure of confidential flight operations data through the Sale Agreement can be expected to chill voluntary compliance by pilots across the industry as it becomes known that such data can be sold to third parties with no expertise or interest in aviation safety and presumably included in databases accessible by the public using artificial intelligence software,” the association warned.

Last week, an AI training data lab, Micro1, put in a last-minute competing bid that it claims resolves all objections to the data sale. Outbidding Google by 25 percent, Micro1 offered $12.5 million in cash, while promising that if debtors pick Micro1 over Google, the bankruptcy proceedings can avoid any further delays.

However, Micro1’s plan notably includes de-identifying the data in-house, which Spirit debtors were opposed to in the auction process. Spirit even chose a lower second bid should the Google sale fall through because the de-identification was completed by independent third parties. It seems, then, that even if the late bid is considered, it’s less likely to tempt debtors. Additionally, Micro1’s claims to resolve all objections may be somewhat exaggerated. In Springshot’s case, Micro1 does not promise to segregate IP, trade secrets, or proprietary data. Instead, Micro1 only says that it will not use Springshot data to create a rival product or ever sell the data to a would-be rival.

Ars could not reach Micro1’s lawyers for comment, but the data lab said it plans to attend the upcoming hearing to entice debtors to take their offer.

Kreuzkamp told Ars that he appreciates that Micro1 acknowledges Springshot’s concerns, but his objective remains scrubbing Spirit’s dataset of any data that Springshot owns.

His company’s lawyers have been in contact with Spirit debtors’ legal team and plan to defend Springshot’s proprietary data at the upcoming hearing. They feel confident the court will take their concerns seriously. But there are no guarantees, as the bankruptcy court prepares to approve this unusual sale. Kreuzkamp said it remains unclear what process a bankrupt company like Spirit should be taking to “ensure that it extricates everything that is proprietary from a dataset.”

“I just think it’s a very complex issue when it comes to extricating the data that’s owned by somebody else,” Kreuzkamp said. However, now’s the time to do it, he suggested, since “once you throw data into an AI model, it’s impossible to trace what the model did with that.”

Physicist does the math on Star Trek’s “Picard maneuver”

Ars Technica September 10, 2026

The trick from Next Generation would be even more effective in real life.

It turns out Jean-Luc Picard was an even better starship helmsman than the writers knew. A physicist has gone through the details of a warp-speed trick from the first season of Star Trek: The Next Generation and found a subtlety the show missed. But instead of a plot hole, the detail he found actually makes the maneuver more impressive… as well as a great opportunity to teach about a lesser-known feature of the theory of relativity.

Níckolas de Aguiar Alves, a physicist at the Federal University of ABC in Brazil, first watched Next Generation as a master’s student. When he got to the episode “The Battle” in the show’s first season, the plot reminded him of his relativity coursework.

In “The Battle,” a Ferengi leader reminds Picard of a battle he fought years ago as captain of a ship called the Stargazer. Under fire from a mysterious attacker, Picard’s ship’s shields were down. He had to get closer without taking a hit, so he made a gamble. Picard ordered the Stargazer to charge the enemy ship at warp speed (meaning faster than light), then stop abruptly and fire. By going faster than light, Picard anticipated that the other ship would see two images of the Stargazer: where it reached warp speed and where it stopped. If they fired on the wrong image, they would miss the Stargazer, and Picard could win the battle.

Later in the episode, Riker mentions that the trick had been immortalized in Starfleet textbooks as the “Picard maneuver.”

As it turns out, it’s also not that far from what you can find in some physics textbooks. While warp speed is pure science fiction, physicists sometimes need to consider what happens when an object goes faster than light, and such an object really does leave two images.

Something about the story bothered de Aguiar Alves at the time. But he forgot about it until years later, when he was working through a more practical problem involving particles in a medium with a slower speed of light. Not trusting that he had done the math right, he started trying to work out the situation visually.

“And after I drew one or two diagrams, I started noticing, ‘Hey, I think I’ve thought about something like this before,’” said de Aguiar Alves.

The idea behind the Picard maneuver comes from the way a faster-than-light spaceship would outrun its own light. If the spaceship were going at a constant, faster-than-light speed, then another ship at rest would see two images, corresponding to two different times when light from the ship could reach them.

But in the story, Picard’s ship isn’t going at a constant speed. He speeds up to warp speed, then stops close to the enemy ship. The Stargazer accelerates twice… and that changes the timing. After diagramming things out, de Aguiar Alves found that the enemy ship would see three images of the Stargazer, not two.

While the details were wrong, de Aguiar Alves was impressed that the episode reproduced the core textbook idea mostly accurately. “The main thing they got perfectly, and I think it is a great illustration.”

Physicists don’t expect faster-than-light space travel to ever be possible. But because light travels more slowly in substances like water, the math of faster-than-light travel is still useful. When a particle travels faster than light can in water, its shockwave emits a characteristic glow called Cherenkov radiation, the blue light seen in nuclear reactors.

For de Aguiar Alves, the motivation was a more elusive physical phenomenon, called the memory effect. First theorized for gravitational waves, the memory effect happens when a wave passes by a particle and leaves a lasting effect on its motion. Theoretical physicists expect it to happen when ordinary electromagnetic waves pass a particle, too, but it requires very specific circumstances and is very hard to detect. Recently, a physicist at the Niels Bohr Institute has argued that the effect should be more dramatic in a medium like water with a limited speed of light. Wanting to understand this better inspired de Aguiar Alves to try to picture how a memory-effect-influenced electron would be detected, and the diagrams he drew helped him picture the Star Trek scenario as well.

“You get a lot of intuition very quickly, and pretty much for free, by just doodling,” said de Aguiar Alves.

Matt von Hippel is a freelance science writer based in Copenhagen, with a background in particle physics. In addition to journalism, he blogs weekly at 4gravitons. com.

Kimmel’s ABC show won’t air interview with Democrat because of Trump FCC threats

Ars Technica September 10, 2026

Talarico talk to be on YouTube to save ABC stations the hassle of dealing with FCC.

ABC’s Jimmy Kimmel said he will be interviewing a Democratic candidate for Senate tonight, but the interview will be on YouTube only and not broadcast on TV because of threats made by the Federal Communications Commission.

Kimmel has been a prime target in the Trump FCC’s attacks on ABC and its owner, Disney. In his monologue last night, Kimmel said he’ll be interviewing Democrat James Talarico, a state representative who is running against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton for a seat in the US Senate.

In previous years, such an interview would have aired on the broadcast show via local stations throughout the country, Kimmel said. This time, it will only be on the Jimmy Kimmel Live YouTube channel in order to prevent further trouble for individual stations that hold FCC licenses, he said.

“I’ll be interviewing James Talarico tomorrow night under unusual circumstances,” Kimmel told the audience on Wednesday. “For a lot of years, for the whole 20-plus years of our show, in fact, I’ve been interviewing Americans who are running for office with no problem at all, just like Letterman did, Leno did, Arsenio, et cetera, et cetera. I’ve interviewed a lot of political candidates, from Hillary Clinton to Ted Cruz to Donald Trump himself.”

But as Kimmel said, “something has changed.” Disney suspended Kimmel briefly last year after FCC Chairman Brendan Carr threatened to revoke the licenses of ABC stations for “news distortion” if they continued to air Kimmel’s show.

Much more has followed. In April, the Carr FCC ordered an early license review for all eight TV stations owned by ABC. Carr did this only one day after Trump and first lady Melania Trump called on ABC to fire Kimmel over a joke they didn’t like, though the FCC says the license review is over allegations that ABC’s diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) practices violate anti-discrimination rules.

The Carr FCC also started investigating ABC’s The View after it aired an interview with Talarico and opened a proceeding in May 2026 to examine whether The View should continue to be exempt from the equal-time rule as a “bona fide news interview program.” The View hasn’t aired any interviews of political candidates since the FCC began the proceeding.

Until Carr took over at the FCC, the agency historically treated talk shows that feature interviews as exempt from the equal-time rule that requires stations to provide comparable time and placement to an opposing candidate if an opposing candidate makes a request. The Carr FCC ordered broadcast TV stations in January to comply with the equal-time rule when airing late-night and daytime talk shows that are “motivated by partisan purposes,” but has not made similar moves against talk radio shows that are predominantly conservative.

“Jimmy Kimmel’s decision to keep his interview with a Senate candidate off the air shows just how far this administration’s campaign of censorship and control has gone,” FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, the commission’s only Democrat, said today. Gomez said the FCC “has no lawful authority to threaten broadcast licenses over guest bookings or editorial decisions,” and that “no host, local affiliate, or network should have to weigh federal retaliation before booking a guest for a newsworthy interview. Any attempt to pressure broadcasters into self-censorship undermines both press freedom and the public’s right to hear from candidates in their communities seeking public office.”

An interview with Talarico was also at the center of controversy in February when Stephen Colbert said CBS forbade him from interviewing the candidate. Colbert put the interview on YouTube instead. CBS denied prohibiting the interview but said it gave Colbert “legal guidance that the broadcast could trigger the FCC equal-time rule for two other candidates… and presented options for how the equal time for other candidates could be fulfilled.”

Disney sued the FCC in August, saying its First Amendment rights have been violated and that “ABC must now evaluate any invitation to a political candidate for its potential consequences, including whether it might later be cited by the Commission as a basis for non-renewal in the Stations’ impending license renewal proceedings.” Disney said the Trump administration’s campaign of censorship against ABC will be particularly damaging during the months before the midterm election.

Kimmel didn’t recount all of that history last night, but referred to it when he told the audience about the upcoming Talarico interview. Kimmel said:

I interviewed Donald Trump when he was running for president in 2015, and at that time when he was the one sitting next to me, he seemed to have no problem with the idea of talk show hosts interviewing candidates. In fact, he was very eager to come back for another interview, which he did just before he became the nominee in 2016.

But for some reason, and I can’t seem to figure out what that reason is, something has changed. Now that he’s president, his FCC has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on simple, traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings it would seem they don’t like.

Kimmel said the decision to put the interview on YouTube was made out of consideration for local stations that could face FCC threats to their broadcast licenses.

“And so out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas who would have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television,” Kimmel said. “It will be posted on YouTube instead. It will not be on TV. So if you want to learn about a candidate for the Senate tomorrow, you will have to go to the Jimmy Kimmel Live YouTube channel where you will see it in its entirety, and thank goodness we have that because in the America we live in right now, that is the best that we can do, until November, of course.”

Disney’s legal fight against the FCC is ongoing. The FCC last week urged a court to dismiss Disney’s lawsuit and let it continue a proceeding that could end in the nonrenewal of broadcast licenses held by ABC-owned stations. Watchdog groups told the court they are worried that Disney will agree to a settlement with the FCC that “limits the content provided by the ABC stations.”

China’s drone supremacy shows in airlifting bodies and food after Nepal flood disaster

Ars Technica September 10, 2026

DJI drones that already supply Mount Everest camps assist Nepal’s flood relief.

Chinese-made drones are flying out the bodies of flood victims and delivering food to survivors in the aftermath of devastating flash floods on the border of Nepal and China’s Tibetan region.

Nepal’s army has been using four DJI FlyCart 100 drones donated from China to make 10 to 16 aid deliveries each day, according to Reuters. This comes after a partial glacier collapse in the Himalayan mountains unleashed a sudden surge of water, mud, and debris that swept through border crossings, valley communities, and hydropower projects on August 26.

The DJI Flycart 100 Drones come with a 98-foot rope and winch system for picking up and dropping off heavy loads. The website of Chinese drone company DJI describes the drones as being able to carry between 187 and 220 pounds, depending on the battery configuration.

The four Chinese cargo drones being used by the Nepal army are currently hauling about 132 pounds of supplies per trip, Reuters reported. That heavy-lift capability has also allowed the drones to remove human bodies from some flood-stricken areas.

The official death toll in Nepal had risen to 1,369 as of September 9, according to a situation report from the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. The Nepal government agency also reported that more than 5,000 people are still missing, including 587 foreign nationals.

The same situation report also mentioned how the drones have helped to distribute 1,591 kilograms of food items across 31 flights. The United Nations is appealing for $20.5 million to help 43,000 people in the aftermath of the flood disaster in Nepal.

Smaller drones have also proven useful in search-and-rescue efforts as Nepal has deployed more than 21,000 police and soldiers to look for survivors. Search teams have occasionally found surviving workers trapped in hydropower tunnels after the floodwaters ripped through both operational hydropower plants and sites under construction.

One drone pilot and filmmaker, Manish Maharjan, told AP News about flying small drones inside hydropower plant tunnels to help search for trapped workers but highlighted the challenges of flying drones through tunnels with many “bends, turns, or zigzags.” Maharjan also described finding some tunnels “filled with mud like toothpaste in a tube.”

The drones carried microphone speakers that allowed rescuers to call out to potential survivors or play music, which helped locate survivors in a few cases, Maharjan said. The Nepal government’s September 9 update described 13,646 people as having been rescued so far.

Chinese officials have reported 43 deaths on the Tibetan side of the border with more than 500 people still missing, according to NBC News.

The flood relief efforts represent just the latest example of Chinese cargo drones operating in Nepal. Since 2024, Sherpas assisting climbers at Mount Everest have been making regular use of Chinese drones—including the same DJI Flycart 100 and the smaller DJI Flycart 30—to deliver oxygen cylinders and other supplies to camps while ferrying out poop bags and other garbage, Al Jazeera reported.

The Mount Everest drone flights have even become a focus of US-China tech competition. On May 1, a US team led by President Donald Trump’s special envoy for South Asia attempted to fly a US-made Freefly Alta X Gen 2 drone from the Mount Everest base camp in a challenge to DJI’s heavy-lift drone dominance in Nepal.

But that flight never happened because Nepal’s government denied the US team permission to fly. The government also canceled the drone flight permits for the Chinese DJI drones for a week before protests from Mount Everest expedition operators prompted the official go-ahead for flights to resume.

The Nepal government’s decision to temporarily ground the Chinese drones, along with denying the US permission to fly, may have represented “an effort to maintain strategic neutrality” between China and the United States, retired Nepali army major general Binoj Basnyat told The Wall Street Journal.

In any case, US drone companies may face some headwinds in winning over the mountaineering expeditions at Mount Everest. Milan Pandey, cofounder of the Nepali drone company Airlift Technology, told The Wall Street Journal that the Chinese-made DJI drones can carry significantly more than the US-made Freefly drone at higher Mount Everest altitudes—the difference between carrying 100 pounds versus just 11 pounds. The Chinese drones are also cheaper than the US-made Freefly drone.

However, Pandey also expressed interest in having his company test the Freefly drones in support of mountaineering expeditions. That test finally happened on the neighboring mountain of Ama Dablam in June. In a post on July 26, the US embassy in Nepal described the drone flights ferrying oxygen cylinders and other equipment between the mountain’s base camp and another camp, but it did not specify how much weight the drones were able to carry.

Meanwhile, Shenzhen-based DJI dominates the world’s commercial drone sales with between 70 and 80 percent market share—although the Trump administration recently imposed a 100 percent tariff on foreign-made drones. The US Federal Communications Commission is also mulling a “military grade” classification restriction that could even prevent US law enforcement and first responders from using DJI’s drones, despite the majority of state and local law enforcement agencies using DJI drones and describing them as irreplaceable.

This story was updated on September 10, 2026 to add more context on DJI’s dominance in the drone market and US government efforts to restrict the use of foreign-made drones.

Artemis II commander and pilot become NASA’s first astronaut emeriti

Ars Technica September 10, 2026

“Artemis II is done.”

The commander and pilot of NASA’s Artemis II mission have gained a new distinction five months after splashing down from the Moon: They’re not fully retiring from the space agency.

Reid Wiseman and Victor Glover are the first astronauts to join NASA’s emeritus program, enabling them to continue to support the work being done at Johnson Space Center in Houston. They will remain available to train and mentor the current workforce while still being able to pursue employment and opportunities outside of NASA.

“I have asked NASA … to not use the term ‘retire’ as much, but technically emeritus is a retirement program,” Glover told collectSPACE. com on Wednesday. “It’s something we have typically done for scientists when they have groundbreaking research, and they want to go back to academia to teach or to research and publish.”

Glover has accepted a full-time administrative leadership position at his alma mater, California Polytechnic State University (Cal Poly) in San Luis Obispo, helping shape the school’s long-term strategies. Concurrently, he has committed to NASA to be available to convey his knowledge of the Orion spacecraft and its systems, among other expertise, to future Artemis missions.

“You can be paid or you can be a gratis service, which is compensation waived, and that’s what I’m doing,” Glover said. “So I’m not going to be paid for it, but I’ll be able to voluntarily be an advisor or a consultant providing insight into what living in Orion is like.”

Glover will be issued an access badge and plans to be present at the training simulation runs and hopes to be a part of establishing a new initiative, the United States Space Academy, serving NASA and the US Space Force.

“I want to work on that as they start building its foundation because that signals exactly what I care about: building the future of the technical workforce leaders,” he said. “So this is really amazing timing.”

According to NASA, Wiseman also plans to use his emeritus status to continue sharing his spaceflight experience with his now-former colleagues ahead of the Artemis III mission, targeted for no earlier than mid-2027. The Artemis III crew will test Orion’s rendezvous and docking capabilities with commercial human landing systems in low-Earth orbit.

Historically, when astronauts wanted to join private industry, run for public office, or return to military service, they retired from NASA. If they wanted to remain at the space agency but were no longer eligible for a flight assignment, either temporarily or permanently, they were categorized as management astronauts.

There have been other exceptions, though.

Mercury astronaut Scott Carpenter took a leave from NASA to briefly become an aquanaut. From August to September 1965, he lived on the ocean floor in the Navy’s SEALAB II. He then returned to the space agency, though due in part to an arm injury he sustained while away, he worked in management positions until he resigned in 1967.

Edward Gibson, who flew on the third and last Skylab mission in 1974, resigned from NASA after returning to Earth. Three years later, he returned to the astronaut office as chief of the scientist-astronaut candidates. He had hoped to fly another mission, but ultimately retired from the agency again in 1982.

Similarly, Tony England was selected as a scientist-astronaut in 1967, but left five years later due to the lack of available flight assignments. England returned as a mission specialist in 1979 and flew on STS-51F, a 1985 Spacelab mission aboard the space shuttle Challenger. He retired from NASA for the second time in 1988.

Anna Lee Fisher, one of NASA’s first six female astronauts and the first mother to fly in space, took an extended leave from 1989 to 1995 to raise her family. The leave was decided on a year-to-year basis. Like Carpenter, Fisher did not fly into space again after her return, but oversaw the design and development of hardware for the International Space Station and Orion spacecraft before retiring in 2017.

Other astronauts, such as Sally Ride and Neil Armstrong, continued to serve the space agency long after their retirement by volunteering their time on blue-ribbon committees that investigated the loss of two space shuttles and studied the direction of the space program.

What separates what Wiseman and Glover are doing from what other astronauts have done is the formality of the service.

“Being an astronaut is already a lifelong commitment, and when you’re a former [astronaut] you’re always one of us, always a part of this small community of people who have flown off the planet, but this is a new way for us to continue to execute that lifelong commitment,” said Glover.

Glover and Wiseman will need to reapply for emeritus status for every year they want to remain in service.

“For as long as NASA can use my services, I will provide,” Glover said. “I love the leaders, and my colleagues are some amazing people. I will always want to work with them and serve them. So I hope they never make me go fully retired.”

What has come to a close is the Artemis II mission that saw Wiseman, Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen fly by the Moon and travel farther into space than anyone else in history. The last of the mission’s post-flight activities was completed last week.

“The training, pre-flight testing, the 10-day mission, and then the post-flight [public appearances] and debriefs and the medical review and all of that—it’s all wrapped up,” Glover said. “Of course, we’re going to continue to analyze the pictures and the science and make changes to the Artemis III and IV missions based on what we’ve learned, but Artemis II is a wrap. It’s the agency’s to learn and grow from, but Artemis II is done.”

Prior to Wednesday’s emeritus announcement, Hansen announced that he was stepping away from his full-time role at the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) to pursue new professional opportunities. He was also transitioning to serve as a reservist within the Royal Canadian Air Force.

Glover timed his departure with his retirement from the US Navy, a move that Wiseman had made before the Artemis II mission.

That leaves only Koch as an active NASA astronaut. She has not publicly said what her post-Artemis II plans are with regard to staying with the agency.

In addition to Artemis II, Wiseman and Glover lived and worked on the International Space Station, the former by way of a Russian Soyuz spacecraft and the latter as the pilot on SpaceX’s first operational Dragon flight under NASA’s commercial crew program. Wiseman also served as chief of the astronaut office from 2020–2022.

As members of the 20th and 21st classes of astronauts, respectively, Wiseman logged a total of 174 days, 9 hours, and 33 minutes in space, while Glover tallied 176 days, 8 hours, and 1 minute.

Xtracycle’s Swoop ASM e-bike brings an automatic transmission to cargo bikes

Ars Technica Long form August 26, 2026

A steel frame cargo bike with a unique twist: You can let it choose your gear.

The Velotric Discover M e-bike we reviewed earlier this year had a feature I found somewhat annoying: It would sporadically block much of the display with an alert telling me I should be in a different gear. While the implementation bugged me, the concept made a certain degree of sense; most e-bikes now know your cadence, how much torque you’re generating, and how that power is being translated into speed. That’s everything you need to know to determine an optimal gear.

Somewhere in the back of my mind, I thought, “If you’re so smart, why don’t you just shift for me?”

I was completely unaware that Shimano had already developed a system that did exactly that. And for the past few weeks, I’ve been using it on a $4,500 cargo bike from Xtracycle called the Swoop ASM that let me see what it’s like to hand control of my gears to an electronic brain.

The short answer is that the electronics on the Swoop really are smart enough to figure out when it should be shifting. But the system is less adept at the actual shifting process, making for rides that are less smooth than they could be when it’s active. But you can shut that feature off, and the Swoop will shine as a fantastic cargo bike.

Xtracycle got its start providing cargo trailers for mountain bikes and then branched into dedicated cargo bikes. The Swoop ASM is a long-tail cargo bike with what’s called a mullet setup: a larger tire up front and a smaller one in back. The small wheel is designed to help keep the weight held by the large rear rack a bit closer to the road. It also has a front suspension to help cushion the ride.

Notably, the bike is built with steel tubes. Most manufacturers’ lineups use a mix of either carbon fiber and aluminum because those two materials can be made into the exact same shape, simplifying manufacturing. But other materials still have their fans, as they can offer distinct combinations of weight, stiffness, and vibration dissipation.

I haven’t owned a steel tube bike since the 1990s, but the Swoop was a good reminder of why it still has its fans. It’s relatively lightweight (just under 70 lbs/31 kg) for its size, its ride is very comfortable, and it was surprisingly responsive when I stood in the pedals to accelerate away from stops. Despite its highly specialized geometry, the Swoop felt like a fundamentally good bicycle.

There are limits to how well a single frame size can adapt to different body sizes, but Xtracycle does its best to widen the comfort window. It includes a double-telescoping seat post to maximize the seat-pedal distance flexibility. There’s also a quick release on the front handlebar clamp, making it easy to tweak the angle where the grips meet your hands. I found settings that were relatively comfortable but still a bit short of ideal for my 6-plus-foot (188 cm) frame—even with the seat post at its recommended maximum, I could touch the toes of both of my feet down while seated.

Beyond that, plenty of nice touches make this a solid cargo bike. These include protective covers for the rear wheel and chain to keep clothing and limbs from accidentally getting entangled. A robust U-shaped kickstand keeps the bike stable even if you park it when fully loaded, and there’s a front cargo rack that can hold some baggage.

The rear rack can be outfitted with a large range of accessories; mine came with the default setup meant for carrying passengers. This means footrests extending out at the level of the rear hub and two handgrip bars running parallel to the bench seating. But remove a soft cover, and the metal beneath reveals a series of slots that allow a wide variety of attachments to be fitted into place.

You can also use one of Xtracycle’s bag attachments in this setup; I was provided one that ran the full length of the rear attachment and held a fair amount of cargo. Adding a second would have handled all of my typical shopping needs. (While having only one bag might seem awkward, the bike performed very well with everything I was carrying loaded on one side.)

The only problem is that this hardware makes the rear wheel extremely difficult to reach. I struggled to lock the back tire to anything, and I considered myself fortunate to not have to figure out how to deal with a flat.

All those basics make the Swoop a solid entry into the cargo bike market. What sets it apart is its use of a Shimano Cues Di2, one of the component maker’s low-end electronic shifting systems. Its mere existence surprised me, since I thought Shimano was reserving electronic shifting for higher-end component lines. But the company not only took it lower in the range; it added a couple of surprise features to its electronic shifting.

First, the basics: the drivetrain uses a single chainring on the cranks and a 10-speed rear cassette. The rear derailleur requires only a power source and control signals—no cable required. Once properly aligned with the cassette gears, it executes a perfect shift every time it’s told to. This shift includes a brief period when the derailleur over-travels to ensure the chain engages the next ring along, then drops back into the optimal location for continued cycling.

Everything in the system—the derailleur, the controllers, and the motor—takes power from a single removable battery. If the battery’s charge is good, you’re set to ride.

The mid-motor offers three levels of assist, adjusted through a controller on the left side that also includes the power button and a simple display. Shifting is controlled by the one on the right, which lacks a display. Separating the two allows each to be fairly minimalist, making it easy to find the control you need by feel.

On its own, the system worked beautifully. Shifting was fuss-free, and each change was blissfully silent. The assist worked well, and its three levels seemed to cover any needs short of going up steep hills with lots of cargo. This is not a bike that lets you skimp on pedaling in hot conditions; there’s no throttle, and even the highest setting of assist still requires you to exert some force on the pedals. But the motor definitely cuts down on the effort you have to make.

The battery, while looking fairly compact, easily handled dozens of miles without needing a recharge, which means several days of typical errands. While the battery lacks a carrying handle, it’s easy to take it out to charge it, as it pivots sideways out of the frame. When in place, it acts as a protector that keeps anything on the left side of the bike from sliding through the frame and getting tangled in the chain.

This is the first Shimano e-bike system I’ve tested, and it was just as good as you’d expect from a company that has come to dominate cycling drivetrains. Shimano Cues may be its lower-end system, but there’s no apparent skimping on the quality. And that’s before the bonus surprises Shimano has included.

Somewhere in one of the controllers, Shimano’s software gathers all the relevant information about your ride: how fast you’re going, how much force your feet are exerting on the cranks, what gear you’re in, and how fast your legs are churning (and possibly more?). And it uses that data to do a couple of interesting things.

One is what it calls Free Shift. Normally, a bike can’t shift to a different gear unless you’re turning the pedals to move the chain, which can potentially create problems. For example, you could move the derailleur down a gear but not complete the shift before stopping, meaning that the shift would be made when you start pedaling again, and the chain is under a lot of tension as you crank away from a full stop. Or you could move the derailleur several gears over without the chain following.

But the whole point of having a motor is to move the chain. So if you shift without pedaling and the bike isn’t stationary, the Cues system will use the motor to move the chain just enough to complete the shift. It does so without speeding up the bike at all.

Practically, this means that as you coast to a stop, you can simply hit the downshift button a few times, and the system will go into a low gear to make it easy to start up again without requiring you to turn the cranks. It’s … weird. Decades of cycling experience have programmed me to instinctually move my legs when I shift. Those instincts are suddenly superfluous.

It gets even weirder if you enable the automatic transmission. Shimano has included two settings, one for general riding and one for hauling cargo or passengers. When the system recognizes that you can get more out of your pedaling in a different gear, it will simply move you into that gear. That includes doing all the downshifting as you’re coasting to a stop and rolling back up through the gears again as you accelerate away from it.

Let me make that clear: You can coast to a stop without turning the cranks or touching the shifter, and you’ll still be in a different gear when you start up again.

The system is remarkably good at matching when I feel a shift is needed—Shimano’s programmers have done a fine job. Because of that, it’s pretty easy to induce a shift by altering your pedaling, as well. You can tell when it’s close, and just a bit more force will cause the system to send you up a gear. It’s kind of pointless to do so, since the buttons that shift up and down still work when it’s in auto mode, but I found myself doing it regardless.

The downside is that these shifts are not situations where instinctual actions are superfluous. To execute a smooth shift, you have to ease tension off the drivetrain by pedaling with less force, allowing the chain to slide over onto a neighboring gear with a bit less stress. Failing to do so can make for a clunky, inefficient shift and wear down components over time.

My problem with the automatic transmission mode was that I could tell when a shift was likely to come, but I couldn’t predict its precise moment. So it typically came while I was pedaling away happily, with full tension on the chain, making for a loud and awkward shift. This was especially unpleasant when accelerating away from a stop, when the bike would make three or four clunky shifts in rapid succession, each emitting a noise that told me I’d just done something I’d spent years learning to avoid. Living in a neighborhood with lots of four-way stops meant I sometimes experienced that every single block.

Shimano is not stupid, and these systems use parts that are specifically hardened to handle the added strain and wear. But it still felt bad every time I heard and felt that clunk.

The Swoop is not an inexpensive bike; at $4,500, it sits somewhere between the Trek Fetch+ 2 and the Urban Arrow Family I’ve reviewed previously. While it lacks the latter’s capacious cargo tub, the longtail form factor provides a much more bicycle-like riding experience. I’d rate its ride as superior to the Trek because of its frame and front suspension made for a more pleasant ride.

I also prefer Shimano’s drive system to the Bosch used by the other two bikes. It just felt better integrated with my pedaling, plus a bit quieter and less intrusive. The electronic shifting is a bonus—it’s not needed, but it definitely makes for a nice experience, and one where Shimano’s integration means you don’t have to worry about the status of the two additional batteries needed by many electronic systems. I don’t think I’d use the automatic shifting, but I could see where a less experienced cyclist might feel they benefit from it.

So while it’s on the pricier side, the cost seems to be in line with the features it offers. If those features are important to you, the Swoop is definitely worth consideration.

In the end, though, I’m not a huge fan of electronic shifting. I hate worrying about battery levels just to ride my bike, and I like the feel of a well-aligned mechanical shifter clicking into place. But even I have to admit that Shimano’s software does a fantastic job of shifting at the right times, and I think the system could really work well for anybody who hasn’t learned to associate a clunky-sounding shift with bad things.

Google Pixel 11 series review: Is the magic fading?

Ars Technica Long form August 19, 2026

Google’s new Pixels make some compromises but still manage to be good phones.

Google’s approach to making smartphones has changed a lot over the years. It started with Nexus phones aimed at the tinkerer and enthusiast niche back when there were countless companies making smartphones. Today, there are far fewer, and Google’s hyper-polished Pixel lineup is seeing less competition and higher sales. So maybe Google thinks it can just keep doing what works. The new Pixel 11 series is Google’s most refined yet, featuring sleek designs, smart software, and incredible screens. They’re also rather boring.

Google made precious few hardware changes in its 2026 phones, shaving off a fraction of a millimeter here and dropping a gram there. The design language has been the same now for three generations, all while prices continue to inch upward. And this year, Google’s hardware has actually regressed in a few key areas. Despite that, the Pixel 11 phones aren’t bad—they’re some of the best 2026 has to offer. But it feels like Google is forgetting that it’s not just competing against Apple and Samsung. It also has to compete against the Pixels of yesteryear.

Just like last year’s Pixel 10 series, Google’s 2026 lineup includes three flat phones and one foldable. The flat Pixels are the same size, and even side-by-side, it’s hard to tell them apart from their predecessors. We’ve got almost identical aluminum and glass sandwich designs, which do admittedly look very nice. They still have Pixelsnap, too.

The Pixel 11s feel extremely solid, and Google has finally managed to make the buttons less wobbly. The base model Pixel also has a flatter camera bar, which makes it a little more pocket-friendly. The three flat phones are all still eSIM-only in the US—the international versions and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold retain their SIM card slots.

The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL keep the taller camera bar on the back, but it’s nice that the cameras are centered on the back, unlike Samsung phones. You can set a Pixel down on a table, and it’s stable enough to poke at. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold still has that off-center camera module, which makes it less stable.

The back of the phone is also home to the Pixel 11’s new HiLight module. This ring of LEDs is inside the camera flash of the Pro phones to act a bit like an old-fashioned notification LED. However, it’s mostly tied to Gemini to indicate when the AI is listening or responding. It also lights up to tell you when one of your favorite contacts calls. And that’s it.

HiLight only works when the phone is face down—if the accelerometer detects any other orientation, it won’t light up. So it really only makes sense if you’re using “OK Google” hotword detection and leaving your phone face down a lot. Annoyingly, you can’t even have the LEDs light up for text messages from your starred contacts.

It’s really a baffling addition to Google’s phones. It would be questionable even if it had all the functionality of a classic notification LED, but it barely does anything as it currently stands. Honestly, give me the thermometer back. That at least had a theoretical use, even if it didn’t come up very often. HiLight has been so hobbled that it might as well not exist. Google says more features will be added later, but why the slow drip? We had notification LEDs figured out 20 years ago.

The displays on the Pixel 11 OLED screens are all fantastic, and Google says they’re twice as scratch-resistant now. While the base model stayed the same, all the other screens got a little brighter this year. These phones are perfectly legible in bright outdoor light, even the Pixel 11 that remained at 3,000 nits. The other phones have a peak brightness of around 3,600 nits. They are a bit more reflective than Samsung’s latest flagship phones, which have an anti-reflective quality, but the Pixels still look great. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold’s internal screen is a bit too reflective due to its plastic top layer, though. So far, Samsung is the only company that has worked to address that issue in foldables.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold saw the biggest chassis change compared to last year’s model, but even here, the difference is minor. It’s a few tenths of a millimeter thinner, but that’s not enough to notice unless you have both phones to compare. It certainly doesn’t look or feel as supernaturally thin as the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, or even last year’s Z Fold 7. Oddly, the two halves of the phone are also slightly different (the side with the cover display is thicker). You can feel the difference when holding the phone, and while it doesn’t affect usability, it’s a little strange from a tactile perspective. The screen also still has a fairly deep crease compared to the Z Fold 8, which has almost none now.

Google is, however, doing foldable durability right. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is IP68 rated for water and dust protection, and the back panel is a new glass fiber composite that Google claims is “nearly impossible to crack.” Still, the Pixel foldable is much heftier than the latest foldables from Samsung or Motorola.

Google’s new Pixel phones ship with Android 17, not that you would know from listening to Google. It doesn’t talk about Android much anymore, let alone Android version numbers. Regardless, Google has the best version of Android on its phones. While you do get the full suite of Google apps that you may not use, there’s no superfluous filler, sponsored placements, or duplicative apps. If you use Google’s products, the Pixel 11 series is ready to go out of the box.

Google’s apps, widgets, system UI, and home screen have a unified aesthetic that even Apple would envy. However, Google has oversimplified some things in recent updates, like surfacing suggested widgets instead of showing you the full list by default and using a larger, less dense home screen grid. Still, the Pixel build of Android has great vibes.

It also has a ton of AI. There are hints of Gemini in numerous apps, but that’s also true when you access these products in a browser. The on-device AI features can be mostly ignored if you just don’t tap any of the buttons with the AI sparkles on them, but that’s getting harder.

For example, Gboard now has AI-assisted voice transcription built in for Pixel phones. When you tap the mic input button (which now has the telltale AI sparkle), you get a feature called Rambler. Rather than directly transcribing your words with all the mistakes intact, it essentially summarizes what you say to remove “ums” and streamline what you meant to say if you have to correct yourself. This works in the way that AI summarization tends to work, making you sound polished, stilted, and sometimes weirdly positive.

Gemini is also a key part of the experience even more so now that Google has announced Assistant will begin shutting down in the coming weeks. Like Samsung’s latest phones, the Pixel 11 series includes expanded AI automation in more than 40 apps, like Airbnb, Best Buy, DoorDash, eBay, Delta, and more. It’s basically a robot that helps you buy things.

The story here is the same as it was on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. Gemini is capable of navigating these apps with some difficulty. It usually gets where it needs to go, adding items to your cart or pre-booking a reservation. However, it takes much longer than it would if you did it yourself, and its decisions are sometimes suspect. You have to carefully evaluate what Gemini does in these apps, which makes the feature much less useful.

Google continues to offer seven years of OS updates, along with monthly security patches and quarterly Pixel Drop feature updates. This is on par with Samsung and a bit longer than almost everyone else. Google’s updates also arrive in a timely fashion, whereas even Samsung may take several months to roll out new versions of Android.

Google is not interested in talking about smartphone performance in the traditional way. It readily admits the Tensor chips are not optimized for winning benchmarks, but it claims the new Tensor G6 offers 25 percent faster web browsing and up to 20 percent better power efficiency. This seven-core Arm chip sports the same middling GPU as last year’s G5, along with a new MediaTek modem.

As expected, the Pixel 11 series doesn’t show well in benchmarks, trailing the flagship phones from other smartphone makers. But those are all just abstract numbers that might describe how the phone performs in some situations.

In daily use, the Pixel 11 phones feel great. Animations are fluid, touch response is instant, and apps open quickly. Google’s phones can feel faster than even the Galaxy S26, which is sometimes inconsistent despite being the fastest on paper. Google’s chip is also more thermally stable than high-end Qualcomm chips, losing under 25 percent of its performance during extended use.

Gaming is more of a problem for Google, though. The company is still using the same PowerVR GPU in the new Tensor chip, which is markedly slower than what you get in high-end chips from Qualcomm or Apple. Consequently, if you’re playing graphically intensive games like Genshin Impact or the mobile port of Red Dead Redemption, you will get lower frame rates with the Pixel. For the simpler, free-to-play games most people play, the Pixel is plenty powerful.

It is notable that Google has backtracked on RAM in the Pixel 11. Previously, Google cited the need for running bigger on-device AI models as a reason to upgrade base SKU Pixel phones to 16GB of RAM. However, the 2026 Google phones start at 12GB, and you have to upgrade to get 16GB. That means you’re looking at a minimum of $1,219 for the Pixel 11 Pro with 512GB of storage and 16GB of RAM.

Heavier apps and games may close more quickly on the 12GB versions of the Pixel 11, but the difference has been minimal in my testing. However, should you have to make that kind of compromise with a phone that costs $100 more than its predecessor? Probably not. That said, Google’s phones are generally better at keeping apps in memory than, say, Samsung, which only has 12GB of RAM in its $2,100 foldable.

Battery life is also complicated with the Pixel 11 series. All the batteries are slightly smaller across the board this year. The flat phones are less than 100 mAh smaller, but the Pixel 11 Pro Fold dropped more than 200 mAh compared to last year’s foldable. Yet Google is claiming similar battery life this year, somewhere between 24 and 30 hours, depending on the model.

In my time with the Pixel phones, they haven’t seemed to run dry faster. So that’s good… sort of. Ideally, we should be seeing battery life expanding beyond this “about one day” window we’ve been stuck in forever. Very few phones have managed to do that, and Google doesn’t seem interested in making the kind of changes (See: OnePlus’ last hurrah) that would support substantially longer battery life.

There is some good news in the battery department. The Pixel 11 Pro XL has finally gotten a charging boost, now topping out at 45 W instead of 30 W. The base model, 11 Pro, and Fold are still at the lower wattage, but now all of them at least have 25 W wireless charging with a compatible Qi 2.2 pad.

Google’s camera hardware has gotten a few minor tweaks this year. The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL have all the same setup—a 50 MP primary, 48 MP 5x telephoto, and a 48 MP ultrawide. However, the main and telephoto sensors are new components that promise better optical quality. The Pixel 11 and 11 Pro Fold have a new 48MP primary sensor. The foldable has the same 10.8 MP 5x telephoto and 13 MP ultrawide from last year, and the flat phone has a new 13 MP ultrawide and the same 10.8 MP telephoto as the Fold.

Most of the changes are in the software controlling those cameras. In general, these changes are clever and could be nice to have for certain situations, but they’re not game changers.

There’s a new feature called Magic Capture that lets you outsource the shutter button to the on-device AI. Once you activate this mode, the phone starts recording a video. When it determines the moment is right, it can snap full-quality still photos as well. This works well in theory, but it’s not infallible. Generally, if the scene isn’t too busy and your subject is around the middle of the frame, the AI will reliably snap a photo. This works a lot of the time—I’ve gotten some genuinely cool shots with Magic Capture, but it also sometimes misses the moment. If a photo is important, I’m going to do the legwork of tapping the shutter myself.

11 Pro and 11 Pro XL photos:

Google also says the Pro phones have a new Instant Night Sight feature, but calling it “instant” may be overselling it a little. You’ll still get a timer telling you to hold the phone still, but the captures are noticeably faster. That could be the difference between a blurry photo and something usable. So while it’s not as fast as a regular photo (and certainly not instant), it’s still a nice upgrade.

However you’re taking photos with the Pixels, the results will be impressively sharp. With quick captures and powerful processing, even moving subjects are clear. Even the most expensive phones from Samsung and Apple struggle here. Google’s dynamic range is also better than you’ll see on other devices, resolving details in light and shadow very well.

Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro Fold photos:

However, Pixel photos have a specific look, and it might not be ideal for every situation. With the Pixel 11, Google has debuted Camera Looks to address the situation, but it’s a little confusing. There are new default styles, like natural and shadows, that are retained each time you open the camera. Then there are the more dramatic filter-like looks you access by swiping in the viewfinder. This includes options like velvet, digi, and editorial. You can imagine this like something akin to film simulations on Fujifilm cameras. You can also edit any of the looks to your liking, changing sliders for highlights, tint, grain, and more.

Camera Looks:

While they’re a bit clunky to access, Camera Looks give you a ton of new shooting options on Pixel phones. They’re perfect if you’ve gotten tired of the super-sharp processed look of smartphone photos.

The Pixel 11 phones are good devices. The regression on RAM is a bummer, but the 12GB phones still feel very fast and keep apps in memory well enough for all but the most picky buyers. Likewise, the slightly smaller batteries are less than ideal, but the battery life doesn’t seem to have taken a dive.

Additions like Camera Looks and stronger displays are nice, but they’re probably not worth an upgrade for current Pixel users. And HiLight doesn’t even figure in. If you have a Pixel 10, Pixel 9, or even something older, you don’t need to run out and buy a Pixel 11. These phones are still more than serviceable, and they have years of support left. With such minor updates in 2026, Google is essentially competing against its older phones.

If you’re due for an upgrade, either because your current phone is in bad shape or you’re thinking about switching to Pixel, you’ll probably like what the Pixel 11 has to offer. However, you’d probably like the Pixel 10 just as much. You’ll probably be able to find last year’s model at a discount, and it still has six years of software support left. Again, Google is a victim of its own success here.

And what about Google’s foldable? That’s a tougher sell. Even in the US, Google has stiff competition. Both Samsung and Motorola offer foldables that are thinner, faster, and have longer battery life. These phones all cost about the same and get similar levels of support, but Google’s software is a bit better overall. Still, I’d probably choose a Galaxy Z Fold 8 with its more compact frame over the Pixel 11 Pro Fold right now, even if it’s a little more expensive.

Terabytes of credentials leaked in massive supply-chain attack

Ars Technica Long form August 12, 2026

The data was scraped and exfiltrated from 2,500 users of a compromised AI package.

Terabytes worth of credentials, many belonging to the world’s biggest and most sensitive organizations, have been exposed in a supply-chain attack on LiteLLM, an open source tool that streamlines AI-driven software development. Microsoft, Amazon, Cisco, Samsung, and Salesforce are only a handful of the entities whose access secrets were exposed.

The revelation was posted on Tuesday and Wednesday by security firms CloudSEK and Hudson Rock. CloudSEK said it found cloud keys, repository tokens, SSH keys, Kubernetes secrets, package publishing credentials, environment variables, and AI provider keys that could allow attackers to gain access to more than 2,500 organizations.

The credentials were extracted during a 40-minute window in March while the victims used compromised versions of LiteLLM downloaded from the package’s official location in the Python Package Index repository. Hudson Rock said it made the discovery after analyzing a 195TB file that it obtained. Neither firm identified the source of the information.

The LiteLLM compromise was the result of a previous supply-chain attack that infected the widely used vulnerability scanner Trivy. Other software infected in the campaign includes KICS and the Telnyx Python SDK. TeamPCP, a ramshackle but extremely capable gang largely made up of teenagers, took credit for the attack, and researchers have largely corroborated the claim.

“I’ve confirmed the data is legit, by the way, multiple victim orgs,” independent security researcher Kevin Beaumont said. “It contains a significant volume of sensitive content at orgs. It’s a massive supply chain breach due to poor AI security—not because AI is the threat, but teens can run circles around orgs obsessed with rushing out AI and poor DevOps security.”

The compromised versions of all four software packages contained code that accessed the memory of infected machines, scraped its contents, and exfiltrated it through an attacker-controlled channel. The data is filled with an assortment of information. Interspersed in the wall of data are credentials to software pipelines maintained by the tens of thousands of organizations that ran LiteLLM during the 40-minute span that the supply-chain attack remained active.

In all, both security firms said some 434,000 CI/CD (continuous integration/continuous delivery) software pipelines had credentials exposed after running the compromised LiteLLM versions. In many cases, researchers at CloudSEK and Hudson Rock had trouble identifying the organizations the credentials belonged to. For instance, an email address in the dump from the domain @siriusxm. com ultimately didn’t indicate a breach at the satellite broadcaster, but rather one within the infrastructure of SiriusXM subsidiary AdsWizz.

A full list of organizations is here. The researchers had high confidence that these organizations had their credentials exposed:

“Many CI/CD pipelines are configured generically,” Hudson Rock said. “The dumped variables contain active database passwords, third-party API keys, and cloud credentials without any identifiable company email, custom domain string, or internal server name. This means countless organizations currently have active secrets sitting in this database, completely unaware of their exposure.”

Both firms are urging all organizations that used the compromised versions of LiteLLM—particularly those listed in the high-confidence section of the list—to thoroughly rotate all credentials in their pipelines. Hudson Rock instructed any organization that uses any AI proxy infrastructure, third-party CI/CD vulnerability scanners, or downstream AI packages to immediately audit their environment for versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 of LiteLLM, the two compromised versions of the software.

The firm advised all those affected to perform “aggressive credential revocation,” assume any secret accessible to the LiteLLM environment is compromised, invalidate and rotate all cloud keys, Kubernetes service account tokens, and GitLab/GitHub PATs, and audit logging and egress filtering.

As a cautionary tale, CloudSEK said that Trivy developers rotated but failed to fully revoke an automation token over a 20-day window. The lapse gave the attackers a nearly three-week period to force-push malicious code to third-party builds that used the vulnerability scanner. As Beaumont observed, organizations’ rush to integrate AI into their software delivery systems has also greatly contributed to the scale of the damage.

Update: There are already signs that some of the affected organizations aren’t taking the disclosure with the seriousness warranted. After this post went live, Beaumont reported:

These creds date from about March. One of the orgs impacted told me they’d rotated them all and it’s a nothingburger, so I looked at their responsible disclosure policy, it allows trying creds, so I tried them all. Almost every one worked. Submitted report. One of the biggest US techcos.

Ultimately, the new revelations concerning the LiteLLM supply-chain attack underscore the growing threat of such campaigns and hence the importance of maintaining vigilance around the use of open source software that, when infected, can spread rapidly across the Internet.

“The key takeaway is how supply chains have evolved to make a single upstream breach affect thousands of companies simultaneously,” Alon Gal, co-founder and chief technology officer of Hudson Rock, wrote in an email. “A window of roughly 40 minutes in which the LiteLLM dependency was hacked led to over 430,000 instances in which millions of secrets were harvested. This magnitude pushes us into a completely new world regarding the type of response required from the cybersecurity industry.”
