Christchurch back to host Super Round in 2027

New Zealand Herald September 10, 2026

Super Round will return to Christchurch in 2027. Photo / Alyse Wright

Super Rugby Pacific’s Super Round will return to Christchurch in 2027 after the city successfully hosted the event this year.

Five games will be played at One New Zealand Stadium across three days for round eight, starting with the Crusaders facing the Brumbies on April 2.

On Saturday, the Chiefs will meet the Western Force followed by the Blues clashing with the Waratahs, while on Sunday, the Highlanders play Fijian Drua before the defending champion Hurricanes take on the Queensland Reds.

The round will again likely have big economic benefits for the Garden City.

Earlier this year, the three-day celebration over Anzac weekend served as a grand opening of sorts for Te Kaha.

More than 73,000 spectators attended.

Of the domestic attendees, 16,570 were from outside of Christchurch and almost 4000 from countries including the United States, United Kingdom and Australia.

A Fresh Info report says spending was more than double predictions – topping $13.1 million.

The event can’t be held over Anzac weekend this year, as the All Blacks face the Wallabies in a Bledisloe Cup fixture on April 25.

Melbourne initially hosted Super Round from 2022-2024, but struggled to draw crowds.

The 2027 season will begin on February 12, with the competition’s 10 teams going head-to-head across an extended 17-week regular season.

The extra week and a reduction from two byes to one will see each team play 16 regular season matches – two more than 2026.

With no Moana Pasifika, the finals format has changed. The top six will still play finals, but the first and second teams will have the week off and advance straight to the semi-finals.

Friday, April 2: Crusaders v ACT Brumbies – 7.35pm

Saturday, April 3: Chiefs v Western Force – 5.05pm

Saturday, April 3: Blues v NSW Waratahs – 7.35pm

Sunday, April 4: Highlanders v Fijian Drua – 2pm

Sunday, April 4: Hurricanes v Queensland Reds – 4.30pm

Ben Francis is an Auckland-based reporter for the New Zealand Herald who covers breaking sports news.

IPCA finds no evidence for sexual assault, stalking claims against Richard Chambers

New Zealand Herald September 10, 2026

Police Commissioner Richard Chambers. The IPCA has found no evidence to substantiate claims against him.

The Independent Police Conduct Authority’s investigation into allegations of sexual assault and stalking against Police Commissioner Richard Chambers has found no evidence to substantiate either of the claims.

The IPCA was referred a complaint from a former partner of Chambers in December last year.

The woman and Chambers had been in a “long term romantic relationship” in the 1990s according to findings released by the IPCA.

The IPCA referred the claims of sexual assault to the police’s National Integrity Unit (NIU), and detectives flew to Australia to interview the complainant.

The IPCA said it had “direct access” to the police investigation and also watched police interview Chambers about the claims.

“The Authority monitored Police’s interview of the Commissioner and independently interviewed him without police present. The Commissioner cooperated fully throughout,” the IPCA’s findings said.

The IPCA said the investigation by police was “robust”, and following standard adult sexual assault investigation protocols.

“When the complainant agreed to be interviewed by Police, she formalised a criminal complaint. After the first Police interview, the complainant made further allegations of historic sexual assaults and she was re-interviewed.”

The IPCA said it agreed with the conclusion of the police investigation.

“We agree with the conclusion reached in the [police investigation] report that the evidential test for prosecution is not met.”

The second component of the woman’s complaint claimed Chambers had stalked her and engaged in digital surveillance.

As part of investigating these claims, the IPCA said its staff examined exhibits the complainant alleged verified her concerns.

“We found no evidence to support any of her concerns about stalking and digital surveillance and found evidence that contradicted many of her claims. Whilst we accept that she genuinely believed what she told us, we conclude that there was no evidential foundation for any of these allegations,” the IPCA’s findings said.

Chambers has been approached for comment.

The IPCA has previously said it’s also investigating another separate complaint made by a different complainant.

The Prime Minister says the new rail extension is set to shape Auckland’s economic growth for years to come while Wayne Brown is having “mixed feelings” at today’s official ribbon-cutting ceremony for the City Rail Link.

Timetables have been revealed, there’s been test after test through the tunnels, the finishing touches have been put on shiny new stations – ahead of Sunday’s opening.

The Transport Minister is brimming with excitement this morning as he describes a feeling of “hubbub and hullabaloo” around the country’s first underground train metro.

The public will be able to jump on board the City Rail Link from early Sunday morning, with the first train departing Otahuhu just before 6am.

At today’s opening ceremony, Luxon thanked all those involved.

“Great infrastructure projects begin before the shovel is in the ground. They require leaders who need to think beyond political cycles.

“It’s so much more than a transport project, it’s about shaping economic growth for years to come.”

Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown said that while he had a sense of pride to lead a “modern city”, he acknowledged the toll it had taken on local businesses and ratepayers.

“[I have] very mixed feelings about today.

“Firstly, relief. I’m relieved to see it’s open at long last and I’ve lived long enough to see it.

“I have some sympathy for businesses disrupted at street level and I look forward to you seeing increased business.”

He then went on to give credit to Auckland’s former mayor, which was met with a round of applause from the crowd.

“I have admiration for the tenacity of Len Brown to get it past the government. Who then took it off him and signed contracts I never would’ve signed,” he said.

Auckland Transport chief executive Stacey Van Der Putten said it was a very important day but acknowledged it had been a “sad week”, referencing the death of a MAGS student near the Baldwin Ave station.

“It ripples through the community, the rail impact and the school and has a lasting impact on how we feel.”

Speaking live on Ryan Bridge TODAY from Auckland’s new Te Waihorotiu Station, based by SkyCity, Transport Minister Chris Bishop said it was a momentous occasion.

“It’s fair to say there’s a bit of hubbub, a bit of excitement building in the city for the official ribbon cutting and hullabaloo at 9.

“People watching will probably say ‘oh that looks like something in London, Sydney, Paris’ or whatever and it’s Auckland, look how good it looks.”

Bishop said despite some anxiety expected for D-Day, Sunday, they were ready.

“Any new timetable, any new change to the network, you’re a bit anxious about it, but we’re good to go.

“There’s been an enormous amount of work done over the last few years to get ready for this day.

“Will there be teething problems? Probably … human nature being what it is we should calibrate our expectations.”

Coalition colleague and NZ First leader Winston Peters was a little more restrained, telling Bridge while he planned to go to the station, “you can’t be excited”.

“This has been massively delayed, it’s massively overpriced but thank God the light at the [end of] the very long tunnel is coming to open today.”

KiwiRail CEO Peter Reidy told the Herald earlier this week he is confident that the system is ready to go.

Train enthusiasts have snapped up tickets to be on that train, alongside politicians and other officials.

About 450 people are expected at today’s ribbon-cutting and opening ceremony.

Commuters will face new timetables and some route changes on the three main services: the East West, South City and Onehunga West lines.

The first weekday timetable will operate on the new CRL-enabled rail network with trains scheduled to run from just after 5am.

The East West Line will connect Swanson with Manukau, effectively joining today’s Western and Eastern lines and running through the new city-centre tunnel.

The South City Line will replace the Southern Line, running from Pukekohe through Newmarket and the city centre.

The Onehunga West Line will run between Onehunga and Henderson off-peak, but terminate at Maungawhau during peak hours.

Members of the public have flocked to open days held at Karang-a-hape, Maungawhau and Te Waihoritiu stations in the lead-up to the official opening.

Katie Bradford is a Senior Correspondent at the Herald. She has been a broadcast journalist for over 20 years and was based in the press gallery for 10 years. She specialises in politics, business and Auckland issues.

AI start-up Partly is taking on the world from Christchurch

New Zealand Herald September 10, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

“I grew up on a farm. The ethos was: If something breaks, you fix it; the number 8 wire mentality,” says the Canterbury-raised Levi Fawcett.

He fixed cars. He fixed farming equipment. At 13, he converted an old shipping container into a sleep-out.

Today, Fawcett (now 31) is still in the fixing-things business, but now his efforts centre on artificial intelligence.

And it’s going pretty well.

His start-up, Partly, has just raised US$50 million in venture capital at a US$500m ($858m) valuation - making it easily the most valuable AI start-up founded within New Zealand.

Partly’s app lets a mechanic at a repair shop take a picture of a damaged vehicle with their smartphone.

The start-up’s AI, “Interpreter”, can then help them assess the level of damage - and whether it’s worth repairing - and identify damaged parts and help source replacements.

To a layperson, taking a photo of a car part then having an AI identify it might not sound that hard.

But Fawcett says with hundreds of makes and models of cars, each with thousands of parts, things quickly get complicated. All told, there are around four billion combinations of parts that can be ordered across different makes and models of cars - and a mix of phone calls, faxes and spreadsheets have been used to try and keep track of them and source the best options. There were some databases, but they didn’t talk to each other or could glitch over different terms, from the well-known - Americans saying “hood” for what we call a bonnet - to countless lower-level erratic naming conventions.

On some levels, things have only been getting worse.

“Over the years, vehicles have become more and more complex, making them harder and harder to repair,” Fawcett says.

Zooming out to the past century, cars have become about 100 times cheaper to make - ignoring the cost of the raw materials - but around four times more expensive to repair, he says.

Fawcett recruited a team of data scientists to automate the process of matching parts.

His team has spent most of five years training Interpreter to recognise parts and recommend the best options - for customers who range from parts makers to wholesalers and distributors to collision repair shops.

It what can be a low-margin industry, Fawcett pitches Partly’s AI as a way to increase profit by making faster, smarter choices about replacement tasks, and by freeing staff from repetitive, time-consuming tasks.

“Contracted revenue has just topped US$50m,” Fawcett told the Herald.

“We’ve got just over 1000 customers now. The UK is our largest market, with around 400. New Zealand is second, on around 300. The US is third.”

The founder says Partly won’t be consistently profitable for another two years or so, “but we’ve already had profitable months.” But for now, like many start-ups, it’s prioritising growth over getting black most of the time.

The Series B raise was denoted in US currency because it was led by DST Global, a venture capital firm founded by Israeli tech billionaire Yuri Milner, which has offices in Silicon Valley, New York, London and Hong Kong.

It followed a $37m round at a $180m valuation [both NZD] that was billed as the largest Series A raise in New Zealand history.

In 2021, Partly just raised $3.7m at a $49.8m valuation in a seed round led by Australian VC firm Blackbird, with Beck also chipping in.

The US$50m in new capital is earmarked for more Interpreter training, and expansion in the US. A Partly office was opened in Texas in June. Fawcett is now dividing his time between Christchurch and Austin.

“We expect that in the next nine to 12 months, the US will become our biggest market,” Fawcett says.

It will also be used to get more bodies on board. Partly currently has around 170 staff (with around 100 in Christchurch; others are in Auckland or offshore satellites). Fawcett will be hiring at least 60 more over the next few months. Many will be in Christchurch, which Fawcett sees remaining his firm’s research and development hub long term.

“Most of our staff are from outside Christchurch. About a third of our core Christchurch team have been brought in from the US,” Fawcett says.

“About 30% have come from Europe and about 10% from Europe.

“It’s not what we planned. We hire locally when we can. We still do, probably once a month. It’s just that Christchurch has quite a small talent pool and we set a very high bar.”

MORE ON CHRISTCHURCH

How does Fawcett sell Christchurch to AI experts in New York, or just north of the Bombay Hills?

“It’s a good family city,” Fawcett says. “It’s safe. The cost of housing is lower and there are quick commutes.” It doesn’t hurt that some of New Zealand’s most scenic spots and best skiing is close by.

“There are a whole group of Americans and Europeans who are keen to get out of the country they live in, for whatever reason, and live in New Zealand - and we’ve been somewhat successful in attracting them,” Fawcett says.

Creating a simple app for mechanics has necessitated hugely complicated algorithms under the bonnet.

It’s fitting to call it rocket science.

Between graduating with an honours degree in engineering from Canterbury University and founding Partly in 2020, Fawcett spent four and a half years at Rocket Lab as a navigation and control engineer.

While working at Sir Peter Beck’s firm, Fawcett had a side-hustle: an online marketplace called AllGoods, which was where he first noticed the problems people had sourcing car parts.

Beck told a group of University of Auckland students last month that he never frowns on staff who have the initiative to found their own start-up. Rather, he’s supported the likes of Craig Piggot (Halter), Jamie France (Outlier Space) and Stefan Powell (Dawn Aerospace).

In 2020, Beck backed a $1.7m “pre-seed” round that helped Fawcett get Partly up and running and agreed to act as an adviser.

The Rocket Lab founder was also good for some press. “They are certainly one of the most exciting start-ups in New Zealand,” Beck told the Herald as the firm banked its seed money.

Having an e-commerce market as a side hustle didn’t mean Fawcett was slacking at his day job.

“I loved Rocket Lab. It was a punishing environment for some people, in that we could work seven days a week. I remember a back-to-back stretch of 60-something days non-stop, but it was super-fun.

“We were trying to be only the second private company to put a rocket into space. SpaceX did it with 2000 people. We were trying to do it with - at the time - 200.”

He slept in Rocket Lab’s Mt Wellington car park to save time.

“I would wake up in the morning at 7 o’clock and read Nasa papers and do research. From midday through to 1am, I’d be building. Then I’d go back to my car for six hours, then wake and do it all over again. I’d eat and shower at work.”

What sort of boss is he at Partly?

“People are not working 60 days straight, but people are still working way harder than average,” Fawcett says.

“An 80-hour week is fairly normal, 100 hours is a big week. 120 hours is a massive week. That’s not performative. That’s just the end result of people caring a lot, being very mission-oriented, and working super hard to solve global problems. Our overall goal is: Anyone can fix anything. That’s the final end state, so it’s ridiculously ambitious.

“We let every new joiner know. They opt in.”

Fawcett adds, “I’m very demanding. I set a high bar, but I give people a huge amount of autonomy to achieve it. There’s a huge amount of freedom, and trust. If someone wants to leave to pick up their kid at 3pm, nobody cares. But they’ll probably be back online at 7pm.”

“We were training AI models in 2021, before it was cool,” Fawcett says.

His firm’s Interpreter is still the only full-blooded product in its niche, “But now there’s a handful of start-ups that are trying to replicate what we’re doing,” Fawcett says.

AI technology can give them a jumpstart - “or at least the impression they can jump-start” - and the venture capital boom around AI means they can now raise more money, sooner, to accelerate their efforts.

And what’s to stop a mechanic just point their smartphone cam at a part and asking ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini to identify it, and help manage a repair?

The Herald obviously isn’t the first to ask this question.

Partly has published benchmarks that find its Interpreter up to 20 times more accurate than the “general purpose” models made by OpenAI, Anthropic and ChatGPT.

“We’ve got 110 people right now collecting all this information, training our model to be just really good at that one thing.”

Venture capital firms seem convinced. Ahead of the June Series B raise, Fawcett spent a week in San Francisco talking to a slate of top-tier VC outfits.

“Then DST said, ‘We’d like to lead.’ We flew over to Yuri [DST’s London-based founder]. We chatted for half a day, then there was a signed term sheet and, six days later, we had the money in the bank.”

Chris Keall is an Auckland-based member of the Herald’s business team. He joined the Herald in 2018 and is the technology editor and a senior business writer.

Passengers were evacuated from Auckland Airport's domestic terminal after sprinkler sensors were activated this morning.

Passengers at Auckland’s domestic terminal have been evacuated this morning after a burning smell was detected.

“Passengers should contact their airline for further details of flight impacts.

“We thank travellers for their patience and co-operation,” the spokesperson said.

On The Up: Napier boy with cerebral palsy takes on 5000-stair challenge for disabled athletes

New Zealand Herald September 10, 2026

Rocco Green, 9, takes on a 5000-stair challenge, two years after taking his first independent steps. Photo / Rafaella Melo

Step by step, 9-year-old Rocco Green is climbing towards a 5000-stair goal, just over two years after taking his first independent steps.

The Napier boy, who was born prematurely at 32 weeks and diagnosed with cerebral palsy at 16 months, is tackling thousands of stairs to raise money for Disability Sport and Recreation Hawke’s Bay, already surpassing his $2000 fundraising target.

Rocco had completed 3749 stairs when Hawke’s Bay Today caught up with him last Friday, adding another 64 during the visit.

He hopes to complete the challenge over five weeks, finishing on Saturday at McLean Park.

The fundraising idea came from Rocco, while his physiotherapist Karen Busch helped turn it into the 5000-stair challenge.

“I said, ‘yeah, let’s do it’,” Rocco said.

“I just thought it would be a good cause to raise money.”

Rocco underwent selective dorsal rhizotomy surgery in the United States in May 2024 before taking his first independent steps without a walking frame.

His mum Ashlee Green said climbing stairs remained significantly more difficult for him than for most children.

“He can walk unassisted for short distances, but going upstairs is quite a challenge for him,” she said.

“They thought 5000 was quite a big goal, but still achievable for him, and something that he had never done before.”

Rocco has been clocking up stairs across Hawke’s Bay and further afield, including at Pettigrew Green Arena, in Ahuriri and during a recent trip to Rotorua.

Some sessions have involved hundreds of stairs. His biggest effort so far was about 1100 in one go.

Asked how his legs felt afterwards, Rocco laughed.

“Broken. It felt like jelly,” he said.

Before his surgery, Rocco progressed from a wheelchair to crutches and then walking aids.

Today, he can ride an adapted bike, play football and basketball, take part in a non-contact rugby programme, and participate in school activities with more independence.

Ashlee said his daily routine still involved stretching morning and night and physiotherapy twice a week to maintain his mobility.

Rocco chose Disability Sport and Recreation Hawke’s Bay as he participates in its programmes, including basketball and skateboarding, and hopes to attend the Halberg Games in Auckland next year.

Disability Sport and Recreation Hawke’s Bay community sport co-ordinator Brandon Clark said donations raised by Rocco would assist with costs for Hawke’s Bay athletes attending the 2027 Halberg Games and future Disability Sport & Recreation Hawke’s Bay events and programmes.

“With his hard work, we hope to create more active opportunities for athletes with disabilities in Hawke’s Bay,” Clark said.

“His determination for self-improvement is a great motivation for others in our disability community to try to improve ourselves a little more.”

Clark said this was Rocco’s biggest challenge to date, but he believed it wouldn’t be his last.

“Rocco is also growing up and finding his voice supporting this community and those around him,” he said.

“We look forward to seeing what he is going to do next.”

A Rotorua retail shop owner says she thought she was having a heart attack after three women stood outside her store warning people she was “evil” and would “do witchcraft on them”.

Doris Elliot, owner of Rotorua CBD shop Muma Dee’z Creations, told the Rotorua Daily Post she called the police about midday yesterday when three women who she understood were religious were in front of her shop “preaching”.

She said they stood outside her Tutanekai St shop and pointed towards it, telling people she and the shop were “evil”.

Elliot said they were trying to intimidate people walking past, telling them not to go in because “I’ll do witchcraft on them”.

She and security asked them to leave but they wouldn’t, she said.

Elliot then called the police and “finally they’ve gone”. An ambulance was also called.

“Today, I thought I was having a heart attack because I had sharp pains in my chest. I couldn’t breathe properly. It was a little bit of a panic attack.”

She said the women took issue with the store’s products, including crystals, tarot cards, sage and “witch’s brooms, which are decor”.

“But I’m not the only one in Rotorua that sells it.”

Elliot claimed the three women did the same thing two weeks ago. She called the police who “moved them on”.

Before that, Elliot said the three women had gone into the shop three times and had “a nice talk with me”.

“They asked like, ‘Could they bless me, could they pray for me’ ... so they held my hand and they prayed and what not. Very nice, and then this happens.”

Elliot said the incidents had made her feel angry, anxious and “really upset”.

“Go preach, I don’t care. That’s your belief but go in the middle of the square or something, you don’t have to do it in front of my shop ...

“You can’t run a business like that, you just can’t do it.

“I hope they don’t come back. I don’t want to go through this all the time.”

Elliot said this was her fourth year owning Muma Dee’z Creations, a “spiritual, holistic store” which sold healing products.

“We don’t practise witchcraft, we never have practised witchcraft ...

“We’re not an evil store - we’re here to help. We’re here for the people.”

A police spokesman said police received a report about three people causing “public disturbance” on Tutanekai St.

“Police attended and spoke with those involved. There were no arrests nor charges.”

Megan Wilson is a health and general news reporter for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post. She has been a journalist since 2021.

Prestigious Hawke’s Bay winery Sileni will close at the end of this year after almost three decades.

Sileni was established in 1997 by Sir Graeme Avery.

The winery has been based in a stunning building and property near Hastings since 1999, in the wine district known as the Bridge Pā Triangle.

The cellar door has been shut since last July, raising questions about the winery’s future.

Booster Wine Group (BWG) is the current owner of Sileni and has now announced plans to close the winery at the end of this year, and cease winemaking at that location.

The Sileni brand will continue, with winemaking shifting to other BWG-owned wineries in the South Island.

“Post the closure of our Hawke’s Bay winery, Sileni wines will be produced at our Awatere River Winery in Marlborough and Gravity Winery in Tasman,” BWG chief executive Craig Langley said.

Following a review of its operations, Langley said the “difficult decision” was made to exit its Hawke’s Bay operations .

“As part of the restructuring process, a number of roles across winemaking and viticulture have been affected.”

Langley did not confirm how many Hawke’s Bay jobs were going.

He said the decision was based on several factors.

“The global wine sector is facing multiple challenges including an oversupply of grapes and wine, alongside reduced consumer demand for wine.

“New Zealand’s wine producers are not immune to these challenges, and we are starting to see wineries respond by scaling back production and removing vines.

“BWG will continue to operate the Sileni winery until the end of 2026.

“The decision reflects the need to consolidate operations, improve efficiency, and ensure the long-term sustainability of the company.”

Sileni is a prominent brand across New Zealand and is also exported to 36 countries.

Langley said Sileni remained “one of our most recognised and established brands” and “a cornerstone of our portfolio”.

“With significant brand equity built over many years, a long-standing reputation for quality, and a loyal customer base in New Zealand and 36 international markets, Sileni will continue to be central to our growth ambitions and long-term strategy.”

The Avery family, which sold Sileni to Booster in 2018, declined to comment on the winery closure.

BWG leased the property and associated Hawke’s Bay vineyards from Private Land and Property Fund (PLP), managed by Booster Investment.

PLP said, in a statement, it was considering the future of the winery property.

“PLP is currently evaluating a range of options, including running the vineyards, partial or full sale, or redevelopment. No final decision has been made as yet.”

Sex, drugs and a legend redefined: it’s time to meet the real Marianne Faithfull

Sydney Morning Herald September 11, 2026

Broken English strips away the scandal to reveal the complex, defiant spirit of the late singer-songwriter.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

When Marianne Faithfull died last year, directors Iain Forsyth and Jane Pollard had been working on a film about her for four years.

Watching Broken English, named for the hit album she made in 1979, you can see what a compelling subject she was. A ’60s survivor, still probably best known to an older generation as Mick Jagger’s ex-girlfriend and the subject of scandal, she emerges as a formidable woman who was also a singer, writer and actor, the kind of liminal artist who popped up in collaborations with professional fans from Metallica to Nick Cave.

In her ’70s, she is in a wheelchair, hooked up to an oxygen tank: the result of long COVID. Whatever, she still commands the room.

Broken English isn’t so much an account of her life as a response to it, pitched somewhere between documentary, essay and fiction. Archive footage is sprinkled between interviews with Faithfull herself. These are set within an imaginary “Ministry of Not Forgetting”, the questions asked by “an archivist” played by 1917 star George MacKay. Derek Jacobi narrates the film and Tilda Swinton plays the head of the ministry, who at one point lists Faithfull’s many achievements before concluding: “And yet, to the world at large, she’s still just Mick Jagger’s girlfriend. Well, f--- that.”

In his role as archivist, MacKay wears an earpiece to hear the directors urging him to push a point or drop it, depending on Faithfull’s answers. Clearly, they never aimed to cover Faithfull’s entire life. The juiciest scandal from her Stones era is left out. Her youthful heroin addiction is in there, but the gruesome details of her life on the street that she described in her autobiography aren’t. And while her first husband, John Dunbar, appears with her, Jagger does not.

“I didn’t know how to make him a part of it,” Pollard says with a short laugh. “I really enjoyed reframing it, looking at that period of her life from the perspective of her childhood, growing up in a commune.”

With the Stones, she says, “they all felt they were all working towards something that felt really important”. But, as Faithfull reflects herself, that wasn’t how she was seen. She was cast as a rock’n’roll casualty. She was the woman arrested in a drug raid wearing only a fur coat. For the tabloids, she was a terrific story.

The filmmakers set out to tell a different story. Their approach to the years Faithfull spent with Jagger, for example, was to shift their gaze away from the usual catalogue of disasters. We learn how Faithfull took Jagger to see the Royal Ballet with Rudolf Nureyev, knowing he would love it; we see that she joined in a poetry event with the Beat poets and became a lifelong friend of Allen Ginsberg.

“All these cultural things that she was absorbed in and that she was sharing with Mick, things that felt a lot more relevant and interesting than just who at the end of the day she was going to bed with,” Forsyth says. “I hope that as much as the film is a story about a life, it’s just as much a film about how we choose to tell that story.”

Forsyth and Pollard are best known to Australian audiences for their inventive 2014 film about Nick Cave, 20,000 Days On Earth. They first became interested in Faithfull because Cave and his musical partner Warren Ellis knew her well; Ellis worked with her as a producer and toured with her, playing in her band.

“In the year before the lockdown, we would chat to Warren a lot,” says Pollard. “He was working on the poetry album She Walks in Beauty with her when she got COVID and went into a coma. He was just heartbroken, in the studio working on the poems, not knowing if she would ever hear them. I think at that point, our hearts found her in a different way. We began to care about her a lot, just vicariously, through him.”

The interviews with MacKay at the Ministry of Not Forgetting were among the first things they did, afraid that Faithfull’s precarious health would collapse again. After that, they worked on the film’s mosaic structure of memories and other interviews, showing her assembled segments as they went along. From the start, they expected that by the time they finished the work, she would no longer be with them, but they never intended it as an obituary.

“The film needed, in some way, to acknowledge her passing, but not to change,” says Forsyth. “We were so determined it wasn’t going to be like a standard text with dates. That felt so at odds with it; it’s so alive with her humour and artistry and brilliance – with her defiance, actually.”

George MacKay is 34. He had worked several times with Pollard and Forsyth on art projects, but he knew almost nothing about Marianne Faithfull. “I knew one or two of her songs without knowing they were hers,” he says.

He threw himself into research. When he saw how she was pilloried and derided in the press during her Stones period, he was aghast. “It was awful, just on a human level, what was said about her,” he says. “The misogyny she came up against was so intense.”

Although he worked from a script, he says the interviews felt like improvisations. “Because Marianne had never seen those scripts – and you have to follow wherever the interview goes.”

The Ministry of Not Forgetting sounds as if it could have come from a Harry Potter novel, but it is a key idea for the filmmakers. “Not forgetting was a deliberate act, to make remembering active,” says Forsyth.

“If you choose not to forget, you make the effort. Whereas remembering something is an accident. Do I remember where I left my car keys?” Pollard chips in. “It’s also about learning lessons. The act of remembering seems loaded with a kind of sentimentality; it feels wistful in a way, whereas not forgetting is a recalibration. It has an urgency.”

Broken English was billed at last year’s film festivals in Sundance and Venice as a documentary, but Forsyth isn’t sure that holds. “For us, the idea of going into a project saying ‘we are going to make a documentary’ just seems so alien, so limited from the start,” he says.

“I think we were going into it thinking, ‘We are going to make a film that tells a story, and we want to make the best film and tell the best story we can.’ For me, ‘non-fiction’ works as well as anything because the story we’re telling is not fiction, although we might be using some of the devices of fictional storytelling. I think the story we’re telling is full of emotional truth. Which is not the same as journalistic truth.”

For Pollard, the real discoveries in the film are the expressions that flicker across Faithfull’s face as she looks at the old footage of her younger self, beautiful and damaged but still holding up her end of things.

“There’s a piece from Weekend World in 1974 or ’75, an interview she probably should have said ‘no’ to, when she had just come out of rehab,” she says. Watching it, Faithfull initially looks dismissive of that young idiot, opining on life. “Then she starts to align with her. And I’m looking from face to face, and I’m seeing the same eyes, I’m seeing the same smile, and I’m seeing the same willingness to be open. We all can all read a face – and cinema is the best way for us to do that. That’s when the film is revelatory.”

Broken English opens nationally on September 17.

Blood, lies and cartels: Five new crime books to read this month

Sydney Morning Herald September 11, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

The noir label has been tenuously attached to all manner of crime fiction of late. But rather than being identified by a landscape (think rural or outback noir), or geography (Nordic noir), or even a setting (domestic noir), the real deal features a hapless character who is always on the outer and for whom things are never going to turn out well.

Michael Caleb Tasker, author of the impressive first novel Just Like the Night (Allen & Unwin, $35), knows this only too well since he has written a PhD thesis exploring the existential roots of noir fiction.

Meet 12-year-old Sera sitting in an El Paso hotel room while her father Ray stacks the decks in preparation for an elaborate sting. “There’s a fine line between being a magician and a card sharp,” he tells her. Despite being as sharp as a knife himself, Ray is routinely rumbled and roughed up. As father and daughter drive the length and breadth of the US, eventually decamping to Sydney, Sera wonders “how he made her feel safe while he was still covered in blood”.

Fast forward a few decades and Sera is coming to the end of her prison sentence. On her own in a cell, “she’s up early before the sun, face washed, push-ups done and bed made, waiting like there was something to wait for”. To discover what that something might be, Tasker takes us on a round trip to discover what unfolded when Sera and Ray came to Australia, what has happened to them since, and how Sera manages her parole when she discovers that her estranged daughter is being used and abused by the kind of bad man her father never was. Just Like the Night is tightly written, occasionally violent and very noir, especially the haunting conclusion.

If violence is not your thing then look away now since The Damned by Matt Rogers (Simon & Schuster, $40) is a veritable bloodbath. While initially a tad hesitant, after reading this sentence “Quadriceps flare beneath faded gym shorts as he balances two hundred and forty pounds of authentic Japanese straw on one shoulder”, I was in. Logan Booth (he of the flaring quadriceps) is a contract killer of Reacheresque proportions and this is his third outing.

Unlike Lee Child’s Reacher, Booth has an offsider, a diminutive, gay, recovering meth addict, whose love and loyalty to Logan ensure we know from the start the latter is a “good guy” despite his propensity to off people at an alarming rate. The fact that the president of the United States wants Logan dead is another tick in his favour. This time, the flaring quadriceps are headed to Colombia to rescue a former lover before Logan finds himself up against a nasty cartel determined to take him out.

The violence inflicted on both sides is surprisingly inventive and beautifully choreographed once you get over the gore factor and the prose style. This is the kind of propulsive crime that might make you burn the soup. I did.

Jessica Mansour-Nahra’s The Burn (Hachette, $25) is of a different order of flammable magnitude. Set in 2030, it imagines an Australia emerging from a five-month lockdown caused by rampant wildfires on a national scale. It’s a timely scenario given the disasters affecting Europe during their summer and dire warnings of worse to come.

After months of enforced isolation writing uplifting social media posts for her university employer’s website, Carmen is suspiciously reluctant to leave her featureless apartment and a dying pothos plant. But her three former high school chums have different plans: a camping trip on the idyllic south-east coast that has so far escaped the fires. What could possibly go wrong?

Lots apparently, but there will also be time for Carmen to ruminate on her chequered sexual history and “her broken, disparate family”. This includes her Finnish scientist father who has remarried and is deeply concerned about the fate of the walrus, her distant scientist mother somewhere in the Indian Ocean with her new German husband, and her horse-loving older sister Anna with whom she has always had a taut and tricky relationship. There’s a lot to work through.

While Burn is labelled as a psychological thriller, and it is indeed that, there are also telling reflections on the power of social media for good and evil. As it emerges, it’s not just bushfires we have to worry about.

Nevertheless, bushfires also figure in Petronella McGovern’s latest suburban thriller, Every Time She Wakes (Allen & Unwin, $35). University careers counsellor, Suzanne Vitale, is sleepless and fretting at 2.30am when the Rural Fire Service arrives to evacuate her and her family ahead of the firestorm. Bundled into a van, it’s not long before Suzanne suspects they are being abducted rather than rescued begging the question: why? There’s scant time to consider the options as the van crashes and Suzanne wakes up.

Although it might be assumed that it was all a bad dream, McGovern is playing trickier plot games. While there’s a clue in the fact that Suzanne’s eldest daughter Frankie is studying a unit on “Metaphysics, Reality, Time and Possibility”, it might be more helpful to think Groundhog Day meets Sliding Doors.

Like most domestic protagonists, Suzanne’s got a lot to figure out about her life and work. This includes how best to handle student complaints concerning a repulsive radio shock jock named Rowdy Mac who has made a bankable career demeaning women. Bells ringing anyone? Rowdy’s been hiring Suzanne’s students as interns, before he moves on to Suzanne’s daughter and her best friend who is a social media influencer. This is another book with something to say about the contemporary media landscape.

Given that Suzanne has to relive the bushfire scenario again and again until she gets it right, it’s tricky to summarise a plot that effectively works backwards rather than forwards. Thankfully it all makes sense in the end although you may be left wondering just how she did it. McGovern, that is.

American author K. T. Nguyen is also playing inventive mind games in her psychological thriller You Know What You Did (No Exit Press, $33) which is heavy on the psychology and light on the thrills. Annie Shaw is a budding artist with a teenage daughter, an entitled war-reporter husband and a Vietnamese mother hoarding all manner of detritus in the carriage house of their large estate. Annie also suffers from punishing bouts of a disgust-driven obsessive-compulsive disorder that is painfully realised. She takes a lot of very hot showers.

Nguyen incrementally replays the trauma experienced by Annie and her mother to explain their present plight. Although they have stuck together through war and displacement, their relationship has always been fraught since her mother has demeaned Annie’s every move. Sadly, Annie is unwittingly repeating this demeaning with her own teenage daughter, Tabby. How this maternal cycle might be broken is the major work of this book.

You Know What You Did has been well received in the US, winning an Agatha and Anthony Award for Best First, although I found it a rather solemn trudge. In its favour, it is illuminating on the experience of forced migration and the debilitating effects of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). I just wish it had been shorter and sharper. More noir even.

The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

More Anthropic researchers warn of AI’s perils as Musk terms fears a ‘psyop’

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 21:51:26 GMT

Insiders at the firm fear tech’s advancement could cause human extinction while others are calling it a ‘setup’

A day after a former researcher at Anthropic made an apocalyptic declaration about artificial intelligence, more researchers and staff members at the AI startup publicly agreed with him and posted their own dire warnings.

In response, Elon Musk and other conservative figures on X, formerly Twitter, called the chorus of concerns a “setup” and a “psyop”.

The Anthropic insiders fear the technology they are building could become so advanced and dangerous as to cause human extinction within the decade, and they assert many of their colleagues feel the same but haven’t said so publicly.

These researchers and staff are posting in response to a now-viral thread from Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who said on Wednesday he was resigning from the company because neither Anthropic nor its competitor OpenAI, also his former employer, were building AI models responsibly and are “gambling with our lives”.

Anna Wang, who works on Artificial General Intelligence Safety at Anthropic and previously worked at Google’s DeepMind, said Thursday that many people at Anthropic want to slow down development to come up with a plan to mitigate the risks that could come with these AI models.

“There is not yet a viable scientific plan to solve risks from recursively self-improving AI,” Wang wrote on X.

Drake Thomas, another Anthropic employee, said that he respected Coxon’s choice to abstain from building these models if he worries they could pose planet-scale risks.

“Things are moving way too fast, we don’t have anywhere near the degree of assurance we’ll want for ASI [artificial superintelligence],” Thomas said.

Musk took a more adversarial stance. “Seems like a setup,” he wrote.

Coxon replied to the world’s richest man with a selfie, writing, “I’m real and these are my real beliefs. You could ask your xAI researchers about me if you hadn’t fired them.”

In a statement to the Guardian, an Anthropic spokesperson defended the company’s strategy. “We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks. To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry,” the statement said.

Musk and others with a more positive view of AI have started to spread theories that Coxon’s post and the resulting fallout are part of a “psyop” to negatively influence the public’s feelings about AI.

“I think the groundwork for this psy op (for lack of a better term) has been prepared for a long time,” Musk posted on X. “This was just the match that lit the fire.”

Musk was responding to a post by Parker Thayer, a researcher at conservativethinktank Capital Research, in which he floated a theory with little evidence that Coxon’s post was the start of a “VERY sophisticated and well-funded PR operation to get support for Democrats to regulate AI into oblivion”. Other notable figures took notice.

Sign up to TechScape

after newsletter promotion

Bill Ackman, the billionaire CEO of the hedge fund Pershing Square, also quoted Thayer’s post, simply saying “Interesting.”

Other Anthropic employees had posted their agreement with Coxon shortly after he declared his resignation on Wednesday.

“AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes),” wrote Samuel Marks, who works on safety research at Anthropic. “This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are.”

Evan Hubinger, who describes himself as a lead in the company’s alignment division, which works on ensuring Anthropic’s AI models function in line with human goals, said Coxon was “correct” and that the industry was falling behind in attempts to deal with the apocalyptic potential.

“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger wrote. “I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.

It’s not exactly clear how Coxon and others expect AI models to usher in the demise of humanity. Some experts doubt that the technology will become so intelligent as to cause the apocalypse. Gary Marcus, a scientist and leading voice in AI, said that it’s time to boycott AI, but because it’s already causing harm.

More than extinction, Marcus said he worried about the “risk of catastrophe” from “from AI-generated pathogens, from wars started or escalated by AI-generated disinformation, from hacks that destroy critical infrastructure, and so on. Nothing I have seen gives any indication that any of that is under control”.

The same day, Anthropic released a report documenting how the company dismantled an operation attempting to build a biological weapon using its AI models.

Sesko soars as Manchester United surge past Sabah on Champions League return

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 21:05:24 GMT

It was a night for romance given the astonishing story that Sabah brought with them to Old Trafford for their Champions League debut. This is a club that did not even exist a decade ago and nobody saw their bolt to the title in Azerbaijan coming last season; in 2024-25, they had finished 41 points off the top. The job that their manager, Valdas Dambrauskas, has done since taking over in the summer of last year is extraordinary.

It was also a night for cold, hard reality. Manchester United were back in Europe’s elite competition after a two-year hiatus and in need of something to soothe them after the trauma of their last-gasp coughing up of two points in last Sunday’s Premier League draw at Everton. And before the extremely serious business of the derby here against Manchester City on Sunday. They got it on the back of a first-half performance that burned slowly before catching fire.

Sabah were game. United were clinical. It was Matheus Cunha who broke the deadlock midway through the first half and the defining moments came at the end of the period when Bruno Fernandes and Benjamin Sesko sent United into half-time with a three-goal cushion. Lisandro Martínez added the fourth late on. It was a case of job done for Michael Carrick, no wobbles. Now for City.

United had wanted to put their best foot forward when they heard the Champions League aria after the chaos and embarrassment of their previous involvement in the competition. Erik ten Hag was the manager in 2023-24 and his team finished bottom of their group with four points, starting and ending with losses to Bayern Munich. It was what happened in between times against Galatasaray and Copenhagen that still causes a few shudders. It was a period when United panicked uncontrollably when they had a lead. When the defensive gifts from them came in crazy clusters.

Carrick took no chances with his starting XI. There was minimal rotation in the midfield and front line, save for a first start of the season for Sesko in the No 9 position. It was easy to think that the manager wanted to groove Youri Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo in central midfield before the City game.

United looked to Fernandes to get them going. As always. There were intelligent runs from him; incision about his passes, that wonderful disguise on some of them. The breakthrough goal stemmed from him chasing a high ball over the top that looked like a lost cause only for him to keep it in play. It was what happened next that quickened United pulses. When Sabah gave the ball away cheaply to Bryan Mbeumo, United moved quickly over to the left. Patrick Dorgu crossed and Cunha’s finish was clean.

Sabah lined up in a 4-3-3 formation; no bus parking. They wanted to ask questions of a United defence that had a makeshift feel about it. There was assurance on the ball from them, the desire to carry it forward. And a huge chance in the 35th minute when Kaheem Parris crossed to the back post. Joy-Lance Mickels was clear of Noussair Mazraoui only to put the header wide. The angle was not favourable. It did not entirely excuse him.

Sabah were harshly treated by the half-time scoreline, even though United played on the front foot and created openings. It was the one-two punch in the closing stages of the first period that changed everything. Fernandes – who else? – made a sidefoot finish look easy after Tielemans had burst on a Cunha pass inside, spun and teed him up. The third followed a first time pass by Fernandes into Mbeumo, who got Sesko clean though. The Sabah backline was high. Sesko went around the goalkeeper to score. He never looked like missing.

There was a lovely scene 90 minutes before kick-off when some of the Sabah players wandered around the pitch, the stadium virtually empty, phones out to capture the quiet before the storm, the sheer scale of Old Trafford. They wore wide smiles. They were determined not to be overawed when it got started. The performance of the strolling central midfielder, Ivan Lepinjica, was certainly impressive. They were just too loose at the back.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

United played some slick stuff at times, Mainoo and Fernandes ever involved. When Carrick’s pass-and-move game clicks, it is easy to feel the possibility. Imposing it against the higher-profile teams is the name of the game. Starting against City.

Carrick introduced Mason Mount at half-time for his first football of the season, Tielemans coming off, his work done. He could be pleased with his impact. Carrick was always going to withdraw other likely starters against City, such as Mainoo. Sesko came off with him on 64 minutes and was warmly applauded. After his goal at Everton on Sunday, has he done enough to make the XI for the derby?

United controlled the second half. The jeopardy was long gone. The fourth goal summed up Sabah’s travails in their defensive third. It was a scooped free-kick by Fernandes for Joshua Zirkzee, on as a substitute, and when his backheel hit Aden McCarthy, the Sabah goalkeeper, Stas Pokatilov, lost his bearings, the ball caught under his feet. It was a tap-in for Martínez. The substitute, Orphé Mbina, headed high for Sabah at the very end. There was to be no fairytale goal.

New battery-powered trains will ‘bring faster journeys to north’

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 21:00:46 GMT

No 10 says 29 new trains to be built in Derby will support 350 local jobs, as well as nearly 6,000 across the UK

No 10 has announced the construction of a new fleet of battery-powered trains that will “bring faster, more reliable journeys to the north”.

The 29 new trains, which will be run by TransPennine Express, are set to be built in Alstom’s Litchurch Lane works in Derby from 2028, which the government says will support 350 local jobs, as well as nearly 6,000 across the UK.

The new fleet will be made up of Adessia Stream trains, a battery-powered model that will be the first of its kind to be used for long-distance mainline journeys in the UK when it enters service in 2034.

Prime minister Andy Burnham, who uses trains regularly to move between London and Manchester, highlighted the need for more reliable and efficient services, with the new trains pitched as making journeys between major northern cities shorter while increasing capacity on rail networks by 30% in the next decade.

Burnham said: “I’ve lost count of the number of times someone has stopped me to tell me about the train that never came. And when that happens, it means missed shifts, missed appointments and missed opportunities.

“Today that starts to change. These 29 new trains will bring faster, more reliable journeys to the north, and thousands of British jobs for the next generation.

“It’s exactly what Great British Railways is all about – taking back control of the basics and getting Britain believing again.”

As well as speed and capacity, the new trains are set to run without emissions even on non-electrified stretches of the network, while also having more accessible step-free boarding and onboard wifi.

Transport secretary Heidi Alexander also praised the announcement, calling it a sign of how Great British Railways “will deliver better journeys for people while backing British business” and allowing passengers to “wave goodbye to overcrowded, delayed diesel trains and step onboard faster electric trains which are fit for the future”.

The Paper season two review – one of the best comedies on TV right now

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 21:00:46 GMT

This spin-off from the US Office is so brilliant that it might even eclipse its mother show. And as for the hilarious Sabrina Impacciatore – just hand her all the awards!

Pity the poor TV writer foolish enough to make a show about journalism. The world is full of inaccurate and illogical medical dramas, but they survive because real life doctors and nurses only tend to grumble about them to themselves. But when you make an inaccurate and illogical show about journalists, real life journalists get to yell about it from the streets. This is probably why Aaron Sorkin’s The Newsroom ended so early, because we all got to bleat about it through our little megaphones.

The makers of The Paper must have been anticipating a similarly rough ride. It is, after all, explicitly a sitcom about the death of print media, and, Lord knows, nothing wounds us like staring the truth in the face. And yet last year’s first season emerged as one of the best new comedies on television.

Technically, a spin-off from the American version of The Office, it centred around the reporters of the dwindling Toledo Truth Teller newspaper. Forced to share an office with a (much more successful) toilet paper company, its skeleton staff were made to either copy and paste wire stories on to its content management system, or write clickbait drivel. It was bleak but, you had to admit, at least it knew the state of things.

Things turned around with the appointment of crusading new editor Ned Sampson ( Domhnall Gleeson), who strived to return the paper to its former glories. Last season ended on a moment of glory, with the paper winning a prestigious local award for journalism. As season two begins, it becomes clear that this did not change much.

This is still very much a show about a struggling operation. A billboard bought to trumpet its success ends up reminding locals to cancel their subscriptions. An obituary of a beloved colleague goes off the rails when it becomes apparent that he had a comically dark secret life. Everyone gets annoyed by overzealous push notifications.

A show with such devotion to an issue – make no mistake, this is a love letter to journalism – always has the potential to come off as unpalatably worthy, but The Paper avoids this thanks to its absolutely stacked cast. Gleeson, in the lead role, has a Leslie Knope-ish can-do spirit that sometimes overtakes him. Tim Key returns as a slightly villainous corporate strategist, although for some reason he only appears fitfully this time around. Lisa Gilroy makes a very strong first impression as an oversharing HR officer.

But, really, the show belongs to Esmeralda Grand, played impeccably by Sabrina Impacciatore. Esmeralda feels like she’s been beamed in from another show entirely. While everything else about The Paper feels like a naturalistic workplace comedy, Impacciatore’s Esmerelda is big and broad and loud. She’s a whirlwind of pratfalls and gesticulations and wildly overcooked reaction shots. At one point this season she gets nailed into a crate. At another she dresses up as a teenage boy and beats up her own son. None of it should work, but somehow all of it does. There are, quite honestly, not enough awards in the world to give her.

The Paper is also becoming a masterclass in the sort of will they/won’t they romantic storylines that tend to propel US sitcoms to the big leagues. The main one exists between Gleeson’s Ned and Chelsea Frei’s Mare, who shared a kiss in last year’s finale and now have to navigate a secret on-off relationship, but this time almost everyone in the cast finds themselves in the same situation. There are definitely two more will they/won’t theys, one of which comes about during an exceptional piece of physical comedy in a tornado, but there might even be more than that. It’s a lot to keep up with.

But, if that’s overload, then so be it. You get the sense that this could be The Paper’s chance to become as big as its mother show, and the producers are throwing everything at the wall to get it there. By no means does the show have a guaranteed future – a recent interview with Gleeson hinted at the uncertainty of a third season – but a show like this deserves to come back year after year. A warm, funny workplace sitcom that actually has something to say is a rare thing indeed. It would be a terrible thing to see it go the way of local newspapers.

The Paper was on Sky One and is on Now. In the US, it airs on Peacock. In Australia it airs on Binge and Foxtel.

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington made the request to Judge William Sullivan six days after the trial ended in a deadlock, and as a fourth member of ⁠the 12-member jury went public to describe how a single juror had prevented the panel from reaching a unanimous verdict.

The jury in Plymouth, Massachusetts, deliberated for seven days before Sullivan on Friday declared a mistrial, following repeated ⁠reports by the jury that it was deadlocked.

Prosecutors have yet to say if they plan to retry Clancy. But Reddington argued that ​Sullivan should decide the matter himself, saying prosecutors during the ‌six-week trial did not present evidence ‌that would allow a jury to find her guilty on the first-degree murder charges she faces.

He asked the judge to hear arguments on his motion during a hearing scheduled ‌for 29 September. A spokesperson for the Plymouth county district attorney, Timothy Cruz, did not respond to a request for comment.

Clancy, 36, has admitted to strangling her three children with exercise bands on 24 January 2023, in ​the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then cut herself with a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to end her own life that left her paralyzed.

Reddington at trial sought to convince jurors she should be found not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility, saying she suffered from postpartum psychosis when she killed Cora, ⁠five; Dawson, three; and eight-month-old Callan.

In his motion, Reddington said that 11 of the 12 jurors ​had been prepared to find her not guilty ​by reason of lack of criminal responsibility but ​could not return a verdict due to a holdout who despite acknowledging having reasonable doubt would not agree ​to find her not guilty.

Canada offered support on Thursday to boost Ukraine’s air defenses and help replenish its drone stocks, as the countries pledged to deepen their alliance during a visit by Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Mark Carney hosted the president of Ukraine in Calgary in the western province of Alberta, where the Canadian prime minister grew up among a large community of people with Ukrainian heritage.

“Canada will always be with you,” Carney assured Zelenskyy.

The leaders signed an agreement to work toward a “hundred-year partnership”.

That deal, to be negotiated over the coming months, aims to codify cooperation in a range of areas, including defense, critical minerals and energy.

“Our two nations have been connected since 1893,” Carney said, referring to a wave of Ukrainians who migrated to the new Canadian nation.

In Alberta, there are an estimated 350,000 Canadians of Ukrainian descent.

“Ukrainians helped build Canada and Canadians will help rebuild Ukraine,” Carney said.

The support announced on Thursday includes C$350m (US$253m) provided through the United States’ Joint Ukraine Multinational Program – Services, Training and Articles Rapid Timeline (Jumpstart) program.

Zelenskyy has emphasized the need for increased air defense as Russia ramps up ballistic missile attacks.

Carney said Canada was also offering C$450m in loan guarantees to enhance the Ukrainian energy supply.

The funds will help repair damaged infrastructure, increase storage capacity and improve power supply to hospitals.

Carney said the goal of the energy support was “to help Ukrainians get through the winter”, a difficult period when the country endures rolling blackouts amid often frigid temperatures.

Canada is moving aggressively to increase its own drone stocks, Carney said, announcing a deal that will see 30% of new Canadian production head to Ukraine.

Zelenskyy told reporters that “these drones will go to Ukraine immediately to [the] battlefield, immediately to our people, our soldiers … to save our children, our families first of all.”

Asked about potential negotiations to ease the fighting, Zelenskyy said he did not anticipate any substantive talks during Russia’s ongoing election period.

But he said he planned to meet Donald Trump in New York City in late September, probably on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, with Washington bidding to revive long-stalled talks to end the war.

“But at the end of September, we will have an opportunity to meet, I think, with the American team in New York,” Zelenskyy said.

“And I think that … I can be more open after the New York meeting with President Trump.”

After the Calgary meeting, Zelenskyy was headed to Banff, a stunning Canadian national park, where he will address a cabinet retreat for Carney’s liberal government.

He then heads to Canada’s largest city, Toronto, and North Bay in northern Ontario.

Florida sues Netflix over misleading parents over minors’ data collection

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 20:11:55 GMT

Lawsuit brought by James Uthmeier, the attorney general, marks latest action by the state against big tech companies

Florida officials filed a lawsuit against Netflix, accusing the streaming giant of misleading parents about its collection of minors’ data and using features that encourage children to “binge watch” content.

The lawsuit, filed Wednesday and led by James Uthmeier, the Republican Florida attorney general, marks the latest action by Florida against major technology companies. The red-leaning state has taken an increasingly aggressive approach toward big tech, particularly during the rise of artificial intelligence (AI).

“Netflix told Florida families they could pay a monthly fee to escape big tech surveillance. That was false,” Uthmeier said in a statement. “Netflix collected detailed data on children and families, designed its product to keep kids watching, and then commercialized that information to launch the advertising business it promised never to build.

“Parents, not corporate executives, direct the upbringing of their children. Netflix should expect to be held accountable,” he added.

In a statement shared with The Guardian, a spokesperson for Netflix said: “Netflix takes our members’ privacy seriously. We comply with privacy and data‑protection laws everywhere we operate and have dedicated safeguards in place for kids who watch content on Netflix. This lawsuit lacks merit and we intend to vigorously defend the matter in court.”

In the 66-page lawsuit, Florida accuses Netflix of carrying out a “years-long bait-and-switch” that has “led the company right to where it promised never to be: addicting children and families to its platform, mining those users for data, and then converting that data into lucrative intelligence for global advertising juggernauts”.

The lawsuit claims Netflix opened Floridians’ data to commercial data brokers and advertising platforms after it launched advertisements in November 2022, allegedly allowing advertisers to “target Floridians by life stage, income, and household composition”. The complaint says Netflix failed to obtain the consent required under Florida law.

It emphasizes that Netflix has in the past made a point to distinguish itself from tech companies that offer “free” services in exchange for data collection such as Google, Facebook, and Amazon, but claims that Netflix has failed to live up to its promises to not track and monetize data similar to other tech companies.

Netflix provides members with its updated privacy statement and terms of use annually, according to the streaming service. Those terms lay out the company’s advertising and privacy practices, along with users’ rights and available controls. It also offers parental controls that allow parents to filter or block content.

The Florida case follows a lawsuit filed earlier this year by Texas officials accusing Netflix of spying on children and designing its platform to be addictive.

Uthmeier has also filed lawsuits against OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, and TikTok this year. He recently kept Florida out of a multi-state settlement involving Meta, saying the $17bn agreement was “not enough to punish” the company over allegations that it failed to protect minor users.

“We’re going to send a message to big tech companies. If you hurt our kids, you are going to have to pay for it,” Uthmeier said while announcing the Netflix lawsuit on Wednesday. “And so, in this lawsuit, we will be seeking billions of damages.”

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 20:04:02 GMT

Broadcaster, 86, had intended to end her life in Swiss clinic after being diagnosed with terminal lung cancer in 2023

Esther Rantzen has said she is no longer able to travel to Switzerland to end her life because she has become “too physically fragile”.

Rantzen, who presented the TV current affairs programme That’s Life! for 21 years and founded the youth support charity Childline, had intended to end her life in a Dignitas assisted dying clinic in Switzerland after being diagnosed with terminal lung cancer in 2023.

The broadcaster, 86, said in a statement on Thursday that her quality of life had deteriorated since her diagnosis, and that she was ready to end her life but was no longer able to make the journey despite having joined Dignitas about a year after learning she was terminally ill.

Rantzen said: “Unfortunately, when I was strong enough to make the flight and go to Dignitas, my life was not unbearably painful, indeed, I was able to relax in my beloved cottage in the New Forest.

“And by the time life did become unbearable, I was too physically fragile to make the journey and go through the Dignitas process.

“So even though I had spent the money and made the plans, I was not ready to end my life back then, and did not realise that would be my last chance.”

Assisted dying remains illegal in the UK, though a bill that would allow it in certain circumstances is being revisited.

Rantzen is a vocal supporter of the bill, which is due to have a second reading in parliament on Friday, and has criticised the current laws that prevent people in her situation from legally ending their lives, calling the rules “messy and cruel”.

Legalised assisted dying in the UK has been the topic of intensive debate since Kim Leadbeater’s bill was introduced to parliament in October 2024.

A June 2025 vote in the Commons saw the bill progress by 314 votes to 291, with both sides receiving votes from MPs from Labour, the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats.

If the bill passes, the UK would join European countries such as Austria, Belgium, the Netherlands, Spain and Switzerland, as well as Australia, Canada and the US, where it is legal in 13 states.

Advocates for the bill have claimed it will enable terminally ill people to enjoy a dignified end to their lives and allow them to die before their health declines too much.

Those against it, however, argue the criteria put forward could change after the law is passed and that the quality of palliative care could decline.

Tiafoe v Shelton US Open semi-final a legacy of the departing Gaël Monfils

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 18:51:34 GMT

Veteran Frenchman bowed out in New York but the clash of two black players in the last four of the men’s singles is testament to his effect

The early days of this year’s US Open can be told in a series of farewells to competitors who plan to end their careers this year. The most moving of them all came in the form of Gaël Monfils’s grand departure inside Louis Armstrong Stadium against the wildly talented 20-year-old Learner Tien. Tien was competing in front of his home crowd, one of the Americans capable of a deep run, but for much of his straight-sets defeat the Frenchman had the American crowd in the palm of his hands.

Beyond the massive popularity he has garnered among tennis fans, one of the most striking parts of Monfils’s long farewell was seeing how highly nearly all of his fellow professionals, particularly his fellow black players, regard him. Frances Tiafoe says he spent his youth looking up to Monfils. Arthur Fils considers Monfils his older brother. Naomi Osaka’s nickname for Monfils, one of her idols, is simply “the Goat”. They all hold Monfils in such great esteem, and for good reason.

While women’s tennis has witnessed the successes of a long line of top black players, Monfils and his retired compatriot Jo-Wilfried Tsonga were, for so long, the standard bearers for black players in men’s tennis. In the same year that the 40-year-old Monfils will finally bow out, the new generation of black men’s players have consolidated their positions at the top of the sport.

Last month, the Cincinnati Open featured two black players competing in a Masters 1000 final for the first time as the 22-year-old Frenchman Fils overcame a year of injuries to defeat Tiafoe and win his first big title. Fils’s victory was preceded by Ben Shelton’s triumph at the Canadian Open in Montreal.

It took three weeks for the Fils v Tiafoe final to be eclipsed by an even more significant match between two black players. Tiafoe and Shelton will compete against each other in the US Open semi-finals on Friday night, with the winner becoming the first black man since Jo-Wilfried Tsonga at the 2008 Australian Open, and the first African American man since MaliVai Washington, the 1996 Wimbledon finalist, to reach a grand slam final. The victor will then attempt to become the third black man to win a grand slam after Arthur Ashe and Yannick Noah. Along with last year’s semi-finalist Félix Auger-Aliassime, there will be four black players inside the ATP’s top 11. The status commanded by Monfils, who never reached did not reach a major final, plainly underlines how important this moment is for future generations of black tennis players as well as themselves.

As Americans at the US Open, two players who have spent their careers being reminded of how far American men’s tennis has fallen since its decades of dominance over the sport, and particularly of Andy Roddick’s triumph at the 2003 US Open, the last time an American man won a title here, the significance of this moment is doubly important to Tiafoe and Shelton. Unlike in their previous runs, there are no multiple grand-slam champions or all-time greats left in the draw, with the earlier semi-final feauturing top seed Alexander Zverev against former top-10 player Karen Khachanov. All four can win this title.

The past few years in New York have been leading up to this match. It is just the fourth time Shelton has competed in the US Open main draw, yet somehow this will be his third US Open meeting with Tiafoe. Shelton won their 2023 quarter-final before Tiafoe exacted revenge in a bruising five-set, third-round match in 2024. They have become great friends, which can be awkward oncourt for some, but they enjoy battling against each other so much that their relationship only makes them even more determined to produce their best. It helps they are such creative, all-court players with great variation and explosive athleticism, which makes for such a complementary match-up. This is a third major semi-final for both players, but neither man has ever been so well prepared. Shelton just delivered the biggest win of his career over the defending champion Carlos Alcaraz and the 23-year-old continues to evolve into a genuine grand slam threat. Tiafoe, meanwhile, has been one of the revelations this year. The 28-year old has spent the season determined to be more professional and focused each week than ever before, and his results are a direct consequence of his growing maturity. Their efforts have yielded by far the biggest opportunity of their careers, and the winner will be decided by which competitor is truly ready for the pressure and weight that accompanies such a massive opening.

Ministers face backlash from hospitality industry over ‘tourist tax’ plans

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 18:14:53 GMT

Many mayors welcome power to impose tourist tax but industry warns of ‘irreparable harm’ and job losses

Ministers are facing a backlash from the hospitality industry after they announced mayors in England would be given sweeping powers to levy taxes on holiday accommodation such as hotels and Airbnbs.

The plan, presented on Thursday by Angela Rayner, the local government secretary, will allow mayors to impose a “tourist tax” without a cap on how much they can charge and with few controls on how they can spend it.

The move, which gives mayors some of their most significant tax-raising powers, was welcomed by regional leaders, who said it would give them a vital revenue stream at a time when local government is facing a funding crisis. Mayors will be expected to lay out their detailed plans for how they plan to use the new powers in early 2028.

But it was met with outrage from hospitality businesses, who had expected the government to put stricter conditions on how much mayors could charge and how the money would be used.

UKHospitality, the industry’s trade body, said a 5% overnight levy across England could result in 33,000 job losses and a £2bn hit to the economy, with regions more reliant on tourism, such as the Lake District, being worst affected.

The owner of Premier Inn, Britain’s biggest hotel chain, said it would be “hugely damaging” and urged ministers to “avoid inflicting what could be irreparable harm on this large and vital sector of the economy”.

Eddie Nelder, a co-owner of the Choice Hotels chain, which has hotels in Blackpool and the Lake District, said: “We’re here trying to stay alive, waiting for a lifeline from the government and we get another hammer blow. It feels like we’re being strangled.”

However, Rayner said the tax-raising powers would help fund local communities. “This measure will give mayors the choice to raise and reinvest funding where it’s needed most,” she said in a statement before a meeting with the country’s mayors at No 10 North in Manchester.

“It’ll help support the local services, public spaces and attractions that both residents and visitors rely on, with decisions taken by people who know their area best.”

In the immediate term, the rate will be set at no more than 5% in almost every major English city after every Labour metro mayor agreed to cap their charges at that level.

In a joint letter to Rayner, they wrote: “Foreign cities visited by British tourists from New York to Paris, as well as hundreds of smaller cities across the world, have long benefited from such levies while continuing to grow their tourism sectors. Granting the power to regions to introduce levies will help level the playing field by ensuring further investment in our cities, contributing to further growth.”

But large parts of the east coast will not have to pay the tax after their mayors – two Reform UK and one Conservative – said they would refuse to impose them.

The move follows a consultation launched by Keir Starmer’s government, and will bring England into line with many European countries and the US, where holidaymakers have for years been paying overnight visitor levies.

Similar levies also apply in Wales and Scotland, though they will be capped in Wales.

Edinburgh became the first city in Scotland to introduce a tourist tax, setting it at 5% in July. In Wales, councils will have the power to charge £1.30 per person a night in tax for most accommodation from April 2027.

Under the proposal, which is expected to be introduced as a bill in parliament within months, mayors will be allowed to charge a levy as a percentage of the price of an overnight stay, rather than as a flat fee.
