Ministers at Westminster will cap the number of nights to which it can be applied in order to avoid hitting long-term rental properties. It is understood the cap is likely to be higher than the 5% that is applied by Holyrood.

Any commercially rented property will face the tax, though there will be an exemption for those that are only rented occasionally on a casual basis.

Mayors will be allowed to decide whether or not to exempt other sites such as festival campsites. They will also be allowed to share revenues with local councils.

Kim McGuinness, the mayor of north-east England, backed the move for a visitor levy, saying it could bring money to the local economy during events such as the Great North Run, which is due to take place this Sunday.

“A visitor levy could help us bring major international events to our region, back local businesses, improve visitor attractions, build on the 90,000 jobs already in this sector and unlock opportunities that come from a thriving visitor economy,” she said.

“Most importantly, the money raised here would stay here, helping us invest in the future of our region rather than waiting for Whitehall to do it for us.”

The move is one of the biggest handovers of power from the Treasury to local leaders in years, and comes before the first budget of Andy Burnham’s government, at which ministers have promised to hand over more tax powers to local leaders.

It comes at a time when many local authorities are struggling for funds. Last year the government gave emergency funding worth £1.3bn to a record 28 councils, without which several said they would have gone bankrupt.

But it also comes after a concerted effort by the government to ease the pressure on the hospitality industry, with many businesses struggling with high inflation and increased national insurance and minimum wage bills.

Earlier this summer, the former chancellor slashed VAT on British summer holiday destinations, in a programme she called the “Great British summer savings scheme”.

Meanwhile, in one of his first acts as prime minister, Burnham announced he would cut business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues.

Many hospitality businesses are struggling with high inflation, as well as additional national insurance and minimum wage costs imposed by Reeves in her first budget.

Allen Simpson, the chief executive of UKHospitality, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “What we’re talking about here is an open-ended power for mayors to set tourism taxes at any level they want … If you go to Paris, if you go to Rome, if you go to Berlin, you’re paying a small tourism tax, but it’s capped.”

Global bond sell-off resumes as surging oil prices stoke fears about inflation

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 18:05:15 GMT

Crude jumps above $107 a barrel amid concerns over Middle East conflict and out-of-control government borrowing

Nervous investors across big economies have been dumping government bonds, driving up the cost of borrowing, as surging oil prices amplified fears about rising inflation.

The cost of a barrel of oil jumped 6% to above $107 on Thursday amid concerns that advances by Houthi rebels along the Red Sea coast in Yemen could choke off Saudi crude exports.

The global bond sell-off that has rocked markets in recent weeks resumed in response to the news from the Middle East – which came against a backdrop of escalating concern about out-of-control government borrowing.

Higher oil prices, which had already climbed since hostilities resumed in the Iran war, are expected to drive up inflation, prompting central banks to raise interest rates and putting the brakes on economic growth.

Donald Trump suggested on Wednesday that the conflict with Iran could continue until “immediately after” November’s US midterm elections, at which point he claimed oil prices would be “tumbling downward”.

The European Central Bank (ECB) raised its main interest rate to 2.5% on Thursday, with its president, Christine Lagarde, saying: “We believe inflation will be longer lasting than we had anticipated.”

“The conflict in the Middle ​East continues ​to ⁠generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to ​remain well above target for ​an ⁠extended period,” she added.

As Thursday’s sell-off gathered pace in London, the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year UK government bonds surged above 5.37% – the highest cost of borrowing since 2007 – creating a fresh headache for the new chancellor, John Healey.

With less than seven weeks to go until Healey’s first budget on 28 October, higher interest rates on the UK’s debt-pile will raise the cost of future investment projects and eat into the Treasury’s fiscal headroom.

At the same time, the prospect of higher energy bills as oil and gas prices rise is likely to intensify pressure on the government to help consumers to weather the winter.

Unleaded petrol prices have already risen by 6p a litre since the start of September, according to the motoring organisation the RAC, while the prospect of higher inflation has prompted some banks to raise their mortgage rates.

Healey has promised to provide a “breathing space” for UK households while also addressing the cost of doing business.

In a speech on Monday, however, he also sought to tame bond market fears by committing himself to “controlling borrowing to bear down on inflation, and reducing long-term pressures on our public finances”.

The cost of longer-term borrowing also continued to surge, with 30-year yields hitting the highest level since 2007, despite the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, intervening directly in debt markets on Wednesday.

Bessent hoped to bring down yields by buying back $6bn worth of government debt; but investors appeared to respond by deepening the sell-off.

Kyle Rodda, a senior financial market analyst at the broker Capital. com, said: “Ultimately, a sustained drop in long-end yields can ​only be achieved by genuine shifts in macroeconomic policy: ​either the US government pulling back on spending or the ​Fed lifting rates.”

Policymakers at the Federal Reserve, the US central bank, will meet under its new chair, Kevin Warsh, to set interest rates next week.

Markets are expecting a rise – potentially enraging Trump, who has repeatedly demanded rate cuts. In a TruthSocial post last week, the president said: “The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart – BE PATRIOTS for a change.”

A plethora of UK data to be published over the next week, including on inflation, jobs and growth, will give an updated snapshot of how resilient the British economy has been in the face of the Iran war.

In the first six months of the year, UK growth was the strongest among the G7 economies. This was despite higher-than-expected oil prices and the absence of hoped-for rate cuts.

Bank of England policymakers will also meet next week, but are expected to leave the UK’s key interest rate on hold at 3.75% for the time being as they continue to monitor the impact of higher oil prices.

The Guardian view on the prisons crisis: moving men into women’s jails is not the answer

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 17:35:24 GMT

Kneejerk reactions to overcrowding will do more harm than good. Ministers should focus on probation

It is not hard to see why ministers are considering converting parts of the women’s prison estate for use by men. While Andy Burnham’s decision to narrow the early-release scheme was born of political necessity, it has made an already acute capacity problem worse. Excluding manslaughter and further sexual offences cut projected early releases from 6,000 to 4,500. The family of PC Andrew Harper, who was killed on duty in 2019, welcomed the assurance that his killers would not be released early. But the change left overcrowded English and Welsh jails with even less room.

The government is trying to innovate. Last week it was announced that £110m will be spent on creating new cells in existing jails, by converting underused spaces such as storage and laundry areas. Deportations are to be speeded up, if foreign governments can be persuaded to cooperate. There is an overdue and welcome commitment to examine how indeterminate imprisonment for public protection sentences can be phased out.

But nobody believes that these schemes will be enough. Demand for places will continue to outstrip supply, while continued overcrowding risks worsening grave existing problems including endemic drug use, high rates of recidivism, violence and low staff morale (which undermines recruitment and retention).

Most of the criminals who the public is anxious to see locked up are violent men. At the same time, there is a growing consensus that it would be better if some of the roughly 3,300 female prisoners in England (Wales has no women’s prison) served their sentences in the community. Most women are imprisoned for non-violent offences and pose no threat to public safety. Two out of three have been victims of domestic abuse; one in three have a child under 10. More than a quarter are on remand, so have not even been sentenced. The social and financial costs of locking them up are shockingly high.

It is good to see these arguments gaining traction. A landmark review by Jean Corston proposed the replacement of women’s jails with smaller local custodial centres nearly 20 years ago. But rushing to close a women’s prison, or part of one, in order to free up space for men would be damaging, as experts have pointed out. Female prisoners are held separately from men primarily for reasons of safety. Already, because there are so few female prisons, women are more likely than men to be held a long way from home. A report by the charity Women in Prison on the closure of Holloway prison in 2016 described it as a “deeply harmful process” owing to the disruption it caused.

The Tories bear a heavy responsibility for prisons’ calamitous state. Criminal justice budgets were singled out for huge cuts under austerity because voters would be unlikely to notice – at least initially. The failed privatisation of the probation service was a disaster. But after two years in office, Labour must focus on the future, and explain to voters why locking people up in squalid, drug-riddled buildings is so wasteful. If they are serious about community alternatives, as plans to shrink the women’s estate would suggest, they need to show that this is more than a kneejerk reaction to overcrowding. Probation cannot be an afterthought: in early 2026, more offenders returned to prison on recall than were released from custody. Mr Burnham’s ministers need a new slogan: probation, probation, probation.

Could he also be about to offer everyone in the country £5,000 in return for electing a Reform government?

Sadly not. Even Honest Bob’s planned welfare cuts won’t cover that. Instead, Nige was treating us all to his reflections on his party conference that had just ended. The only drawback was that there appeared to be some gaps in his memory. Let’s be kind and assume he was pushed for space. So let’s help him fill in the blanks.

Dear John. ‘Wow.’ That’s what I kept thinking as our conference closed. Good start, Nige. Because that’s what I was thinking too. It’s not every party conference that is completely derailed by an undercover investigation into allegations of illegal sources of party funding. And it came completely out of the blue. Who would have thought that a party leader under investigation over a £5m gift from a Thai crypto billionaire, and a party whose main funder is Ben Delo – who was convicted in the US for failing to comply with legislation against money laundering – might be implicated in possible wrongdoing?

It’s obviously massively reassuring that you say you can’t be bought. But you can clearly be rented.

Robert Jenrick nailed it when he said: “Boohoo.”

Zia Yusuf and I will put the Royal Navy in the Channel and stop the boats. Do you really think the Royal Navy is going to participate in operations to turn back the small boats that could result in the deaths of dozens of migrants?

It’s so good to see Reform turn over its political allies abroad. A reminder to Johnny Frenchman that when we left the EU it was to put some distance between us and him.

It was a masterstroke to write the memorandum in both English and French, and sneakily adding a clause in English agreeing that France would take back all migrants who had arrived in England. And as Jordan’s English was not that good, he never noticed! Chapeau! Or perhaps he’s a bit thick. Either way, he’s a lot less odds-on to be the next prime minister because Marine Le Pen is furious with him and there’s an almighty row going on in the National Rally party.

In our first 100 days, Richard Tice pledged to cut £250 off your energy bill by scrapping the mad levies on them. No one thinks Dicky is going to do anything. Everyone inside the party thinks he is just an afternoon TV presenter from the 1980s. A man born to be your hype person. Who owes his entire existence to you. The same goes for Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman. Politicians too mediocre even for the Tory party.

It’s looking like we’ll need 10,000 candidates for the general and local elections. Recruiting that many candidates will be a mammoth task. So I need more of you than ever to step forward. It goes without saying that the 6,000 of you in Birmingham are already on the list. But we still need 4,000 more. Yours, Nigel Farage

World Rugby wants a Six Nations match to be staged in the US and has offered financial incentives to the unions to do so – but England have effectively ruled themselves out on the grounds that fixtures at Twickenham are too lucrative.

Insiders also point to how the RFU owns its home stadium whereas New Zealand and South Africa do not.

If there was appetite among the other unions, however, the Six Nations committee would have to agree as would the tournament broadcasters, though ITV’s recent £1.6bn takeover by Sky, which is owned by the US telecoms giant Comcast, may help in that regard.

“In terms of the matchday economics, [South Africa v New Zealand] is like a Six Nations match,” the World Rugby chief executive, Alan Gilpin, told the Telegraph. “It starts to show that [financial return] is not the barrier. It is all part of the new World Athletics Ultimate Championship, a three-day event with a prize fund of $10m which is designed to pit the best against the best, and kick off a minor revolution in the sport.

When Usain Bolt, who is a global ambassador for the event, was told that anyone who wins the 100m, 200m and mixed 4x100m relay here will walk away £250,000 richer, he smiled – and recalled a conversation he had just recently had with another legendary Jamaican sprinter, Asafa Powell.

“I was chatting to Asafa before I came here and we were like: ‘Jeez, we missed out on a big cash prize,’” he said. “I won a fair few championships and it still doesn’t add up to all that cash. I am sad I missed out on it, but I’m happy for the athletes.”

The idea is the brainchild of World Athletics president, Sebastian Coe, and chief executive, Jon Ridgeon. But this is just the start of plans to make the sport richer – and more popular.

“We will deliver magnetic indelible moments that will travel around all four corners of the globe, and I think we will see a compelling glimpse into the future and the potential of this sport, which at its best is untouchable,” said Coe.

“We also want this championship to be an incubator for change. As a proud Sheffielder, I would describe it as a blast furnace, ultimately shaping what our sport will look like going forward. And we want to take some of these innovations into the world championships and Olympic Games.”

So what could be next? The Guardian can reveal there is growing clamour for Coe to stay on at World Athletics in some capacity when his presidency ends in September 2027. One plan being discussed is for Coe to lead a new commercial arm, which aims to sell World Athletics’ own rights for the first time and add substantial external investment and revenues.

Such a move could come about because at the end of 2029, World Athletics’ commercial contract with the sports marketing agency Dentsu, which is worth around £14m a year, will end.

While it has been a happy relationship, the current deal means that even if World Athletics wants to use footage from its own world championships at its own awards ceremony it has to pay Dentsu.

But in three years’ time World Athletics will have control of its commercial and broadcast rights for the first time in three decades, allowing it to explore fresh options on how best to fund the sport.

It is understood that Coe, who has transformed the governance and fortunes of World Athletics since taking over from the corrupt Lamine Diack regime in 2015, is undecided as to whether he would take on such a role.

In a statement to the Guardian, World Athletics said: “At the end of 2029, most of World Athletics’ commercial contracts and broadcast relationships will come to an end, as will our current contract with Dentsu, who has owned our commercial rights since 2014, and we will be in a position to sell our own rights from 2030 onwards.

The Guardian view on falling birthrates: cash alone cannot buy belonging

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 17:30:19 GMT

Young people still want partners and children. Governments must address the insecurity and isolation preventing them from building families

Why are people in one of the world’s richest, safest countries having so few children? Singapore is asking that question. In 2000, its fertility rate matched America’s at 1.6 children per woman. By 2025, it had dropped to 0.87 – almost half the US rate. Singapore’s leaders, worried about population collapse, have reached for the chequebook. Each child, including those born to unmarried parents, will get $55,000 in government support by the time they turn 17. Yet a quarter of Singaporeans say they do not intend to have children. Wealth and security, clearly, don’t guarantee more babies.

UN data shows that global fertility fell from 5.3 births per woman in 1963 to 2.2 in 2023. But this masks a growing divide. In some poor sub-Saharan African countries there are around six births per woman. Compare this with England and Wales, where the figure is just 1.39. More than half of the world – including a billion women in India and China – have a fertility rate below the global 2.1 “replacement level” needed to sustain populations without migration. But even in poor countries with high mortality rates and consequently higher replacement rates, births outpace deaths. In Nigeria, for example, the fertility rate of 4.4 exceeds its replacement rate of 2.6 children per woman.

To understand this phenomenon, the UN asked 100,000 18- to 39-year-olds from 73 nations their views on relationships and having children. The results, released in July, were striking: two-thirds said they want to marry or live with a partner. Those who did not have children overwhelmingly wanted them. Yet about a quarter of those aged 25 to 39 said they wanted a partner but were single and not dating – a status reported more by men than women. More than half said the biggest barriers to a durable relationship were economic constraints. Young people want partnership and parenthood, but questioned achieving the “emotional and financial” stability needed for a shared life.

The Nordic region – consisting of five states and three territories – is viewed as a good place to have children thanks to generous parental leave and subsidised childcare. Yet fertility rates have fallen by up to third since 2010, against 12% across the EU. The Polish sociologist Anna Gromada wrote in the Guardian that despite her country’s economic success, its fertility rate was 1.05. While the state transfers cash worth 10% of the median wage for every child born each month, Poland’s population is shrinking. Prof Gromada argues that people are not just deciding against children; many never form lasting relationships in which the question arises. Almost half of under-30s are single. Cash paid after a family exists cannot create the togetherness needed for a family in the first place.

The world is not running out of people. The UN expects today’s 8.2 billion people to become 10.3 billion by the mid-2080s. What is emerging is a demographic divide between ageing, shrinking rich societies and population growth in poorer ones. Getting richer seems to mean lower fertility. The baby bust may indicate a wealthy country’s failure to reproduce itself socially as well as biologically. People ask not only whether they can afford children, but whether they fit in, can trust each other and believe in a future. This loss of confident belonging poses questions that politics across the rich world has yet to tackle.

The Crown Prosecution Service described James’s crimes as “a sustained pattern of predatory behaviour against children in her care” and praised the teenagers she targeted for coming forward.

During her trial at Winchester crown court, jurors were told that James, from Chippenham in Wiltshire, flirted with a 16-year-old boy in class at a school in Southampton.

They began exchanging Snapchat messages and arranged for her to drive him to a promenade, where they kissed in her car.

Later they went to her house where they cuddled while watching the Wimbledon tennis championships on the television before going to her bedroom where they had sex. She told him she loved him and wanted him to move away with her.

Edward Culver, prosecuting, told the trial the school was made aware of the incident after another student showed a teacher some text messages apparently sent between the James and the complainant.

He said: “They suggested a sexually charged relationship. He [the boy] was named as ‘number 8’ in the messages as a cover. She acted not only in an unprofessional and overfamiliar way, but failed to recognise any boundaries, exploiting her position to engage in sexual activity with one of her young students.”

In a police interview, the boy said he had been “groomed” by the defendant.

James was convicted of three counts of sexual activity with a child by a person in a position of trust.

Before the trial, James pleaded guilty to offences against two girls. One was a pupil at the same Southampton school as the boy, the other attended a school in Wiltshire that James had also taught at.

The offences included sexual activity with a child, sexual communication with a child and making an indecent photograph of a child. The victims were 13 and 14 at the time.

England bat Pakistan out of third Test before Robinson moves in for the kill

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 17:10:30 GMT

Brook, Lawrence and Smith miss out on centuries

Ollie Robinson takes two wickets in first over

Friday is the only sold-out day of this third Test but whether that translates into a full house remains to be seen. Much like the series itself, the contest is long since over, set in motion by Pakistan’s howling collapse on the first day and then compounded by England’s ruthlessness on the second.

Although for all that England’s march to a 3-0 clean sweep appears a formality, there should in theory be a decent chunk of cricket to enjoy. Joe Root’s side are still eight wickets away from enjoying a weekend at leisure, with Pakistan, set to resume on 52 for two, 268 runs away from making them bat again.

It follows a dominant outing with the bat from England that turned 156 for four in the morning into 453 all out by tea. That said, three men still trudged off despondently. Harry Brook needlessly ran himself out on 75, Dan Lawrence chopped on for 65, while Jamie Smith fell for 69 after batting through the pain of a suspected broken finger. In all three cases, a Test century went begging.

When Ollie Robinson, fresh from a trolley-dash half-century of his own, chugged in after tea and knocked over two batters in his first over, it looked like the match might be over in two days. Saim Ayub sent his first ball flying to Harry Brook at second slip to complete a pair for the parachuted-in opener, before Abdullah Shafique then gallingly feathered the fourth to Root at first slip.

The daft thing was this dramatic double-wicket maiden was not even Robinson’s best opening salvo of the summer, having knocked over three New Zealanders in his first over at Lord’s back in June. Swapping a few words with Shafique on departure, Robinson looked like a man in the mood for a quick kill.

As it was, rain that swept in from the west cut the evening session to only 12.4 overs and the final image of the day was not Robinson’s wild-eyed celebrations but the covers spread over the outfield. One chance did go down before they came on, however, with Shan Masood dropped by the diving Ben Duckett at third slip on 13.

That Root had returned to first slip to claim his 220th career catch – reclaiming the outfield record from Steve Smith in the process – may have been down to two drops by Duckett there on day one. Equally, it might have been a realisation that his bowlers no longer need his input from mid-off, such is their hold over Pakistan.

Although Gus Atkinson, the man denied by Duckett’s leaky buckets, could probably have done with Root’s arm around his shoulder. In a series where England’s quicks are chewing up their opponents like it is a speed-eating contest, Atkinson has somehow claimed one for 172. The poor bloke has bowled alright too.

Root will doubtless stress that the end result is everything, even if Brook, Lawrence and Smith were probably still chuntering about their dismissals as the team bus made its way back up the Pershore Road. England trowelled 143 runs on to their stash in the morning, 154 more after lunch. But unless something absurd happens, Duckett’s 113 at Trent Bridge in June will remain their only century this summer.

Brook was most culpable, adding 23 to his overnight 52 before setting off for a single that never was and throwing his bat in disgust when this was confirmed. The 27-year-old is England’s top scorer this summer, the only guy averaging over 40, and is the No 1-ranked batter in the world. But more than a year has passed since he last tasted three figures and the brain-fades are still a factor here.

That suicidal single off Ayub’s part-time off-spin was a bonus for Pakistan, likewise Lawrence’s playing on to hand the all-rounder Mohammad Imran his maiden Test wicket before lunch. The No 6 had been purring up to this point, whipping or driving his nine crisp fours during England’s sprightly start. Little wonder he let out an audible cry when he heard the stumps shatter behind him.

Unbeknown to all, Smith had suffered a finger injury on the opening day that later saw Jordan Cox deputise with the gloves. Emerging after the fall of Brook at 229 for five, Smith played and missed a bit early on but soon got going with some lusty blows off Ayub. In the end another promising innings was ended by a bit of nip and leading edge that the giant Razaullah gobbled up in his follow-through.

Pakistan’s sole bright spark on day one, Razaullah finished with four wickets in his first outing, even if 148 in the runs column from 23 overs underlined how raw he still is. The 21-year-old’s full-throated celebrations point to a fast bowler with fire in the belly, at least. Given his attributes – tall, strong, and whippy – Pakistan’s sorry tour may in time at least be remembered as the start of something significant.

With so much time left, there was no need for Root to even consider a declaration even after the tailenders started to appear. And in a rare period of afternoon sunshine, they made merry against weary bowlers. Robinson, 50 from 47 balls, and Jofra Archer, 32 not out from 27, certainly enjoyed themselves, both men launching the second new ball into a Hollies Stand that has been light on numbers this week.

Atkinson, 19 from 36 balls and a solid ally to Smith earlier, was therefore outdone by his peers with the bat too. Unlike the batters whose work is likely now done for the summer, at least he still has a chance to buff up those curious bowling figures when the third and likely final day begins.

The USA have won only once on European soil since 2007, when they triumphed in 2015. Eleven years have passed since “Gimme-gate” but Alison Lee’s reappearance in a United States team in Europe gives cause to reflect upon the chaos that unfolded in Germany. “It was a shell-shocking week for me,” Lee recalls.

This weekend, Lee will be the sole playing survivor from the US contingent in 2015. Back then, aged 20, she picked up her ball before the supposed formality of a concession from Europe. Suzann Pettersen seized upon the moment, claiming the hole for Europe amid tears and ferocious backlash. The USA had the last laugh, winning the Solheim Cup by one point as Pettersen spent the evening sobbing in a hotel room.

“I had been thrown into a team where I didn’t really know anyone very well,” says Lee. “I just felt really grateful that the team around me, the US team, were just so supportive of me. They had my back and they were so welcoming.

“All that stuff happened on Sunday morning because there was a delay and we had to finish the Saturday afternoon session in the morning. So we had a couple hours before singles where we all came together and I was very rattled, obviously, with everything that happened. I think everyone just saw me as a little sister and they just really cared for me. They not only wanted to win, for the US, but we wanted to win for each other. And so I feel like that meant a lot.

“I was so young. I remember just being on the team was such a cool thing to be a part of. Less than a year before that, I was watching them all on TV so I was a little scared to be on the team, to be honest. Winning was super special.”

Pettersen’s redemption came in 2019, when she holed the winning putt for Europe at Gleneagles before announcing her retirement. The French Football Federation’s president, Philippe Diallo, said Gianni Infantino had “seriously damaged the image and the unity of football” as he announced the end of France’s support for the Fifa president’s re-election.

The FFF’s executive committee unanimously voted on Thursday to withdraw its backing, which had been formalised at the end of June. Diallo referred to “events during the World Cup” which had “flagrantly gone against the way we believe our sport should be run” and to Infantino’s World Cup sell-off plan, which was revealed in July and scrapped after a widespread backlash.

During the World Cup the suspension of the US forward Folarin Balogun was overturned by Fifa after lobbying from Donald Trump. The US president said he called Infantino to recommend that Balogun be allowed to play. Fifa has said the decision taken by its disciplinary committee was “a balanced measure” and “based on an explicit provision of the applicable regulations”.

Diallo outlined the reasons for the loss in confidence: “From July onwards, the conditions which led to us to support his candidacy had been disrupted. Does the withdrawal of the [sell-off] project solve the issue? I don’t think so. His initiatives during and after the World Cup have seriously damaged the image and the unity of football. As a result, we believe that trust has been broken.”

Diallo said of the initial decision to support Infantino: “It would be wrong to say that certain developments in football were not made under his mandate.” But he added: “When you are making changes to the game itself, in a unilateral and opaque fashion to sell our shared asset, that changes our appreciation.

“France is one of the founding members of Fifa, and as such we have a historical legitimacy to intervene when we feel that Fifa and its president are deviating from our vision of how world football should be run. We also have sporting legitimacy, as one of the top three teams in the world rankings over the last 10 years. We wanted to make it clear that we refuse to go in a direction which does not correspond to the general interest of our sport.”

When reports of the sell-off project came to light, the FFF expressed “doubts and deep concerns”. Uefa threatened a boycott of Fifa competitions and several European countries, including Wales and England, withdrew their support for Infantino but the FFF had not until Thursday publicly disavowed him.

Diallo indicated France would play an active part in Uefa’s search for an alternative candidate for the Fifa presidency before the 18 November deadline. The election will take place in March during Fifa’s next congress.

Before then, Diallo said, the FFF would reach out to figures it considers experts in “transparency and good governance” in football and beyond as part of France’s “contribution to the debate”, as it pushes for “far-reaching reform” of Fifa.

‘I’ve got more of a sense of humour than Ralph Lauren’ – nine things we learned from Paul Smith’s new memoir

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 17:00:41 GMT

He put personality into boxers, collaborated with the pope (sort of) and is to thank for novelty socks. The British designer’s new book reveals there’s more to Smith than his stripes

In July, the British designer Paul Smith celebrated his 80th birthday and he has now released a memoir to mark the occasion. Threads: My Life in Style tells Smith’s story, from growing up in Nottingham and leaving school with no qualifications to selling suits to celebs, including Gary Oldman and David Bowie.

Here are nine of our favourite lesser-known takeaways from the book.

1. He made boxers something you want to be seen inIn the 70s, Smith reimagined boxers in clashing prints and colours, such as polka dots and stripes rather than drab greys and whites, catapulting them from the back of the underwear drawer to the pages of fashion magazines. “I always describe my early success as nudging rather than shoving the British male into appreciating the fact that you could be a little different,” he writes.

2. He has a love/hate relationship with stripesSmith describes the multi-stripe he has become synonymous with as “both a joy and a curse”. It was a design detail forced upon him in his early days due to budget constraints, but quickly became popular among his customers. “It began to take on a life of its own,” Smith writes. However, it “became a bit of a burden to me if to no one else. You meet people who say, ‘Oh, you’re the one who’s famous for the stripes.’ It’s like being Calvin Klein – you can make beautiful clothes every year but someone will always say, ‘Oh, you’re the one who makes underpants.’ You find yourself having to work around it.”

3. He’s to blame for the rise of novelty socks

In the 1980s, Smith says men only bought two types of socks: plain or argyle patterned. After coming across a pair with a paperclip motif in Japan, he brought the design to the UK. Now he sells more than 700,000 pairs of socks a year. “Quite often when I’m introduced to someone new he’ll say, ‘Oh yes – I get your socks for Christmas,’” Smith writes.

4. His office is the original example of curated chaosPiles of vinyl records, 28 bicycles (including the yellow Pinarello Chris Froome rode to victory in the Tour de France), a model train set, hundreds of books and oil paintings and a Snoopy telephone are just some of the curiosities you’ll find in Smith’s office. And then there are the rabbit figurines in all shapes and sizes, the result of a joke, which got out of hand, about how they were his lucky charm. “Every week I get rabbits of all kinds,” writes Smith. “They’re everywhere. Rabbits made of bronze, felt, plastic, wood, stone. A man in Italy sends me four or five a month, even though I’ve never met him.”

5. David Bowie hated small talk

Bowie became a big fan of Smith’s two-piece suits, including one in a lemon and pink overcheck. After turning up to the store unannounced several times to shop, Smith invited him for a cup of tea in his studio. It was the beginning of a friendship. Bowie never called Smith by his first name – instead, it was always Smithy. “Was he an easy person to be with and to talk to? Only if you were interesting,” writes Smith. “There was no small talk.”

6. He accidentally created Instabait

Even if you’ve never been to LA, you’ll probably recognise Smith’s Melrose Avenue store. Five years after it opened in 2005, Instagram launched and the store’s hot-pink wall became a selfie sensation. There have been thousands of snaps taken at the #pinkwall, making it one of the most Instagrammed buildings in California.

7. He’s not keen on comparisons to Ralph Lauren Smith describes getting “pissed off” in his early days when the press kept comparing him to the American designer, and renowned anglophile, Ralph Lauren. “I’ve got far more of a sense of humour, for a start,” he writes. “His shops were always so serious, with the stately-home image and the good-looking models. There was nobody that English in England.”

Sign up to Fashion Statement

Style, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solved

after newsletter promotion

8. He collaborated with Pope Francis (sort of)

As a huge cycling enthusiast (he hoped to become a pro until he had a nasty accident aged 17), Smith was thrilled to be asked to design the leaders’ jerseys for the annual Giro d’Italia bike race in 201. It included the “maglia rosa”, a pink jersey that is (sort of) equivalent to the Tour de France’s yellow jersey. Smith added some red piping around the edge, signature striping on the left sleeve and a tiny sketch of a cyclist. It was sent to Pope Francis to be blessed. Smith writes: “I’ve done a lot of collaborations over the years, from cars to crayons, from carpets to cycles, but only one of them, so far as I’m aware, has been personally blessed by the pope.”

9. Despite all his success, he remains a doerCase in point, during lockdown Smith continued to work from his office, albeit alone. One day he was met by an unpleasant smell and discovered that 18 containers of forgotten milk had exploded all over the kitchen floor. He spent three hours cleaning it up. At one stage he found himself thinking: “I wonder if my friend Giorgio Armani is doing something like this now?” Still, when Smith told colleagues about his wiping marathon, “they all said the same thing: ‘Oh no! Only Paul Smith.’ And I took that as a compliment.”

Shabana Mahmood urges police to curb far-right, anti-migrant protests

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 16:51:07 GMT

Home secretary tells officers to make ‘full use’ of their powers after masked vigilantes cause weekend of chaos

Shabana Mahmood has urged police to curb the activities of far-right, anti-migrant groups which have “obvious malign intent” after a weekend of chaos caused by balaclava-wearing vigilantes.

In a meeting on Thursday, the home secretary told senior officers to make “full use” of their powers, including bans on face coverings, after police were assaulted and ports were disrupted in Kent and Hampshire.

She signalled the need for “strong deterrence” and improved intelligence in light of new tactics being deployed by groups such as Patriot Platform, led by the convicted kidnapper Daniel Thomas, which helped to organise the protests.

Mahmood told the officers: “These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents. This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons.”

The Home Office and police were criticised in the aftermath of the weekend for failing to take a hard line on the far right. Environmental campaigners and civil liberties groups have complained that there appears to be a “two-tier” approach, with peaceful climate protesters prosecuted more aggressively than far-right agitators.

Police in Dover on Saturday and then Portsmouth on Sunday were taken by surprise when hundreds of protesters wearing black clothes and face masks massed to oppose what they say is illegal immigration via small boats.

Both protests are believed by police to have been far-right inspired, with evidence emerging that those behind them were determined to avoid detection.

Thursday’s online meeting was held ahead of this weekend, when further disruption is predicted to take place.

Mahmood told senior officers to make better use of intelligence to ensure they have the correct resources and expertise in place, and made clear the government’s expectation that police should make full use of the powers at their disposal to ensure anyone who is committing a criminal offence is dealt with “robustly”.

The home secretary urged police to make full use of digital evidence, including body-worn video, facial recognition technology, CCTV, ANPR and other intelligence products to identify offenders.

The move raises the possibility that Hampshire police will insist that protesters due to meet in Portsmouth at 12.30pm on Saturday will be ordered to take off any face coverings.

Forces have planned an “enhanced and coordinated approach to intelligence gathering and operational planning” ahead of the weekend – laying the groundwork for a more proactive response.

Labour’s Crime and Policing Act, which took effect in April, gave police powers to create mask-free zones at protests, backed by fines of up to £1,000 or one month’s imprisonment, or both.

The power only applies to people who are trying to conceal their identity, rather than those covering their face for reasons of religion, health or work, and officers must take reasonable steps to notify the public of the restriction.

Saturday’s protests in Dover, which Thomas claimed to have organised, blocked the town’s roads for several hours, disrupting traffic heading to and from the port.

Kent police initially claimed that they had no warning of the Dover protest. That claim fell apart when the force admitted there were warning calls to police on Friday evening which were not acted upon.

Commenting after the meeting, the deputy chief constable Andy Mariner, the NPCC lead for public order, said: “Policing is continually assessing and preparing for protests and any potential impact on public safety. This includes working closely with local forces, specialist teams, communities and partners, monitoring publicly available information, and ensuring the right resources are available where needed.

“We have stepped up this activity this week at a national level, supporting local forces to ensure we have the right information, support and operational capacity in place to respond should we need to.

Visitors got a first glimpse of the medieval artefact after it went on display at the British Museum in London

On the day Bayeux tapestry tickets were released, Megan Stockwell was at the beach. She was so determined to lock down her spot, that she sat with her toes in the sand for an hour, waiting in the online queue.

“The whole ticket buying experience felt like what other people would do to get Taylor Swift tickets. I was like, ‘oh God, am I, like, the geek version of this?’” she recalled.

Like any committed Swiftie, Stockwell felt confident the experience would be worth the hassle and cost. As a self-professed Francophile, she was fascinated by how the tapestry, which is temporarily housed at the British Museum until next July, tells the story of the Franco-British relationship through the Norman conquest, culminating in the battle of Hastings.

“You just grow up learning so much about it – at primary school, in history studies. You’ve always got some mention of the Bayeux tapestry, the Normans, the fact there’s even three lions on the back of our pound coins comes from Normandy.

“We’ve got such a close connection between French and British culture, our language and everything. This sort of feels like a visual representation of that,” she said.

Stockwell’s dogged pursuit of tickets, fascination with the Franco-British relationship, and childhood memories of learning about the battle of Hastings, were experiences shared by many of the visitors on the exhibition’s opening day.

Cydney, who lives in Texas, also drew inspiration from her experience queueing for concert tickets to secure a coveted opening day spot. She had woken up at 3am local time to join an online queue for an hour and half to secure them when they were released.

She anticipated it would be worth it: “It’s going to be life-changing, we’re so excited.”

Cydney had studied history for her undergraduate degree. “So I just really am interested to see what a significant artefact would be and to see how this is basically where the history of England and the UK as we know it really all began. Seeing something so old is just incredible and honestly such an honour.”

Her feelings were echoed by Adrian Harris, who was so moved to catch the exhibition that he signed up for British Museum membership purposely to gain early access to tickets. He ended up the second person through the doors on Thursday morning, after joining a “really jolly” queue at 9.30am.

“It was incredible. It was very, very moving to walk down the steps and to see the length and breadth of it. And I think they’ve done it so well, the British Museum. It was very profound to see it,” he said, adding he had been especially thrilled to spy Westminster Abbey, where he works, on the cloth.

He noted that although he was one of the first through the doors, he felt that 40 minutes was a restricted timeframe to see the 68-metre tapestry, though he observed that attendants were diligent in ushering people along.

A number of ticket holders for the Bayeux tapestry at a special first viewing last weekend were reportedly turned away after other visitors took too long to view it. The French owners of the tapestry have issued strict orders on when lights must be turned off in order to preserve the work.

Richard and Madeleine Abramson, who were in the first group alongside visitors dressed in Norman costumes, agreed that 40 minutes was a short time, but that it was being well policed. “They’re very clear at the beginning there’s a maximum time … they’re very carefully moving you on,” said Madeleine.

However, the oversight did not dampen the pair’s enthusiasm. “It was pretty awe-inspiring,” said Richard. “It’s very well presented, it develops like a film. It’s got a story to tell: it starts quietly, then it gets more intrigue and then you get to the action and it builds up to the battle, which is quite violent.”

Madeleine felt the tapestry loomed large for many former English schoolchildren. “Of all the history lessons you have, every child remembers 1066,” she said, adding that the fact the tapestry was woven by female embroiderers also resonated. “[That they] told this whole story is still phenomenal,” she said.

Vivien and Karen had travelled from Hampshire to see the tapestry, also buoyed up by memories of their school days. “We learned about it at school. It’s something that’s always been in the back of your mind, then all of a sudden it’s here, so why not?” said Karen.

The hospitality industry fears a tourist tax will deter visitors – the evidence says otherwise

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 16:37:25 GMT

Studies from hotspots across Europe that have introduced levies suggest they have no impact on visitor numbers

If you wandered down Las Ramblas or lazed on a beach in the Balearics this summer, you probably paid a tourist tax for the privilege. In fact, if you enjoyed any of Europe’s beauty spots in recent years, it is likely that an overnight levy was added to your bill.

Britons have become used to paying these fees abroad but ministers have shied away from introducing them in the UK. The furious response from UK hospitality bosses helps to explain why.

The trade body UKHospitality estimates that a 5% tax on overnight stays in England would result in 12m fewer visits and 33,000 job losses, piling further pressure on an industry battling an increase in taxes and employment costs, as well as the effects of war, Covid and Brexit.

In places like the Lake District and the Yorkshire Dales, which rely heavily on tourism, businesses are concerned that visitors will instead go to other parts of the country that choose not to impose such a levy.

Large parts of England’s east coast, for example – from the seaside resort of Skegness to the town of Hartlepool – are expected to remain levy-free after their mayors, from Reform UK and the Conservative party, opposed the proposals on Thursday.

But are overnight levies a success? The evidence suggests that it depends what mayors want to achieve, but they could be very lucrative.

They were introduced in cities including Amsterdam, Barcelona and Venice as a way to prevent over-tourism. But there is little evidence they kept visitors at bay: trips to all three destinations have risen consistently over the past decade (despite Amsterdam charging an additional 12.5% for an overnight stay, believed to be the most expensive tourist tax in Europe).

In April 2023, Manchester became the first place in the UK to introduce an overnight visitor levy, charging £1 per room per night in the city centre. A study published in the journal Tourism Management in 2025 found that the tax had had “no significant impact” on the occupancy of hotels in the city.

In sharp contrast to the vocal opposition of national trade bodies, in Manchester it was hospitality businesses that introduced the levy through a business improvement district.

Local leaders say the £1-a-night levy has raised £10.5m in its first three years of operation, with the revenue ringfenced for cultural projects such as the Brit awards and Mobo awards, both hosted in Manchester this year.

When Labour MPs visit Liverpool for their party conference later this month, they too will be paying a tourist tax: a £2-a-night charge was introduced by its hospitality firms last June, raising more than £2m for projects in sports, culture and conferencing.

Councils in Scotland already have the power to introduce local overnight levies, with Wales following suit next April.

Only Edinburgh has taken the plunge so far, introducing a 5% tourist tax on 24 July, although Cardiff, Glasgow and three other regions of Scotland are expected to follow next year.

Allen Simpson, chief executive of UKHospitality, said on Thursday that Edinburgh’s new charge was “already having damaging effects” on the city.

after newsletter promotion

However, Edinburgh Tourism Action Group, which represents the city’s tourism industry, told the Guardian it was “too early to draw any meaningful conclusions” on its impact. It said many of the cities that had adopted the scheme, including Manchester, had “not experienced a decline in visitor numbers” as a result.

While there is little detailed international research on the economic impact of tourist taxes, a study by Bangor University in Wales in 2024 found no evidence to suggest they deter visitors.

Researchers found they had been introduced in 125 destinations and 26 countries across Europe by 2019, with exceptions mainly in the Nordics and Baltic region. The modest nightly charges were being used to fund hundreds of millions of pounds worth of public projects, they found.

In the Balaeric Islands, for example, the tourism tax had funded €263m (£226m) worth of projects since 2016, including social housing and scientific research.

Zoë Billingham, the chief executive of IPPR North, a thinktank which has campaigned for a tourist tax, said it was wrong to assume that the entire hospitality industry was against the move, pointing to Manchester and Liverpool, where local businesses led the charge.

She added: “With climate change and other uncertainties in the world, I would expect visitor numbers in the UK to increase – that’s not just domestic holidays, but also people from other countries coming here. This is a real way to share in the benefits of tourism growth in this country.”

Henri Murison, chief executive of the business lobby group Northern Powerhouse Partnership, said there was little evidence tourists would be put off by an extra few pounds on their hotel bill.

“The current system, where all the tax paid by businesses goes to central government and none of it benefits the destination, is wrong. It’s just wrong,” he said.

What internal exclusion really means for school pupils

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 16:13:41 GMT

Readers respond to a report that said use of the disciplinary measure had almost tripled in England’s secondary schools

Your article quotes Tom Bennett, “a leading expert in behaviour management”, suggesting that internal exclusions are “a form of inclusion” (‘Internal exclusion’ of England secondary school students almost triples in three years, 3 September). That does not reflect my own experience. If a student is internally excluded, it must be as a last resort. I spent several months in the isolation room at my secondary school, and it didn’t feel inclusive to me.

Like many of the students disproportionately affected by internal exclusion, I was from a disadvantaged background. I also had undiagnosed dyslexia. For me, internal exclusion meant I was unable to learn alongside other students – I’d simply get a printed handout from a teacher of the lesson notes and was told to read them.

I finished my education in a pupil referral unit, but was able to go on to college thanks to the support of one of my teachers, who also mentored me. I am now in my final year of studying neuroscience at university, and I am working as a youth adviser with Lewis Hamilton’s charity, Mission 44. We are calling for internal exclusion to be properly recorded and scrutinised, alongside suspensions and permanent exclusions.

Schools must also have sufficient resources and clear guidance on what good internal exclusion looks like, as well as how to address the causes of poor behaviour, so they can intervene before a young person reaches crisis point and is removed from the classroom. Faysal YusufLondon

You have to experience being in a classroom when significant disruption takes place. It is devastating. It wrecks the learning of the pupils who want to learn. It ruins the confidence of teachers who want to impart a love of their subject and enable their pupils to progress. It takes up valuable senior leadership time when a pupil has to be extracted. Dysregulated and verbally or physically disruptive children are not the product of schools. They are often the product of severely challenged family units.

In such cases, internal isolation, as a strategy, has the best outcome. Pupils and teachers can resume learning and teaching in a calm atmosphere. The internally isolated pupil has a chance to recognise what triggered their outburst, and can resume learning in a fresh classroom climate that can include attention to their specific needs. And they are still safe on the school premises.

Authorities and commentators should therefore not start to demonise internal isolations in schools without examining the deep-rooted socioeconomic and political causes behind them. Jo WestFormer secondary school headteacher, Virginia Water, Surrey

Imagine if, at work today, you had to commit at all times to looking at the boss (never out of the window or at the floor), to nodding, to walking corridors in silence and to asking questions at least five times a day. Pupils in secondary schools can be banished to internal detention for failing to do these things, among other reasons.

The government’s special educational needs and disabilities reforms are based on making mainstream schools more inclusive. To achieve that, it must accept that the tyranny of rigid, non-evidenced rules does not work for 21st-century children. That doesn’t mean a reduction in standards – it means better and less harmful interventions to manage behaviour. Jane HarrisVice-chair, Disabled Children’s Partnership

We were pleased to see you draw the public’s attention to the new data showing that poorer pupils and those with special educational needs and disabilities are disproportionately affected by internal exclusions in secondary schools.

We are very concerned that the government remains mute on this and is not doing more to promote practices that are trauma-informed and grounded in modern neuroscience. Some schools are already managing to do this, investing in staff training to use relational and restorative approaches that balance both high challenge and high support. Plenty of organisations are ready to provide this training.

But real change needs leadership from the very top of government. Too often, poor behaviour is still seen as deliberate defiance for its own sake. We need to see it instead as a symptom of a system that fails to promote empathy, understanding and taking responsibility for how our actions affect others. Ben HarperPeacebuilding in schools coordinator, Quakers in Britain

Highs and lows of Keir Starmer’s time in office

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 16:13:29 GMT

Warren Brown lists some of the former PM’s achievements, but Stuart Finegan signals deep disappointment with his legacy

Zoe Williams may be right to describe Keir Starmer as a poor politician, but what did we expect (Farewell Keir Starmer, a terrible politician whom we desperately wanted to be something more, 2 September)? After 14 years of economic stagnation and a succession of career politicians as prime minister, we had a leader who previously had a proper job and career outside politics. Starmer’s legacy might be to demonstrate why we need to invest in a better cadre of skilled professional politicians.

Those still pining for Starmer may remind us of achievements such as removing the two-child limit on universal benefit, more free school meals, Best Start family hubs, greater employment rights, increases in the minimum wage, renters’ rights, more GPs, lower waiting lists, the Hillsborough law, better relations with Europe etc. But they shouldn’t bother – no one was listening then, and they certainly aren’t now.

However, history might record his period in office as the first time the cabinet were nearly all state-educated – a massive achievement, for which he deserves our gratitude. Warren BrownIlkley, West Yorkshire

Zoe Williams rightly highlights the deep disappointment many people feel about Keir Starmer’s political legacy. For a politician who promised principle and integrity, he too often appeared willing to abandon commitments when they became politically inconvenient.

His stance on Israel’s war in Gaza remains one of the clearest examples. Rather than showing moral leadership and clearly condemning the suffering of Palestinian civilians, Starmer seemed reluctant to challenge Israel’s actions, leaving many questioning where his principles truly lay.

Equally troubling was his approach to criticism. Many longstanding Labour supporters, including elderly members who opposed the war, felt ignored or dismissed. Leadership requires engagement with dissent, not contempt for it.

Starmer also struggled to connect with the public. In an age that values truth and conviction, he often appeared scripted and detached. It frequently felt as though he was delivering the conclusions of advisers rather than expressing his own beliefs.

Beyond returning Labour to government, it is difficult to identify a lasting achievement. He may ultimately be remembered not as a leader, but as a manager of other people’s ideas. Stuart FineganLewes, East Sussex

Sailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln had it a lot easier than Nelson’s crews

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 16:13:24 GMT

American sailors who were at sea for 286 days really have nothing to complain about, insists Chris Hardy

You report (4 September) that sailors from the USS Abraham Lincoln spent a “record uninterrupted 286 days at sea”. That’s nowhere near a record: Nelson and his fleet blockaded Toulon for two years, 1803-05, without going ashore.

The American sailors complain about the food on their carrier; Nelson’s ships were exposed to terrible weather in which they pitched and rolled violently, and were cold, wet and plagued by rats. No electricity, let alone fridges; they ate salt pork and rock-hard bread full of weevils, drank green water, and every so often fought a battle or sailed to the Caribbean and back.

Apparently the Americans are behaving respectably in the red-light port of Pattaya, Thailand. That’s another difference: the British sailors certainly did not when they came back to Portsmouth and were given two years’ pay in cash. Chris HardyWest Wittering, West Sussex

Trump promise of $5,000 for US citizens after midterms decried as ‘bribery’

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 16:13:11 GMT

Critics react to bid for Republican votes with incredulity and point to potential $1.2tn cost atop existing national debt

Donald Trump’s promise of a $5,000 “Trump dividend” for every US citizen if Republicans retain control of the US Congress in November’s midterm elections has sparked incredulity and accusations of bribery.

“If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000,” Trump said during the unprecedented Republican midterm convention in Dallas. “It will be called the Trump dividend.”

It comes amid extreme concern over the US national debt, which exceeded $40tn for the first time in August.

Speaking to Politico, Chip Roy, the Republican US representative from Texas, sounded skeptical. “Well – I would like to know how they would plan to pay for … back of envelope … well over $1tn,” he said.

In the moments after Trump made the announcement, Marc Goldwein of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget wrote on X that “this would cost about $1.2 TRILLION in just one year. That’s more than ALL THREE ROUNDS of COVID relief checks, despite no recessions. The result would be a huge spike in the deficit, and almost certainly in the inflation rate.”

The US has roughly 240 million adult citizens, suggesting the cost of $1.2tn. The federal government spent about $7tn in fiscal year 2025, with about $2tn taken on as debt.

“The 10-year [treasury bond is] approaching 5%,” Goldwein said on Thursday morning. “Inflation is not under control. We spend more on interest than we spend on defense or on Medicare at this point. Social security is six years from insolvency. Just about the last thing we need is to borrow another trillion dollars to send checks to everybody.”

Spending like this risked an economic sugar high followed by a recessionary crash, he said. But Goldwein was most concerned about what might happen if Trump’s gambit is effective.

“If this works, the lesson for every future politician is going to be: if you want to win an election, promise a trillion dollars. And multiply a trillion dollars times the number of elections we have coming up, that is a recipe for bankruptcy.”

Democratic political leaders reacted with blunt condemnation.

“After making you sicker and poorer with his war, Donald Trump now wants to buy your vote with $5,000 in taxpayer-funded blood money,” the California governor, Gavin Newsom, said. “The most corrupt man ever to occupy the Oval Office.”

The Democratic National Committee (DNC) pointed to Trump’s record on similar pledges, from $5,000 stimulus checks as a result of the work of the so-called department of government efficiency (Doge) to $2,000 stimulus checks from revenue from tariffs.

“Donald Trump and Republicans are once again offering empty promises to Americans,” said Kendall Witmer, the committee’s rapid response director. “The only people reaping the benefits of Trump’s economy are himself, his family, and his ultra-rich elite donors. Meanwhile, working families get nothing except sky-high receipts at the grocery store and the pump, unaffordable healthcare premiums, and wages that aren’t keeping up with inflation.”

The Bipartisan Policy Center has been tracking tariff revenue since Trump began raising rates in 2025. As of 8 September, the US has collected about $210bn in tariff and excise tax revenue in 2026. At a rate of $21bn a month, the US federal government would have to collect tariffs for nearly five years to cover a $5,000 payment, assuming every dollar of tariff revenue went to the payment, and discounting tariff payments refunded to retailers in legal challenges.

Peter Schiff, chief economist for Euro Pacific Asset Management, said that Trump’s pledge had already begun rippling through financial markets.

“Even though bond investors know that, even in the unlikely event Republicans retain control of the House, Trump’s promise to borrow over $1 trillion more to buy votes won’t be kept,” Schiff wrote in a post on X. “The promise itself is so reckless that they’re dumping Treasuries, sending yields to new highs …

“Making his promise even worse, Trump referred to his $5,000 bribes as ‘dividends’, as if his policies had been so successful that the US now has surpluses to share. Instead, his reckless policies have produced massive deficits. Trump needs to send Americans bills, not checks.”

JD Vance appeared to walk back Trump’s pledge, suggesting that the benefit would be means-tested.

But the US senator Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, promised support for Trump’s idea. “I will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election,” Moreno wrote on X.

Hamilton confirms no rules of engagement at Ferrari despite Monza clash with Leclerc

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 16:12:40 GMT

‘When I was at Mercedes we had written rules’

British driver held positive talks with teammate

Lewis Hamilton has said there remain no rules of engagement between the drivers at Ferrari, despite the 41-year-old calling for the team to employ them after he clashed with his teammate, Charles Leclerc, at the last round in Monza.

Hamilton was forced wide by Leclerc at turn two on the opening lap at the Italian Grand Prix, which he felt had been unacceptable. Speaking before the first meeting for the Spanish Grand Prix at the new Madring circuit in Madrid this weekend, Leclerc admitted he had been at fault and Hamilton said the pair had talked frankly and cleared the air in a forthright fashion.

In Monza Hamilton had unfavourably compared Ferrari to his former team Mercedes, stating: “When I was at Mercedes we had written rules of engagement. Here there are no rules. That’s something that needs to probably change.”

Hamilton noted that he had positive discussions with the team principal, Fred Vasseur, but when asked if there was an agreement on rules of engagement between the two drivers, he was unequivocal. “There was not,” he said. “I’m sure at some stage we’ll discuss how we can be better, but we’ve not had a lot of time to just turn around. You can’t change things in two days.”

The seven-time champion said in Monza he believed Leclerc had forced him off track and pointedly noted that he had always tried to race cleanly. In Madrid Leclerc took responsibility for what happened. “I obviously know I went too far in turn two,” he said. “I said it to Lewis and I think it’s very clear what we should do or should avoid going forward.”

Hamilton praised his teammate’s attitude in clearing up the issues. “What’s great is that there was no shying away from having a discussion,” he said. “We sat face to face, just him and I, talked about it and we were just both open and honest. We squashed it and we can move on.

“That shows the maturity from him. I think it’s healthy. It’s a relationship we have built over time. I’m sure there’ll be more times where we’re close because we’re very close in pace. We both want to win just as much as each other and we both want to do well for the team as well. But it’s real positive.”

The race in Monza was won by Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli, who now leads Hamilton, who is third in the championship, by 76 points, a gap the British driver conceded was all but unbridgeable. He had also called on Ferrari to make changes to sharpen procedures and execution, operationally and strategically, after Monza to maximise potential points but conceded that it would not be achievable overnight.

Don’t sashay away! The BBC’s decision to cancel Ru Paul’s Drag Race UK is sickening in all the wrong ways

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 15:25:17 GMT

The hyper-flamboyant and hilariously filthy show is an inclusive, celebratory platform for queer culture. The broadcaster’s choice to nix it is giving stupidity

The BBC is canning RuPaul’s Drag Race UK – a decision that, in my household, will bring the number of regularly watched programmes on the Beeb down from one to zero. It’s a decision that will no doubt please enemies of LGBTQ+ culture, but otherwise seems inexplicable. For a start, Drag Race UK regularly pulls in 1 million viewers a week, which hardly seems like a show in its death throes (even if this is down from a previous high of 1.5 million).

RuPaul’s Drag Race is also a bona fide cultural phenomenon. Since the US version started in 2009, it has brought tons of performers to national, or even global, attention who would otherwise still be plying their trade in provincial gay bars. Jinkx Monsoon from the US is now starring in Oh Mary! in London’s West End; the UK’s La Voix made it on to Strictly; and Bimini Bon-Boulash, who “stepped their pussy up” to astonishing effect in season two, has made records, modelled and written a book.

More importantly, the show gave a TV platform to ballroom culture – the New York City-born tradition in which impoverished, young, largely Black and brown gay men and trans women, usually ostracised by their families, formed their own “houses” and transformed themselves into the glamorous characters they dreamed of being. Ballroom culture gave the world vogueing, the documentary Paris is Burning, and a whole argot which, more than 30 years on from its popularisation in the film, is mainstream. “It’s giving”, “she’s serving”, “throwing shade”, “spilling the tea”, looking “snatched”. We’ll never know what the queens who invented this lingo would think of its incredible resilience, since they perished in the Aids crisis.

RuPaul’s Drag Race UK fused this underground culture with Britain’s venerable drag tradition to often hilarious effect. Who could forget characters like the acid-tongued, high fashion queen A’Whora from season two, whose comedy routine was so filthy it managed to make judge Alan Carr wince? Or Cheddar Gorgeous, the historically minded and hugely articulate queen from season four, whose Act Up themed costume I last spotted on display in Manchester’s Whitworth gallery? Or even Nyongbella from season seven, delightfully random and usually almost naked, strutting her stuff on the BBC in defiance of her disapproving relatives in Cameroon, where gay sex can get you a five-year jail sentence? In what other context would such characters have made it on to the BBC?

That’s not to mention the amazingly high-profile celebrity guests (Andrew Garfield, Mel B and Michaela Coel have all served), and the always-fabulous judges Michelle Visage, Graham Norton and Carr. There is also, of course, the positive impact on scared young LGBTQ+ people on seeing out gay and trans folk living their best lives on screen, working – or rather werking – hard and being unapologetically themselves. Isn’t that something worth preserving?

Along with the girl group challenges, Snatch Game episodes and spectacular looks, Drag Race UK has seen its contestants discuss their experiences of being non-binary or living with HIV. And while, as a cynical Briton, I often cringe at the climactic moment when the queens who make it to the final talk tearfully to pictures of themselves as children, it’s a reminder that self-acceptance is something many LGBTQ+ people still struggle to achieve, especially in the midst of the current global backlash against our hard-won rights.

Prudes and homophobes might say that BBC licence-payers don’t want to pay for a bunch of drag queens telling filthy jokes and bitching about one another on the small screen. Well, I also pay the TV licence fee and I do. It doesn’t seem much to ask that, as a gay person, I get one programme on iPlayer that is unabashedly queer – especially since the BBC also canned I Kissed a Boy and I Kissed a Girl for bad measure. As the arts editor of the Guardian, I guess I could watch the BBC’s amazing slate of arts programmes – were it not for the fact that most of them have also long been chopped.

Drag Race UK has an ardent fanbase of all backgrounds and generations. Of course, not everyone in the LGBTQ+ community likes it – Travis Alabanza’s play The Sound of the Underground entertainingly railed against it – but it has expanded its definition of drag considerably, featuring trans and one female performer among the legions of cis gay men. A contestant in season one even had a girlfriend at the time – and if that’s not inclusion, what is? BBC, RuPaul’s Drag Race UK should not be allowed to sashay away.

Tschabalala Self’s Lady in Blue review – this striding scupture fills the fourth plinth with humour and life

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 15:09:09 GMT

Trafalgar Square, LondonThe swaggering statue’s luscious collision of brown and blue could stop traffic – and serves as a reminder of the big, beautiful, multicultural world we enjoy

It hit me like a thunder clap. One moment I was bored and irritated by the official speeches before the unveiling of Tschabalala Self’s sculpture on the fourth plinth, which so insisted on its sociopolitical worth it sounded like Soviet propaganda. Then the covering slid off and I was in love with the Lady in Blue.

Self has created one of the most beautiful sculptures put on Trafalgar Square’s empty plinth – and I don’t mean that in a cool, formalist way. There is a serious danger of traffic accidents as drivers passing the square stare a little too long at the Lady’s generous proportions, her long stride in platform shoes, her intensely physical, confident being.

Lady in Blue brilliantly exploits the potential of the long rectangular plinth, built in 1841 for an equestrian statue that was never erected, to encompass a lolloping human gait. This is a homage to walking, and to Umberto Boccioni’s futurist strider Unique Forms of Continuity in Space, with Self’s figure extrapolated upward from her wide and fast walk, a massive curved leg thrusting forward out of her draping blue skirt, her head held high, but not absurdly high.

This is no colossus but a statue that takes its scale and life from the surrounding city. There, I’ve said it: statue. The most memorable works on the fourth plinth, ever since it became a site for temporary art works back in 1999, have usually been human figures. To Mark Wallinger’s Ecce Homo and Marc Quinn’s Alison Lapper Pregnant, we can now add Self’s Lady as proof that what we really want and maybe need to see on a plinth is the human form, alive, profound and sexual.

What you first notice is the sheen of this polychrome woman: sunlight glints on her polished, plasticky surface as if she were covered from head to toe in nail varnish. Then your eyes adjust to the glare and you feel the luscious collision of brown flesh and heavenly blue. The blue is that of lapis lazuli, the rare mineral mined in Afghanistan that for millennia was coveted for jewellery and, then, for the most ethereal and expensive painter’s blue: ultramarine.

It connects Lady in Blue with the paintings in the National Gallery behind it, many of which use ultramarine, maybe most of all with Bronzino’s brazenly erotic Allegory With Venus and Cupid, which sets hard flesh against silky blue. Self’s statue has the same provocatively fetishistic power.

But this Lady is not a vulnerable object of anyone’s gaze. She swaggers in space with commanding girth, her bottom facing the National Gallery with flamboyant magnificence. This is the opposite of smooth classicism or catwalk perfection. In fact, it may be the opposite of traditional western sculpture. For all its apparent simplicity, Self’s figure seems rooted in African wood carvings, with their free transformations of the human body. On top of that is a head whose beauty and grace recall the bronze faces of the medieval queens of Ife.

Lady in Blue appears at the heart of a London where we’ve seen Tommy Robinson supporters march for a mono-racial, white nationalist UK. For all my impatience, it’s hard to disagree with the speeches at the unveiling – that we urgently need to uphold diversity and equality and reject intolerance.

The question is how a work of art can help. Just putting up a positive image of a Black woman won’t silence racists, and might even offer them another horrible talking point in the culture wars. But Self’s achievement goes beyond good intentions. You can view it as a seductive and funny comment on our big, beautiful, multicultural world.

Or you can just enjoy Lady in Blue aesthetically as a stonking sculpture that manages to meld multiple art histories to fill the fourth plinth with humour, fun and life. This is a carnivalesque masterpiece. But in a frightening world it also throws us a lifeline, something human to hold on to.
