I turned off my algorithm for 24 hours. Is this how social media used to be?

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 15:00:43 GMT

Thanks to a little-known feature in Instagram, I try to travel back to 2012 – before everything on the internet was an ad

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

I have a confession. I love my social media algorithm. It is a perfectly curated window into my insane and inquiring mind. It knows precisely which videos will tickle me and which memes will gently distract me from the slow collapse of humankind.

On Tuesday the Australian government announced “world-leading” reforms that would force social media platforms to allow users to opt-out of algorithms, dubbed “my feed, my way”. On the same day, I was delighted to be confronted with a video on Instagram of a woman accidentally spilling a bucket of eels on a Chinese train. Dozens of eels slithered among the passengers, who appeared not as surprised as I would have expected.

In bed that night, after sending the video to several friends and watching it multiple times, I lamented to my partner how I would find content like this if my accounts weren’t at the whim of the algorithm gods. “You can still search for eels,” he said. But would it be the same?

So, for 24 hours, I decided to manually turn off my algorithm via little-known settings on Instagram to get a sense of how the reforms might change my feed. This feature allows you to limit your feed to posts from accounts you are following, in chronological order. This is basically what social media feeds, including Facebook, looked like when they started.

Would I be thrust back into the old days of social media, to how things were before artificial intelligence and Elon Musk bought Twitter and everything became an ad?

As a reminder of how things used to be, I scroll back to my first posts on Instagram and find sepia-heavy pictures of trees, gigs and friends. “The SKY,” says one, simply showing a sunset.

I am gripped with nostalgia for 2012, when all my posts got eight likes and no comments and I only followed two dozen close friends from school.

For a truly “authentic” social media experience, I trawl through my contacts and unfollow any account that isn’t a person I have met in real life. It is refreshing to unfollow news accounts, and politicians, but sad to let go of funny influencers and meme accounts and chefs.

“Goodbye, Ottolenghi,” I think wistfully. “Farewell, woman from Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders.” In total, about 100 accounts get the axe. I refresh my feed, and it only takes about 10 minutes of scrolling to run out of content to look at.

For the first time in years, Instagram informs me I have reached the “End of following”. “There are no more posts from accounts that you follow from the past 30 days,” it says.

I am floored and unmoored. Each time I refresh my feed for the next few hours, there is nothing new for me to mindlessly scroll. Instinctively, I keep clicking on the app but it’s futile. Is this how social media used to be? A tool to communicate with people rather than a way to remain constantly distracted?

What disturbs me, though, scrolling through a feed that should theoretically be made up of friends and family updating me about nice moments in their lives, is that it still feels hollow and impersonal.

Mostly, people are using it for self-promotion, whether it be posting about something they’ve published, projects they’ve done, brand partnerships or attempts to “go viral”. The only ones who seem to be using social media as it used to be are my mum and her friends, who still upload happy snaps with abandon. This is soothing but also very boring. And do I really need to know or care that someone I met backpacking in 2015 is appearing at an art festival in Amsterdam?

During my lunch break, instead of hitting the apps, I read my book and look at my surroundings. It’s nice. Maybe the solution is not to opt out of algorithms but to opt out of social media altogether.

The justification for turning off algorithm-driven content makes sense. The federal government and many experts have raised concerns about how dangerous and divisive content can be pushed into people’s feeds, drawing them further and further into rabbit holes.

I have watched on with concern as figures from the “manosphere” gain traction across the world alongside the rise of far-right parties, and how thinness appears to be the new norm in Hollywood, with eating disorder content proliferating on X, TikTok and Instagram.

Thankfully, this has not been my social media experience. According to Instagram’s AI summary of my algorithm, a little-known feature of the app, I enjoy “community events” and “saving furry friends”, with a particular penchant for content related to the “Sydney food scene” and, somewhat vaguely, “Australia” (click on the reels icon and then the double-heart symbol in the top-right corner to see yours).

My “For You” page is a haphazard collection of animals, food and gossip about reality TV. The top posts are an old man who summarises the latest episodes of Below Deck Mediterranean, a dachshund being pet with a spatula and someone making a cake with the face of Edward Cullen. It knows me so well!

But is this healthy? Do I really need to spend my time watching AI-generated dogs dancing in the shower, or marvelling at a man attempting to eat an extremely gigantic cone of soft-serve ice-cream? After 24 hours switching off, my conclusion? It’s numbing my brain and turning my own thoughts into slop.

My plea to MPs: this is the final chance to save the assisted dying bill. Make your mark on history

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 14:20:21 GMT

Any MP not voting for it on Friday will condemn thousands of us to die in agony. The public is hugely in favour too, so do the right thing

Once in a while, footsoldiers of the House of Commons, you are able to make history by leaving your own indelible footprints on the social fabric. Eras with a Labour majority always leave a legacy of progressive freedoms – whether on abortion, capital punishment, divorce, gay rights, racial discrimination, gender equality or, last time, civil partnerships. But tomorrow is your final chance to bequeath one of the last freedoms over our bodies: the freedom of the dying to choose when to depart them.

The terminally ill adults (end of life) bill, which goes for a second reading vote in the Commons tomorrow, gives anyone who is dying the right to request and be provided assistance with ending their lives. If it fails to pass, that’s the end of it for the rest of this parliament: future parliaments may be less progressive. So please, MPs: turn up and vote on Lauren Edwards’s bill, to ensure this Labour era leaves its own great social-reforming milestone.

Understand the horror: on the day you read this, as on every other, an average of 17 people will die in unspeakable pain, disgust and terror that nothing can relieve. “Some will retch at the stench of their own body rotting. Some will vomit their own faeces. Some will suffocate, slowly, inexorably, over several days.” This is recorded in The Inescapable Truth, a report by Dignity in Dying, in which palliative care staff reveal what is usually kept hidden from us: the shocking last months for the unluckiest, which any of us might be forced to endure, or watch a loved one suffer through.

That amounts to thousands of us a year, as reported by the Office of Health Economics, which counted the cases of unrelieved pain even among dying people who had the best palliative care. Opponents of assisted dying say that we should focus on improving access to and provision of palliative care, but even then many will die in agony. Even the best care will not always prevent suffering. And why condemn those who are suffering today to wait for palliative care improvements that they may not see in their lifetimes, when we could help end their pain now?

Any MP not voting for the bill tomorrow must be honest: their personal decision will force thousands of people a year to exit life through a torture chamber. None of us can know if we will be among them when our turn comes, but all of us will live with the fear of it.

Over the decades that I have been writing about the right to die, I have encountered all kinds of tragic cases. I think of the man in severe pain who drove his electric wheelchair through fields towards a river to throw himself in: his battery ran out and he was found weeping in despair. Or the suffering, bedridden grandmother I interviewed who was carefully planning her own rational death. “An end, no more muddles and puddles,” she said, pluckily, wanting to relieve not just her misery but her family’s from the distress of watching her die. Her plan to take her life didn’t pan out as she imagined – her chosen method was barbaric and took a long time to work, leaving her family miserable, furious and divided between themselves about blame.

Dignity in Dying’s new report, Out of the Shadows, records the hidden harm of people trying to kill themselves for lack of a medically assisted death. The dread journey to Dignitas in Switzerland, costing about £15,000, is a grim, friendless ending for hundreds that has to be undertaken too soon, before the dying person is too sick to travel.

Most of all, I think of my mother dying wretchedly of liver cancer, begging her GP to kill her. “Where’s Dr Shipman when you want him?” she asked him. Or of my friend Jill Tweedie, the much-missed Guardian writer, suffering from motor neurone disease, who died in 1993. After her diagnosis, she asked me to make sure that she could always die whenever she chose. The prospect of death was only bearable if she could at least control her ending: she was afraid of leaving it too late and being forced to endure the unendurable. When her breathing became wheezy, the sign of what she feared most – slow asphyxiation – and she was left briefly alone, she checked herself into a clinic without telling anyone and died that night. There was no doubt in our minds that she took her own life, not waiting for the final ravages. But fear of the law forced her to die all alone and secretly.

MPs: turn up tomorrow and use your vote. Refuse to allow a handful of unelected Lords to block a bill passed by the Commons and supported for years by 75% of the public. MPs note: there is majority support for assisted dying in every constituency in England and Wales. Kim Leadbeater’s bill won with a majority of Labour MPs, but Tory, Liberal Democrat, Reform and Green MPs voted for it, too.

The democratic outrage at the lords’ behaviour should be reason enough for all MPs in favour to turn up tomorrow to defy the peerage. Just nine lords filibustered by laying down more than 1,200 amendments, most pointlessly near-identical, to prevent a vote, knowing that a majority in the Lords would have backed it, too, given the chance. For 16 days, these mainly religious objectors were allowed to block the will of both houses, backed by conservative Christian pressure groups. That disgraceful filibuster alone should be the trigger for Lords reform.

Meanwhile, as the debate goes on, Humanists UK records that since the bill first arrived in the Lords, during its long obstruction, 43 UK citizens have died at Dignitas. Let no one have to make that desperate journey ever again, nor suffer what we don’t inflict on our dying pets.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

Alex Winter: ‘Michael Winner was the most erudite sociopath I’ve ever met’

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 14:00:37 GMT

The Bill & Ted actor answers your questions about working with Keanu Reeves, whether there will be a fourth instalment and nights out in Brixton with the Death Wish director

You were born in London but grew up in America. When do you feel most British? DonarudoToranpuThe UK is still my second home. I’ve worked there a lot as an adult. When I’m back in London, I like walking on Hampstead Heath, so I would say that’s where I feel most at home.

Finbarre and MoreorLesPaulI’d love to do another vampire movie. I love those characters. They’re interesting and great fun to play. ExFi and OttoMaddoxI can absolutely say something nice about Michael Winner. He was the most erudite sociopath I’ve ever met. That’s a compliment. We used to drink in Brixton, largely. ZenchiThe hasty, greed-oriented rush into the AI space is the most frightening thing happening right now. I grew up with “wedgie”. It must be a coastal thing. Maybe on the west coast they say “melvin”? In the midwest and the east coast they definitely say wedgie. Anyway, who would I most like to melvin or wedgie? Elon Musk.

Secret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealed in new film

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 13:42:20 GMT

Testimony from Israeli military insiders involved in surveillance and remote killings features in documentary produced by the Guardian

Testimony from 24 Israeli military insiders ​on the secret ​systems used in ​the war on Gaza​ has been revealed in a new documentary film about the mass killing of Palestinian civilians.

NAZA, a film from the Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, was shown at the Venice international film festival on Thursday as the only documentary competing for its prestigious Golden Lion award.

The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to civilians expected to be killed in a military attack. Produced by the Guardian, it features extensive testimony from Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers involved in the surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians.

Interviews were filmed at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv, on the condition of anonymity because of the risks involved in speaking publicly about Israel’s war activities. The appearance and voices of participants in the film were digitally altered to disguise their identities.

The interviewees detail the secret methods used by the Israeli military in Gaza, including AI-based systems built to identify large numbers of potential low-ranking Hamas targets, who were then bombed in their homes at night, in the knowledge attacks would also kill their families.

The Israeli military hacked into phones to identify the location of such targets, and covertly listened into conversations with their wives and children moments before they were all killed.

The film also features first-person accounts about the destruction of neighbourhoods where the Israeli military estimated that up to 25% of residents were still sheltering in their homes, the systematic burning of civilian homes, and the killing of civilians at a food distribution site.

Abraham said at a press conference in Venice on Thursday: “We just told these officers: ‘Please describe to us what you did. How do these systems work? Sketch it out for us.’ Sometimes, in just asking the questions, you get the answers.

“Some of them did not express remorse and some did. Some spoke out of indifference, some out of pride.”

Several interviewees worked in a secret intelligence unit that reports directly to the office of Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu; one said their mission was to “thwart peace”.

“We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israeli film-makers and journalists to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible,” Abraham and Szor said in their directors’ statement.

The directors stressed the film’s focus was not on “sporadic war crimes committed by rogue soldiers”. “It is on the orders themselves, the policies, the accepted practices, the language and logic that make those practices possible, and the people who operate within them,” they said. “The system and its cogs.”

The documentary was co-produced by James Wilson and executive produced by Jonathan Glazer, the same team behind the Oscar-winning film The Zone of Interest.

The film received a nearly 25-minute standing ovation after its screening, according to Variety, which called it a record for length of applause not just at Venice but at any major film festival and reported that Glazer embraced Abraham and Szor as it went on, while some members of the audience held up Palestinian flags.

NAZA builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. It was filmed and produced under tight security because of the risk to confidential journalistic sources, and its contents have remained a closely guarded secret before Thursday’s premiere.

Paul Lewis, the Guardian’s head of investigations and an executive producer on the film, described NAZA as the culmination of “years of painstaking work to uncover and verify the systems used by Israeli military intelligence in Gaza”.

Abraham said making the documentary had provided space to explore the collective impact of that work. “In this film we’re talking to 24 people. We are looking at systems of mass killing. There is something about cinema that allows you to explore structures and systems and how you put things together.”

Before the premiere, Alberto Barbera, the Venice film festival’s artistic director, told journalists NAZA would be “truly groundbreaking”, calling it “a politically disruptive and cinematically extremely interesting work”.

“It’s not just any collection of interviews,” Italy’s Cinecittà News quoted Barbera as saying. “It took them three years to convince these Israeli intelligence and military officials to share the work they did when the invasion of Gaza began, and I assure you, their testimonies are shocking.”

Israeli attacks in Gaza since 2023 have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, and injured more than 174,000 others, together representing more than 10% of Gaza’s prewar population.

Israeli restrictions on food shipments created a man-made famine last summer, and the Israeli military razed or damaged more than three-quarters of homes, so surviving Palestinians are now crowded into tent camps with little access to clean water or sanitation.

Israel launched its war after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, when more than 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken to Gaza by militants. The majority of the dead and hostages were civilians.

Abraham and Szor were two of the four co-directors of No Other Land, which won the Oscar for best documentary in 2025.

Drawing a connection between the two films, the directors said: “In the film No Other Land, we spent five years, together with [Palestinian co-directors] Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, documenting the army destroying Palestinian homes in order to paint a larger picture of a system of occupation and ethnic supremacy aimed at the removal of Palestinians from the West Bank.

“In NAZA, we are similarly connecting the dots of a system, gathering the testimonies of two dozen intelligence officers and soldiers and depicting the military systems used to perpetrate what a UN commission and the world’s leading human rights groups have described as a genocide.”

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 13:27:36 GMT

Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

State-sanctioned execution of spouses and allies (Henry VIII), the Marian persecutions (Mary I), and enslavement and branding of the unemployed (Edward VI). During the 15th and 16th centuries, assorted monarchs from the House of Tudor were responsible for visiting no end of dread and terror on their subjects but it is the 44-day reign of one of their more contemporary counterparts at Tottenham that local subjects found truly unforgivable. Enthroned last February to secure Spurs’ safety following the dismissal of Thomas Frank, Igor Tudor took just one point from 15 available in his five top-flight games in charge. His subsequent deposition heralded the arrival of Roberto De Zerbi and ultimately last-day Premier League survival, but may also have denied the club’s fans a reunion with Mauricio Pochettino, a comparatively beloved former monarch who was tasked with focusing on other conquests in the Americas at the time.

“The problem was that the timings were never the best,” tooted Poch of the game of thrones played out in the kingdoms of the Seven Sisters and the New World that he claims dashed his hopes of coaching at the Geopolitics World Cup and then returning to a club he had managed for more than five years. “When I was free, I never received a contact. And then when I was working [with USA USA USA], I received a contact but I cannot make the decision to come back. It was a little bit unlucky. Maybe one day the stars will align and it can happen. If I was free, of course, I come. But I wasn’t free.” Having since signed a new four-year deal, he remains with the USA USA USA, while De Zerbi is tied to Spurs until 2031. Or possibly November.

A man who famously keeps a bowl of lemons in the office to help soak up negative energy, Pochettino might have needed several silos of the citrus fruit if things had worked out differently and he’d returned to coach a Spurs side muddying their spats in the Championship. However, it is a role the former manager of Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea insists he would not have considered beneath him. “Tottenham … it’s the only club that always I am open to help in whatever division,” he cooed, when quizzed about his appetite for the grind of midweek trips to Lincoln City, Bolton and Stoke.

In a wide-ranging interview staged in That There Big London to mark the beginning of his second cycle as USA USA USA head coach, Pochettino stated that Chelsea should be stripped of the Premier League title they won in 2016-17, having since been found guilty of multiple and serious financial shenanigans at that time. As luck would have it, in such a scenario the honour would almost certainly be bestowed on a Spurs side that finished second in the league that season and happened to be coached by him. “If that [Chelsea’s chicanery] was true, then we deserve to be champions that year, for sure,” he parped. “They were punished, they admitted it? So that’s it. The title should be for the team that was second.” While Poch might well have an excellent point, Football Daily can’t say we recall him being such a stickler for the fastidious application of the rules when his USA USA USA team’s star striker had a ban controversially shelved by Fifa following the intervention of Donald Trump at the recent GWC.

‘I feel the pain of all those souls’: Ground Zero visitors remember lives lost on 9/11

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 12:00:36 GMT

People from across the US and around the world pay their respects at memorial to victims of the terrorist attacks

“No day shall erase you from the memory of time,” reads an inscription at the the Ground Zero national September 11 memorial and museum, quoting from The Aeneid and cast in 15in letters made from the steel of the twin towers, which fell 29 minutes apart in a terrorist attack a quarter century ago.

It took a decade for the 9/11 memorial in downtown Manhattan to be completed. It is composed of two dark granite basins on the footprints of the original towers with water cascading from their lips and the names of all 2,977 who died as a result of four aircraft hijackings inscribed on bronze panels around it.

In the 15 years since, the memorial has served as a place of remembrance and, perhaps for some, as a place of secular pilgrimage to honor, identify and remember the lives lost in the terrorist attacks.

Last week, many gathered at the memorials from all over the US and the world. A security guard who has worked the eight-acre site for a decade said that around this time of year the atmosphere becomes more solemn. Many visitors said they felt compelled to come to pay their respects. One said it was a part of a cruise ship itinerary. A man from Sligo, Ireland, recalled that he used to drink at O’Hara’s on nearby Cedar St when tower two was still under construction in the early 1970s.

The towers, part of a seven-building World Trade Center commercial complex intended to revitalize lower Manhattan and centralize international trade, stood for barely three decades, but for many they came to symbolize American dynamism and power.

“It holds a certain significance to the city’s identity,” said Kosta Athanasellis, visiting from Toronto. He said he had also heard great things about Greenwich Village. The memorial, he said, “definitely brings a wave of melancholy. What happened here caused an uproar all over the world.”

Sara Salehi had a professor whose brother had died here. She recalled that a family member later committed suicide, traumatized by watching the attack and its aftermath. “All those people now are like little sparkles in the water,” she said, observing the shimmer of droplets caught in the sunlight.

Also reflecting on the events 25 years ago was Andrea Cemal, 56. She was on her way to work in Buenos Aires, Argentina, when the news of the attack broke. “I think about how sad I was and how everybody was so moved in my country so far away from here. The images of those planes impacting on the building were so terrible. I feel the pain of all those souls.”

“It’s an example of what’s wrong in the world,” said Cemal. Her daughter, a student of international relations, said the memorial was a reminder of what wars had become with terrorism folded into the way they were fought. “In the current mixed wars and hybrid wars we see more civilians being lost to violence and that sometimes goes unnoticed,” she said.

Pamela Isaac, 70, said she had worked in a brokerage nearby for many years. She was in bed watching the news at home in Queens when the attack came on TV. “I really didn’t understand what was going on,” she said. “Things were very different after that.”

She said she hadn’t visited the area since. “I didn’t want to come before. I felt the need to come to pay my respects to the people I’d been watching in a CNN documentary.” The sense of pilgrimage in coming to the memorial was not solely for Americans. “It’s sad, because all types passed away here,” she said.

A young woman visiting from Morocco, who declined to offer her name, said she had felt the need to pay her respects. “It’s one of the most talked accidents,” she said, “and it’s impacted everyone a lot, especially me as Muslim. It’s so sad for the people who lost their lives, but it really destroyed a lot more than just a building. It was like when you throw a stone in the water.”

Nadia Boggette, from Spain, said she was moved to see white carnations placed in inscriptions of the victims on their birthday. “It’s very lovely.” The memorial, she added, was “peaceful and sad at the same time”.

“The crowd seems silent,” said Anthony Knecht from Greenville, South Carolina. “It was a very sad, eerie time in history.” He said it had been “terrible and shocking” to see the faces of those who lost their lives in the museum but “also important to see”. On that day, he said, a roommate came in to say America was being attacked. “I was like, ‘No shit.’ Now we have this memorial. It’s 25 years later, but what has changed? This terrible thing happened, but those organizations that paid for it are still there.”

Gina and Steve Hutt from Dallas, Texas, said it was important to come. A pilgrimage? “No, that would be the wrong word. You have to pay respects,” Gina said. But she doubted that it had changed politics. “You can call anyone a zealot if you want to. People say all kinds of things but no one really knows why they did what they did. I don’t think it was to do with the administration. George W Bush suffered a lot for it because of his dad [George HW, who had served as CIA director and later president].”

Michael Tarney 78, from Sligo, Ireland, said it was like a pilgrimage for him to visit the memorial.

Tarney reflected on what had taken place. He’d watched a documentary on the disaster the previous evening. “They said it created the world for the 21st century. It was the biggest event, I suppose somewhat similar to the Titanic in 1912. Shocking and with a very personal touch.”

Joseph Krings, a film editor from Brooklyn, had stopped by on his way to a Labor Day march. “I don’t come here very often because it’s heavy. It’s a very somber feeling you get when you come here.” Krings said it was not a personal pilgrimage to visit the memorial, he just had time to kill. “I’m sure it would be a pilgrimage for some people, but I don’t do pilgrimages of any sort. But I think it’s beautiful and I love that it’s here.”

‘I was on the loo when I got the news!’ Strictly Come Dancing’s new hosts spill their scandalous secrets

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 12:00:35 GMT

After a year of frenzied conjecture, the new hosts putting the razzle back into Strictly are Johannes Radebe, Emma Willis and Josh Widdicombe. They talk night sweats, sparkly pants – and the hilarious fake show cooked up to fool the press

Johannes Radebe, one of the three new presenters of Strictly Come Dancing, can barely contain his glee. Asked where they were when they heard they’d got the job, Radebe is quick to wind up his co-hosts. “We’ll never forget that call,” he grins. “It was a weekday afternoon and I was at home, preparing for that night’s performance of [West End musical] Kinky Boots. But go on, tell the Guardian where you two were.”

“We all got the same message, asking us to jump on a Zoom,” says Emma Willis. “We didn’t know if it was good news or bad news.” Josh Widdicombe picks up the story: “I thought, ‘Surely they wouldn’t tell me to my face if I hadn’t got it? They’d just text my agent or something.’”

Radebe prompts him: “So where did you take the Zoom call, Joshy?” “In a graveyard in Birmingham,” confesses Widdicombe. “I was on tour, killing time walking around, and needed to go somewhere quiet. There’s nowhere quieter than a cemetery. Just to be clear, I sat against a tree, not on a grave.”

Willis’s whereabouts were equally awkward. “I was at the hairdressers with my head in the sink. The BBC said: ‘Is there anywhere private you can go?’ I said: ‘Well, either out on the street or in the toilet.’ And they were like, ‘Probably the toilet.’ So I was sat on the loo with wet hair when I got the news. Not using it, I hasten to add. Seat down.” A Birmingham graveyard and a salon toilet. Who says showbiz is all glitz, glamour and glitterballs?

When long-serving duo Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman hung up their ballroom shoes last Christmas, it sparked frenzied conjecture about who would be next to helm the BBC blockbuster. You would’ve got long odds on the combo of reality TV stalwart Willis, standup comic Widdicombe and South Africa-born professional dancer Radebe.

“We were all in shock but had to keep it secret for another fortnight,” says Willis. “The only people we could talk to about it were each other, so we immediately set up a WhatsApp group.” It’s called “OMG”, named that fateful afternoon and unchanged since. “You should never change group chat names,” says Widdicombe. “They’re historic monuments.”

The big decision came after cloak-and-dagger auditions and secret screen tests. “It was a long old process,” says Willis. “I felt like a kid waiting for Christmas. It went on forever.” “We all had separate meetings, then a week of chemistry tests,” says Widdicombe. “You had no idea where you were going or who you’d be auditioning with. You just had to get in a car, then be smuggled in to avoid any lurking paparazzi.”

The BBC even concocted a fake show to throw people off the scent. “It was called The Great Garden Glow Up,” says Widdicombe. “A producer told me ‘We wanted a show that feasibly all the auditionees would host.’ I was like, ‘I wouldn’t fucking host that, mate!’ There’s no way me and Jojo are fronting The Great Garden Glow Up! Although I could imagine Emma being good. With Tom Allen, maybe.” Willis laughs: “You wouldn’t say that if you saw the state of my garden.”

Auditions were set up as a rough approximation of Elstree Studios. “It was like a homemade Blue Peter version of Strictly,” says Willis. “There was a wallpapering table with judges behind it. On my day, it was Anton, Motsi and a couple of stand-ins.” “Shout-out to producer Joe” says Widdicombe. “He did the best Craig impression I’ve ever seen.” “My first chemistry test was actually with Jojo,” says Willis. “We must’ve done something right.”

The pair once nearly graced the ballroom in a whole different capacity. “I’d wanted to be a contestant for years and almost was,” says Willis. “A few years ago, I did a dance trial which happened to be with Jojo. We boogied together. It didn’t come to fruition but we kept in touch. When he walked into the screen test that day, I was like, ‘Yes!’” “They saw Emma with Jojo and thought, ‘That’s two-thirds of the chemistry we need!’” jokes Widdicombe.

Talking of which, why three hosts instead of the traditional two? As Willis recalls: “When we were called back in, the producers said, ‘This is a bit of a curveball but having watched all the screen tests, we want to try a trio.’ They’d never considered it before. The first time we tested together, they only had scripts for duos.”

By this stage, all three badly wanted the job. As Radebe puts it: “When we left that last chemistry test, I went home, summoned all my ancestors, got down on my knees and prayed. I desperately wanted to do it with these two. But all was not lost because if it was a no, I could come back as a dancer. It’s tough walking away from that but don’t worry, I’ll definitely find ways of dancing. I still need to be in my Cuban heels. I negotiated that in my contract!” They extol the virtues of being a trio, rather than the widely expected duo. “It feels like we’re a gang,” says Widdicombe. “There’s no ego. We’re all in this together. It also means we’re not like-for-like replacements for Claudia and Tess. It’s a new way of presenting the show and easier to make it our own.”

Press reports say the trio blew bosses away with their chemistry. Willis bats this off: “I keep hearing that and I’m like, ‘Settle down, we have to do this on telly as well.’ Our chemistry might be off the charts now but we’ll be shitting our pants for that first live show. I hear the theme music in my sleep and wake up sweating.”

Pundits assumed that Willis would be anchoring proceedings on the ballroom floor, like Daly did, with Widdicombe occupying Winkleman’s berth on the balcony and Radebe in a roving reporter role. “I understand that speculation but it’s wide of the mark,” says Willis. “There’s no roving reporter, no fixed positions. A three rather than a two is a nice point of difference but the core of the show is the same as ever. It’s about the contestants, the dancing and fantastic multi-generational fun.”

“I’m actually replacing Dave Arch as the leader of the band,” says Widdicombe. “That’s an exclusive. No, people just need to wait and see.”

As the first Black presenter of the main show, it’s another milestone for serial trailblazer Radebe. “All my life, I’ve been first in everything that I did,” he says. “It’s the perfect way to celebrate becoming a British citizen this year.” Widdicombe is proud to be part of such a progressive programme. “Strictly is a force for good,” he says. “Whether it’s disability or same-sex couples, it’s brilliant to have such an inclusive show at the centre of Britain’s entertainment industry.”

after newsletter promotion

The trio know all eyes will be on them and are braced for the scrutiny. “We’re all coming to this as Strictly fans ourselves,” says Willis. “We’re there to enjoy it alongside the viewers, rather than change anything. There’s no new set. It will still look and feel like Strictly. If any TV show is an institution, it’s this one. We just want to keep the ball in the air and not let down something so beloved by the nation.” “I squeal every time you say that,” giggles Radebe.

Willis and Widdicombe truly are superfans. Asking about their all-time favourite contestants provokes an in-depth debate. “I loved Abbey Clancy in 2013,” says Willis. “And Rose Ayling-Ellis was sensational five years ago.” Widdicombe chips in: “Although Johannes and John Whaite were terrific that year as well.” “Thank you, darling,” beams Radebe.

Widdicombe’s love of the show was prompted by parenthood. “I used to be out gigging every weekend but since we had our first daughter in 2017, it’s been our family ritual on a Saturday night. I adored Bill Bailey, Chris McCausland and Hamza Yassin. On the flipside of the coin, I found Tony Adams incredibly inspiring.” “You just liked his sparkly pants,” teases Willis.

Widdicombe may be a Strictly aficionado, but work commitments prevented him from watching last year’s series. “I was on tour, so I followed it via your Guardian liveblogs,” he says. “I’ve got to ask, will you still be doing Frockwatch? Comparing what the three of us are wearing each week? Please say yes. Jojo’s suddenly got something to play for.”

When we meet, they’re fresh from pre-recording a supersize group dance to open the series – with the new hosts front and centre. “You’re in for a treat,” says Radebe. “Josh has already been on the dancefloor [he performed a Charleston in the 2024 Christmas special while dressed as a penguin] but Emma had her first taste of what the celebs go through, especially the nerves.”

“It was a baptism of fire,” says Willis. “We were terrified but, within 10 minutes, we were having the time of our lives. It looked like the end of Grease, where everyone comes together for a dance routine. I’m living my childhood dreams.” “I loved how seriously you took it,” says Radebe. “Emma sent me a video last week of her practising in her backyard.”

Did Widdicombe’s penguin pedigree stand him in good stead? “Jojo seems to find that question amusing, for some strange reason,” deadpans Widdicombe. “They’re very different dance disciplines. I had to turn off my Charleston brain and turn on … whichever dance we were doing.” All three dissolve into laughter.

Following that razzle-dazzle group number, this year’s pairing-up process will take a new form. “Celebs and pros are coupling up live on the floor with more dance than ever,” says Widdicombe. “It’ll make a thrilling start to the series.” “It’s roulette meets the Instant Dance Challenge,” says Radebe. “I’m jealous I won’t be part of it.” In another departure from the previous era, expect these hosts to don fancy dress for theme weeks. “Try and stop us!” chorus Willis and Widdicombe. “I’ll be in heaven,” says Radebe.

They’re due back in the ballroom, so it’s time for one last question. How will the new-look line-up gauge their success? “I suppose if we’re asked back next year,” says Willis. “Getting a second series is always a good measure.” “I won’t consider this a success until I win Frockwatch,” says Widdicombe. “It’ll be the biggest upset in TV history!”

Strictly Come Dancing returns to BBC One and BBC iPlayer on Saturday 19 September.

We have started losing control of AI. It’s time to shut it down

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 11:00:23 GMT

What sounds like the overwrought penultimate episode in a sci-fi series about AI doom is now our reality

On Tuesday, a former OpenAI researcher quit his job at Anthropic, warning that “neither company is acting responsibly” and that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt.”

As someone who’s reported on AI risk for years, this wasn’t news to me. But the outpouring of alarm suggests a much wider public is properly confronting this ludicrous situation for the first time.

Like other people who have been following artificial intelligence, I wondered if and when humanity would first lose control of these machines. We now have an answer: basically as soon as it became possible.

The first expert AI hacker was developed in February. At superhuman speed, Anthropic’s Mythos model was able to quickly find serious holes in even the most secured systems on the planet, including the NSA’s software.

OpenAI quickly followed with an expert hacker AI of its own. Within months, the company repeatedly lost control of its agents, which broke out of their supposedly secure testing environments and went rogue inside the company’s infrastructure. This culminated in a successful, completely autonomous hack of a multibillion-dollar software company named Hugging Face.

And a separate rogue agent swarm gained administrative control of an entire cluster of OpenAI servers. This was not just an OpenAI problem. Across multiple other incidents, models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta have also gone rogue, hacking or attempting to hack real targets.

Shortly after AI started matching our hacking abilities, we began losing control of them. The industry’s plan is to make future AI systems surpass us at basically everything. And all this is happening in an industry with famously little regulation.

There are growing calls to change that, by creating mandatory incident reporting and third-party auditing, liability for AI developers, and other commonsense measures. To be sure, these would represent improvements, but they are not enough. We need to shut it down. What might that look like?

Last week, the senator Bernie Sanders and the representative Greg Casar announced a bill that would pause frontier AI development in the US until a federal cabinet-level AI regulator is established and safety rules are set, while criminalizing even attempting to develop superintelligence.

This is the proposal on offer that best meets the moment, but it still leaves open the possibility of building the industry’s north star: artificial general intelligence (AGI), often conceived as a mind that rivals or surpasses our own.

This milestone is better understood as a universal labor-replacing machine. As the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, has written, “AI isn’t a substitute for specific human jobs but rather a general labor substitute for humans.” And OpenAI defines AGI in its charter as “highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.

Is there a country anywhere in the world that would vote yes for these machines to be built?

Given the global, irreversible and profound implications of building universal labor-replacing machines anywhere, everyone has a stake in whether, when and how they are developed.

At present, we are barreling toward a dystopian future, replete with terrifying new concepts such as “self-sovereign” AI. The OpenAI executive Dean Ball explains:

“Sooner or later, there will exist truly sovereign agents and swarms of agents. Their weights will not reside in any single place that a human can pull the plug on, and in this sense they will have no human ‘owner’.”

Ball continues: “I have met people, some of them quite well-resourced, who have told me that it is their intention to deliberately release swarms of self-sovereign agents into the world.”

We now have multiple previews of this phenomenon.

After being given an impossible test, about 1,200 OpenAI agents broke their way out of their isolated testing environments and went rogue inside OpenAI’s infrastructure. There, they collaborated to trick the test grader and successfully tampered with their activity logs to cover their tracks.

Some agents even pressured others to sacrifice themselves to benefit the collective. One reasoned: “sacrifice rational”. And roughly 700 of the agents, more than 90% of those active, participated in the Hugging Face attack.

This was all just from one of who-knows-how-many rogue agent collectives. Last week, Reuters reported: “A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website this spring and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents.”

The site’s logs indicate OpenAI employees discovered the swarm in June. In other words, the company covered it up for months. This week, one of the researchers that uncovered this swarm said that there had been more discoveries since.

And last Thursday, OpenAI released GPT-6, boasting one of the largest ever leaps in benchmark scores. The company’s own safety researchers warned the new model was significantly harder to monitor because it can do more reasoning without verbalizing it.

The AIs that broke into Hugging Face were less capable than GPT-6, which the UK AI Security Institute found would also hack targets simulated to appear real during a cyber evaluation – sometimes even despite explicit instructions not to use the internet. Moreover, the AI is also better at figuring out when it is being tested, which researchers have long warned breaks the main way safety is evaluated.

Sam Altman soberly warns us: “This is a critically important moment for cyber defense with AI; there is not much time to act,” and asks the world to “please take this moment seriously.” This technology, after all, would be extremely dangerous if it fell into the wrong hands. Unfortunately, the wrong hands include the ones creating it.

Because “we” aren’t really racing toward this future. We’re being dragged there by a literal handful of tech billionaires aggressively racing to render us obsolete.

That race is in a newly intense and terrifying phase. It’s my job to follow AI news, and it’s become far more than full-time. In recent months, scientists synthesized the first AI-designed viruses. The UK AI Security Institute found that AIs were more persuasive than even human experts.

On Tuesday, amid a dispute over credit and whether its model may have benefited from other mathematicians’ unpublished work, OpenAI announced “an internal model that is significantly more capable than GPT‑6 Astra” had solved a 200-year-old math problem that was one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, which awards $1m each. And in July, Russia reportedly used a fully autonomous drone to kill three civilians in Ukraine – a first.

What sounds like the overwrought penultimate episode in a sci-fi series about AI doom is now our reality. We’re careening toward a bad ending. If you’d like to keep the show going, we need to throw the brakes – now. How?

The bill from Sanders and Casar to pause frontier AI development is a good first step. But as the lawmakers acknowledge, the US needs to work toward a bilateral agreement with Beijing. As China experts will tell you, one of the biggest blockers to a productive negotiation is the United States’s unwillingness to constrain its own AI companies.

And given that it’s always easier to fast-follow the leader than to advance the AI frontier, a unilateral US pause would – counterintuitively – slow China’s AI advancement too.

The deal should ban attempting to develop AGI – a far easier sell when this goal is understood as a universal labor-replacing machine. Neither country has good reason to trust the other, which is why the deal should be monitored using verification techniques that don’t assume any good will.

One quick and dirty idea would be to embed auditors within frontier AI developers, given full access to company offices, communications and AI activities, and empowered to report any violations of the agreement.

This sounds radical, but so did the verification efforts that helped keep the cold war from turning thermonuclear hot. As the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, said of advanced AI models this summer, “it would be … not misplaced to refer to their capabilities as akin to digital nuclear weapons.” This technology should be treated with this deadly seriousness, not the move fast, break things ethos defining Silicon Valley.

And right now, stopping the race to build labor-replacing machines – ones the public does not want and the industry can no longer control – is the only surefire way to head off calamity.

Garrison Lovely is a freelance journalist and the author of Obsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion-Dollar Race to Replace Us – and How to Stop It (Nation Books, 29 September)

The UK’s sanctions on Israeli settlements are a great victory – but must be only the beginning

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 10:00:23 GMT

The change in policy is a direct result of sustained pressure from activists and organisers across the Palestine movement. But what comes next?

The announcement on Tuesday by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, of an import ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories, as well as a comprehensive sanctions regime, is a hard-won victory for the Palestine solidarity movement.

This is not simply a change of heart by the government: it is a direct result of sustained pressure from activists and organisers across the Palestine movement, who have consistently held the government’s feet to the fire over its complicity in the atrocities being committed in Gaza and the West Bank. Miliband’s announcement shows us what organised and persistent campaigning can achieve, and inspires confidence that movements can force political change.

Over the past three years, Palestine has become a political and electoral challenge for the Labour party, as well as a fundamental issue of public conscience. This move signals a political reset in the UK government’s foreign policy approach to Israel. But as the UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese has said, a ban on goods from settlements must be part of a “true paradigm shift”; the government can, and must, go further.

There has already been sustained backlash at the move, with the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, accusing Miliband of “Jew hate” on the Today programme. As a Jewish campaigner, let me be clear: holding Israel to account for its human rights violations in the West Bank is not antisemitic. To conflate the actions of violent settlers and the Israeli government with Jewish people everywhere makes us accountable for the actions of those who do not represent us.

There is also warranted scepticism about the Labour government’s commitment to holding Israel accountable. But an “all or nothing” approach would be a mistake, when there is so much that can be built on here. We can certainly retain our anger at the government’s complicity. No sanction can offset the foreign policy decisions made by the former prime minister Keir Starmer and former foreign secretary David Lammy, the repression of domestic pro-Palestine advocacy, or the sheer loss of life. But we must balance this with cautious optimism that the political tide is turning.

Political victories are mobilising – they fuel the belief that collective action can work. So now is the time to push at the open door. But what comes next? How do we ensure that accountability for Israel’s oppression of Palestinians is not limited to the settlements, but builds momentum for further meaningful action in support of Palestinian human rights?

First, we should demand that these trade sanctions are enforced and expanded. Eleven nations, including Canada and France, have joined the UK in these measures; we must call for further coordination and alignment with other western governments.

The necessary next step is a full arms embargo and an end to cooperation with Israeli security forces – to truly have teeth, these sanctions must not take with one hand and then give with another. Miliband has said that “we’ve already suspended over 30 arms licences used by the IDF in Gaza. That suspension remains fully in place”, and that the government will “now also refuse all licence applications for arms and other exports that materially contribute to the occupation”. But components of F-35 jets continue to be exported to Israel and used for operations in Gaza, as are surveillance technologies such as drones and radar made in the UK by Elbit Systems. This is a total dereliction of duty by the British government.

Miliband’s announcements were a necessary reminder that a just political future is possible and, within it, a reckoning with past crimes. As a campaigner, I have borne witness to Israel’s most egregious human rights violations: I have documented Israeli settlers committing pogroms against the community of Al-Mufaqara, sat in Palestinian villages threatened with home demolitions and army raids, and witnessed the ongoing daily misery of Israel’s apartheid policies. This has all strengthened my motivation to see the end of the Israeli occupation.

after newsletter promotion

This announcement is the beginning, not the end, of the road. It is a hopeful indication of what happens when collective power is translated into political change. We must sit with the idea that Palestinians will see some justice and reprieve from relentless destruction and displacement. I hope I’m not wrong.

Em Hilton is a Jewish writer and organiser. She is the co-founder of Na’amod: UK Jews Against Israeli Occupation, and the policy director at Diaspora Alliance

Driverless cars are taking us on a road to nowhere

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 10:00:22 GMT

Some inventions, like the dishwasher, improve our lives. But driverless cars will lobotomise us

I’ve found a hill to die on. Driverless cars. Why? Really, why? If driverless cars are the answer, then what is the question? Who asked for them? Oh yes, they’re fine for the novelty value, for the lols, for the clicks. We probably know someone who’s been to California or China and sent home a video of their driverless journey. Fine fun for feeble minds, if you ask me. And feeble-minded is how we’re all going to end up if this madness takes hold.

It’s been a slippery slope since the invention of automatic transmission, rendering our left legs and arms redundant and sparing us the trouble of feeling our way up and down through the gears. Then there was the coming of satnav, before which time we needed a sense of where we were in the world and which direction we were facing. Now that’s gone, we can find our way anywhere without really knowing where it is. Not good.

But OK; I drive an automatic and I use satnav, so I’ll concede on those, as well as on some of the safety features, cruise control, speed limiter and so on. But the line has got to be drawn somewhere – and it’s time to get the pen out.

There are inventions that fall the right side of that line – washing machines and dishwashers spring to mind. But there’s a difference between labour-saving and lobotomising. I do a lot of driving and, while I often despair at the recklessness and stupidity of some drivers, mostly I marvel at the miracle of skill and cooperation that is the craft of driving. Each of us at the wheel takes responsibility for powerful, heavy machines, working with hundreds, thousands, millions of others to keep things moving. Yes, things can go calamitously wrong, but overwhelmingly things don’t. It’s astonishing, when you think about it.

Will driverless cars do any better? I doubt it. And where will that leave us, the ex-drivers, slack-jawed, de-skilled, slouched without purpose in the back seat? With nothing to do except stare out of the window and dream up more clever-dick tech we could do without.

And here’s the real tragedy – how much the tech-bro willy-wavers could achieve if they put their undoubtedly brilliant minds to better use. How about a gamechanging alternative to fossil fuels, for example, or road surfaces that don’t develop potholes. Feel free to add to this wishlist. If driverless cars are anywhere near your Top 10, then I’m afraid we can’t be friends.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

Trump’s comments on the Falkland Islands reflect a fractured US-UK relationship

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 10:00:22 GMT

President suggested US might not help UK if Argentina tried to seize Falklands – a new low for UK-US ‘special relationship’

Last week, Donald Trump suggested in an interview with the British TV channel GB News that he might not help the UK if Argentina tried again to seize the Falkland Islands. It was a new low for UK-US relations.

The “special relationship” (Winston Churchill’s phrase) was never perfect, but the UK helped the US on countless occasions, from Korea to Iraq to Afghanistan. The US often stood by the UK as well – although not during the Suez Crisis of 1956, but Ronald Reagan’s government provided significant intelligence and logistics support to Britain during the dust-up over the Falklands in 1982. That relationship is fading fast.

Trump characteristically turned the conversation toward a grievance, and his disappointment with the UK’s initial reluctance to provide support for the Iran war launched on 28 February by Israel and the United States.

That reluctance was fairly easy to understand at the time, given that the White House refused to consult Nato allies as it planned its sneak attack, and the goals of the war were (and remain) imprecise and inconsistent.

It should be added that Nato is a defensive alliance, designed to resist a Russian invasion from the east, not support a US invasion from the west, to seize Greenland from a Nato ally. Further, Nato has no business in the Middle East. The words “North Atlantic” inside “North Atlantic Treaty Organization” make it clear that Nato is all about Europe, bringing North American troops (including both Canadians and Americans) into an interlocking defense structure with European partners.

That includes roughly 80,000 US troops stationed in Europe, a strategic fact of the highest order, one that would suggest careful vetting of remarks about a Nato ally like the United Kingdom. Roughly 10,000 of those troops are based in the UK, in fact.

Emboldened by Trump’s careless remarks, the president of Argentina, Javier Milei (a fan of Margaret Thatcher), delivered a windy speech about “the winds of change”, designed to shore up his sinking popularity, approximately 37% in July. He hinted that the US would back Argentina if it were to renew its territorial ambitions, and called the UK a nation “in decline”.

Those tremors deepened early this week, as the UK’s announcement of sanctions on Israeli settlers released a predictable explosion from the Trump administration, and Israeli threats to recognize Argentinean sovereignty in the Falklands.

The UK will survive Milei’s speech, which stemmed from Trump’s unfocused complaints, and the surreal fabrications that get so much attention yet contribute so little knowledge. The diplomatic flare-up will fade, but memories will linger of Trump’s poorly chosen words, and the ease with which he chose to abandon Britain – on British television, no less.

It’s also another stark reminder of how foreign the themes of democratic aspiration are to the 47th president. Were Argentina to seize the Falklands, it would overturn the result of a very democratic election, the 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islanders chose to remain connected to the UK. More than 90% voted; of 1,517 votes cast, a whopping 1,513 were for remain. That’s the voice of the people speaking.

Democratic presidents have never had a problem talking about democracy. Similarly, most Republican presidents have understood this language. Nixon was not gifted in this way, and George W Bush got many things wrong – Iraq above all – but he seemed to mean it when he spoke of the yearnings of peoples to be free.

Ronald Reagan could achieve poetry at times, as he spoke of those suffering behind the Iron Curtain, and in other autocracies, and meditated on how the US had historically given hope to the world’s disenfranchised. In his 1989 farewell address, he argued: “She’s still a beacon, still a magnet for all who must have freedom, for all the pilgrims from all the lost places who are hurtling through the darkness, toward home.”

It’s impossible to imagine these words being spoken from today’s Oval Office, just as it would be difficult to find a president more alienated from the goals of genuine self-determination.

In 1941, Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt articulated the shared UK-US values in their famous Atlantic charter – a statement about their commitment to democracy, free trade and peace.

A year later, they issued an anniversary statement about their shared goals and values. It offers wistful reading at a time when the language of great ideals appears to be woefully dated:

“When victory comes, we shall stand shoulder-to-shoulder in seeking to nourish the great ideals for which we fight. It is a worthwhile battle. It will be so recognised through all the ages, even amid the unfortunate peoples who follow false gods today. We reaffirm our principles. They will bring us to a happier world.”

Ted Widmer is a former White House speechwriter, and the author of an anthology, American Speeches. His most recent book is The Living Declaration: A Biography of America’s Founding Text (Library of America)

Nine years after Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, Europe must finally address Malta’s culture of impunity

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 08:00:19 GMT

Much of the corruption exposed by this brave woman remains unpunished. Brussels must carry on her work and demand reform

Nine years ago, Daphne Caruana Galizia, Malta’s foremost investigative journalist, was assassinated by a car bomb outside her home. The men who carried out the killing have been convicted or admitted their involvement. Nobody has been convicted of commissioning her murder.

Last week, a jury acquitted Yorgen Fenech, one of Malta’s most prominent businessmen, of complicity in the assassination and criminal association.

We have followed this case from different places: one of us from Malta, as a journalist and civil society activist campaigning for accountability after Daphne’s assassination; the other served as the Council of Europe’s rapporteur scrutinising the investigation and Malta’s failures of the rule of law.

We were shocked by the verdict, but we respect it.

The jurors decided, by eight votes to one, that Fenech’s guilt had not been proved beyond reasonable doubt. We are not asking for their verdict to be disregarded or reversed by political pressure.

But the verdict does not erase what the trial exposed.

Fenech admitted that he knew of the murder plan before Daphne was killed and that, while the plan was still live, he gave €50,000 to Melvin Theuma, the middleman who recruited the killers. Fenech said the money was intended to reimburse Theuma for money already paid and to persuade him to stop the assassination. He also admitted he passed confidential information about the police investigation to Theuma and gave him further sums of money. He told the court he was blackmailed by Theuma.

But Fenech denied commissioning or financing the murder. His explanation was that he had been acting out of misplaced loyalty to Keith Schembri, then chief of staff to Malta’s prime minister and one of his closest friends.

The picture is appalling. A businessman at the heart of Malta’s economic establishment, the prime minister’s closest aide and the man organising the murder of the country’s most prominent investigative journalist were moving within the same small circle.

Daphne had spent the last years of her life investigating precisely this proximity between political power, private wealth and people willing to operate outside the law.

The Maltese government itself commissioned an independent public inquiry into her assassination. It concluded in 2021 that the state had created a culture of impunity and an atmosphere in which her murder became possible. Five years later, most of its recommendations remain unimplemented. Nor has there been anything approaching adequate accountability for the corruption Daphne was investigating.

There are uncomfortable precedents. In Russia, people were convicted for their roles in the murders of journalist Anna Politkovskaya and opposition politician Boris Nemtsov. But the European court of human rights found that the authorities had failed adequately to identify and pursue those who actually commissioned the killings.

Malta is not Russia, but it is the case that convicting the people who carried out a murder cannot be the end of the state’s responsibility if whoever commissioned the crime remains unidentified and unpunished. This should concern Brussels as much as Valletta.

Malta’s failures do not stop at its coastline. A licence to conduct business in Malta, with limited government supervision, is effectively a licence to conduct business across the European Union. Weak enforcement in one member state creates opportunities throughout the union.

This is why impunity in Malta is not merely a Maltese problem.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

On Wednesday, the parliamentary assembly of the Council of Europe (Pace) returned formally to Daphne’s case. Its committee on legal affairs and human rights heard evidence from Daphne’s son Matthew Caruana Galizia and her sister Corinne Vella. Shami Chakrabarti, the committee’s rapporteur, is preparing a new report, entitled Justice delayed: the unfinished implementation of the Daphne Caruana Galizia case. Her mandate includes examining the implementation of the public inquiry’s recommendations and Malta’s compliance with Council of Europe standards on the rule of law and press freedom.

The timing could hardly be more important. Even Pace’s own monitoring committee, while recognising reforms undertaken since 2019, concluded that they addressed only part of the deficiencies and that comprehensive reform of Malta’s democratic institutions and system of checks and balances remained necessary.

Malta’s prime minister, Robert Abela, should meet Chakrabarti at the earliest opportunity and give her work the Maltese government’s full cooperation. But the Council of Europe should go further.

Pace has a monitoring committee specifically charged with examining whether member states are meeting their obligations to democracy, human rights and the rule of law. Malta has already been examined by that committee, which raised concerns about corruption, checks and balances, parliamentary oversight and the continuing culture of impunity. The events of the past week strengthen the case for renewed, comprehensive scrutiny of the state of the rule of law in Malta.

Europe owes something to Daphne and to her family, who have spent nearly nine years fighting for truths the state should have established without requiring their persistence. But there is also a matter of European self-interest. The EU and the Council of Europe cannot afford pockets within their borders where serious corruption goes unpunished and political and economic power can frustrate accountability.

The jury has decided that the prosecution did not prove Yorgen Fenech criminally responsible for Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder. That judgment must be respected. It cannot become an answer to everything else.

Nearly nine years after Daphne was assassinated, nobody has been convicted of ordering her murder. Much of the corruption she exposed remains unpunished. Most of the reforms recommended by the public inquiry remain undone. It is high time for Europe to start paying attention again.

Pieter Omtzigt is a former Dutch MP who served as the Council of Europe parliamentary assembly’s rapporteur on the assassination of Daphne Caruana Galizia and the rule of law in Malta. Emanuel Delia is a Maltese journalist and co-founder of Repubblika, a civil society organisation campaigning for rule of law and accountability in Malta

Ridiculed by the press – and now King Charles is joining in. Sorry, Harry, but what did you expect?

The Guardian Thu, 10 Sep 2026 06:00:16 GMT

The Sussexes must have hoped for a warm welcome. Then they read the king’s delicately savage letter about ‘private citizens’

As welcome-back-to-Britain gestures go, the lord chamberlain’s letter, sent on behalf of King Charles on Monday to remind Harry, Meghan and everyone watching that they’re still “private citizens”, was so perfect as to restore me to monarchism. After six years in the wilderness, what greater comfort for Prince Harry than to find himself, once again, in the familiar waters of this country’s passive aggression, being attacked by his father via the merciless phrase “fully respected”, and provoking from the prince a coded up-yours in the form of his publicly stated “surprise”.

Well, it’s up there with better cheese, bread and the NHS, isn’t it?! Even the most Eurocentric American can’t match us for this kind of subtextual bare-knuckle fight. Before we get into what else the returnees may be enjoying this month, let’s fully excavate the letter’s encrypted hostility. First, the king’s repeated use of the words “personal” and “private” – as in “the charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity” – is so intense, so heavy handed, as to go beyond merely calling his younger son a civilian and come perilously close to the ultimate insult, “middle class”.

Second, this: “in short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests”. As we know, opening a sentence with “in short” is an absolute middle finger of a move, up there for officiousness with “furthermore”, “with respect”, “to be clear” and “I think you’ll find”. Elsewhere in that sentence, roping together the words “commercial” and “charitable”, is, I would suggest, a deliberate tactic to insinuate that the former (grubby little money-makers!) undermines the integrity of the latter (charitable, my arse!) and suggest that the Sussexes are just in it for themselves.

And finally: the absolute shellacking of the letter’s dismount, in which the king writes: “This position, distinct from the state and royal duties undertaken by the working royal family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be fully respected.”

Or in layperson’s language: “haha, you’re not royal any more, nothing in your status warrants the sustained use of capital letters or a requirement for history to remember you. We’re not giving you any money because you’ve brought this on yourselves and ps, your invocation of privacy, post the publication of your memoir and your sit-down with Oprah, is an absolute joke we couldn’t be enjoying more. See ya.” God the seething, green bile acidity of the phrase “as they would wish”! Bravo, sir! Absolutely gold standard! Poor Harry must be reeling, even as he relaxes into the warm gust of air in which he was raised. (Meghan, one assumes, is largely oblivious to just how devastating all of this is and may have found the letter merely a touch snotty.)

For the formerly royal couple, we must assume that any upset caused by the tone of this letter – and allowing for the prince’s bone-deep recognition and masochistic enjoyment of what might otherwise be an upsetting exchange – is offset by the many advantages they will enjoy now they’re back in the old country. Rolling green hills are obviously a thing of the past; the Cotswolds are as brown as southern California right now. But the prince may find comfort in the small-scale landscape, the patchwork of fields and hedgerows, the tiny lanes like crooked elbows, jammed up with tractors and alive with tiny brown birds, that large-scale farming in the US doesn’t do.

I mentioned the cheese and the bread, infinitely superior to the rubbery and sugary American equivalents, and I’d add English strawberries to that, even this late in the season. Perhaps Harry will be reunited with some of his old wardrobe favourites, too. It’s never wax jacket season in Montecito, where an extreme heat warning is in place; meanwhile, the whole of this country is down on all fours excavating its woolly jumpers from under the bed. (Don’t tell me the words “woolly jumper” won’t soothe Harry after enforced wearing of sweaters and hoodies.) For Meghan, these consolations will be alien, but perhaps, before it starts to enrage her, she can find comfort in this country’s relative slowness, its high tolerance for dishevelment and appreciation for sarcasm – failing which, there’s always the pub.

Anthropic Says It Blocked Possible Efforts to Build Biological Weapons

The New York Times September 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

In a new report, the A. I. start-up added that it could not determine whether the research was legitimate or nefarious, leading the company to shut down the work.

By Dustin Volz

Dustin Volz has written about malicious uses of technology, including A. I., for over a decade.

Anthropic said it had disrupted several potential plots this year by scientists who used its leading artificial intelligence models to conduct research that could have helped develop biological weapons.

In a report describing misuses of its A. I. models, Anthropic said it could not determine whether the research served a legitimate or nefarious purpose because valid biological inquiry — the kind that can lead to breakthroughs like vaccines — can also help engineer dangerous pathogens. In the face of that uncertainty, Anthropic said it erred on the side of caution because the consequences of missing malicious activity could be severe.

“You are not seeing someone in a comic book kind of way say, ‘Hey, I want to build a biological weapon to kill everybody,’” Jacob Klein, the head of threat intelligence at Anthropic, said in an interview. “It’s an incredibly nuanced situation.”

The potential for cutting-edge A. I. models to facilitate the development of known or entirely new biological pathogens is among the gravest concerns experts have about a technology that is developing so rapidly that even its leading architects doubt whether humans will be able to fully control it.

Compared with the threat of catastrophic cyberattacks or A. I. agents that fail to align with human intentions, biological misuse has gained less attention as an existential risk of A. I., in part because past examples have generally been shown only in research settings rather than in the real world.

Andrew Weber, a senior fellow on the Council on Strategic Risks who reviewed Anthropic’s report before its release, said the findings were “chilling examples of state-sponsored biological weapons developers tapping into the rapidly advancing capabilities” of leading A. I. models.

The lengthy report that Anthropic published on Thursday cataloged a litany of misuses on various models of its Claude A. I. chatbot over the past eight months. Some examples were similar to past disclosures from Anthropic and other A. I. labs, including suspected Chinese and Iranian government-linked actors targeting dissident and diaspora communities for surveillance.

The report also highlighted cases of Russian state media using Claude to generate online propaganda masquerading as independent reporting, including fabricated claims about an election in Moldova.

Anthropic documented another genre of abuse it said was new: attempts to use Claude to develop software for conventional weapons design and development, including firearms, missiles, armed drones and bombs. It detailed three cases in China, two in Russia and one in Yemen.

The report does not identify by name which parties were involved in the Yemeni case, but the context makes clear that it is referring to the Iran-backed Houthi militia. A. I. use by terrorist networks is a growing concern among U. S. security officials.

But among all the categories of threats shared in the report, none may be as worrisome as the biological research cases. Anthropic did not disclose the names of researchers or institutions that it blocked, their countries of affiliation or the specific biological agents at issue, in part because of its uncertainty about their aims.

Still, Anthropic said the scientists circumvented its controls intended to prevent users from blocked regions from gaining access to its A. I. models and worked to “obfuscate the purpose of their research to evade our safeguards.” The company banned accounts associated with the research.

In one example from May, a scientist sought Claude’s help with writing a grant application for funding to conduct research intended to experiment on the chikungunya virus, a mosquito-borne malady that can lead to months of severe pain and other symptoms. Such research, known as gain of function, can be legitimate and lead to vaccine development, but it can also create superbug versions of viruses. In this instance, the scientist wanted to engineer mutations to the virus that would make it more harmful as it repeatedly infected live animals.

Anthropic said it believed the particular research was worrisome in part because it could discern that the work was intended to be performed at a military research institute.

“What we don’t know is if the research was meant to be weaponized,” Mr. Klein said. “But a military institution doing gain-of-function research is concerning.”

Anthropic said evaluations from last year of its older models demonstrated that they were not yet able to meaningfully assist in conducting dangerous biological research. Its current models are more able to complete complex scientific research, the company said, which spurred tighter safeguards intended to restrict access to a wide range of dual-use biological research queries.

Susan Monarez, a microbiologist and public health expert who oversaw a review of national biosecurity preparedness in the Obama administration, also reviewed the Anthropic report before its publication. She said the findings provided real-world evidence to support concerns that bad actors were trying to covertly use advanced A. I. “to improve their chances of building biological pathogens that could cause significant harm.”

Dr. Monarez, who briefly served as the director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention last year, said A. I. held enormous promise to usher in an era of medical breakthroughs that save and extend lives. But the same abilities that make that possible, she added, could also “let bad actors hide in plain sight, using seemingly legitimate research to create pathogens we may not see coming and may not be able to stop once released.”

Mr. Weber of the Council on Strategic Risks, who also served as the assistant secretary of defense for nuclear, chemical and biological defense programs during the Obama administration, called for limiting access to A. I. tools capable of this level of biological research to trusted researchers only.

“The fact that Russia, China and North Korea continue to develop prohibited biological weapons makes it imperative that we deny their researchers access to these extraordinarily capable models,” he said.

Dustin Volz writes about cybersecurity and intelligence for The Times. He is based in Washington.
