The Next Terrorist Attack Is Predictable

The New York Times September 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Philip Bobbitt

Mr. Bobbitt is a legal scholar and was the senior director for strategic planning at the National Security Council under President Bill Clinton

On Sept. 11, 2001, I was in an airplane at Kennedy International Airport bound for Europe, scheduled to leave at 8:30 a. m. For some reason, we were removed from the rotation and sat on the tarmac as other planes took off.

As I glanced over the shoulder of my seatmate, I saw a dark gray wafer-shaped explosion, two or three floors thick, violently thrust forward from one of the World Trade Center’s two towers. Some minutes later, as I watched intently, a huge golden sunburst erupted from the second tower.

I knew what had happened. Sept. 11 was not only predictable; it had been predicted.

When I drafted my final memo to the president’s national security adviser, Sandy Berger, at the end of the summer of 1999, I wrote, among many other observations, that the United States would be struck on the American homeland by Al Qaeda within two years. I wrote this not because I was a specialist in counterterrorism; on the contrary, I was simply repeating the convictions of my colleagues at the White House who had tried desperately to mobilize the government against this threat. As the principal leader of that group later testified, we failed.

Now America faces another set of predictable attacks from two looming perils. Both stem from the emergence of artificial intelligence and its widespread availability to those who would harm the country. The first is an A. I.-designed cyberattack on U. S. critical infrastructure that could imperil the financial and health care systems, or any other internet-connected network on which we rely for our national well-being. The second is a biological attack mounted by small groups or even nihilistic individuals using A. I. to design and deploy a deadly and highly contagious pathogen.

Once again, we are failing to take the steps that can prevent or preclude the effects of such atrocities. At the same time, the democratic cohesion on which our defenses ultimately depend is eroding. And as the reaction to the Covid pandemic tragically suggests, disinformation and conspiracy theories could undermine the ability of experts to limit the damage from an A. I.-driven biological attack. They also increase the possibility, present at the attacks 25 years ago, that not only American lives, but also the continued functioning of American government itself, could be at risk.

Osama bin Laden’s revolution was enabled by the globalizing internet. He transformed the recruiting, financing and sheer reach of terrorism, moving from the narrowly vertical, nationalistic structures of terrorist groups like Northern Ireland’s I. R. A., Turkey’s P. K. K., Algeria’s F. L. N. and others to a decentralized, horizontal model. This greatly increased the potential for attacks. Radicalized Muslim communities were well suited to such innovations because they were global, but there was no reason that the threat of global terrorism would end with the demise of Bin Laden and the defeat of his movement.

Diffuse networks, now with access to even more powerful technological tools, remain a threat. If Flight 93 had hit its target — likely the United States Capitol — instead of being brought down by heroic passengers over Pennsylvania, it would have struck during a business session of the House of Representatives. Countless members of Congress would have been killed or disabled and, unlike the Senate, the House could not have been reconstituted without new elections. Months would have passed without a functioning federal legislative branch. The possibility that only the executive would rule after a catastrophe is a threat to our constitutional order and remains with us today.

The challenge of taking the steps necessary to limit the damage of an attack has only grown in the 25 years since Sept. 11. We have been lulled into thinking that another attack will not occur. As misinformation, disinformation and the denigration of expert opinion make preparation far more challenging, the environment of confusion, division and fear, as much as any potential attacker, is an equally insidious danger.

The interrogation of Dr. Anthony Fauci by a Senate committee in July is just the latest example of the dangerous attack on expert opinions. Dr. Fauci’s heroic efforts to prepare for a potential pandemic at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases from 1984 through 2022 were crucial to our enduring the Covid crisis. The contemptuous — and contemptible — harrowing of him on Capitol Hill is bound to have a paralyzing effect on taking the kinds of precautionary steps that can minimize the consequences of cyber and biological attacks.

Those who want to limit the potential damage of an attack nevertheless have a place to start. After the carnage in 2001, the independent Continuity of Government Commission, led by Lloyd Cutler and Alan Simpson, created a road map for enduring another terrorist attack. One of the proposals of the commission, on which I served, would speed the replacement of members in an emergency. Another was to reconstitute a devastated Supreme Court by enlisting the chief judges of the 13 federal circuit courts. But in the period following the defeat of Al Qaeda, a sense of urgency for preparedness faded. Congress failed to act on these proposals.

After the shock of the Covid pandemic, a second Continuity of Government Commission was constituted in 2021. It restated the case for congressional action to protect against a mass attack. It also made recommendations about the continuity of government during a pandemic, including protecting the succession to the presidency in the event of a mass attack on the cabinet and congressional leaders. The commission, on which I also served, also explicitly identified infectious disease as a continuity of government problem and devised constitutional machinery to cope with the inability of officials to assemble in person. Lawmakers should urgently revisit these recommendations, and they should be stockpiling laws and protocols to anticipate these crises as well as sharply increasing the funding of research.

Seven years after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks I wrote that “the developments that empower terror are gaining — as markets increase, as weapons technologies diffuse, as clandestine communications become more effective and infrastructures more fragile — at a faster pace than our defenses, our pre-emptive strategies and our legal institutions are adapting.” Now, 18 years later, the same indictment has become even more critical. On the anniversary of the attack, Congress should determine to anticipate the tragically predictable.

Philip Bobbitt is a professor of law at Columbia University specializing in constitutional law and strategy and worked in the federal government during seven presidential administrations.

Oil Prices Surge as Stocks and Bonds Wobble

The New York Times September 10, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Crude oil hit its highest levels in months, bond yields continued to rise and stocks fell for a fourth consecutive session as investors worried about energy supplies and inflation.

How much the international benchmark costs

Notes: Data shows future contract prices for Brent crude oil. Gaps indicate nontrading hours. Data is delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

By Gregory Schmidt and Jenny Gross

Gregory Schmidt reported from New York and Jenny Gross from London.

The price of oil rose to the highest level in months and stocks and bonds slumped on Thursday as the escalating war in the Middle East and intensifying fears about inflation weighed on investors.

Oil prices surged to $109 a barrel, about a 50 percent increase since the start of the war in Iran in late February. The rise in energy costs threatens to push prices up more broadly, squeezing consumers and businesses already grappling with stubbornly elevated inflation.

Investors are looking to a crucial report on U. S. inflation, set for release on Friday, that could alter expectations for the Federal Reserve’s decision on interest rates at its meeting next week. Traders believe that a rate increase is more likely than not. The European Central Bank raised its key interest rate on Thursday, the second time it increased rates since the war began.

Fears of accelerating inflation and forecasts for higher Fed rates have been major factors behind a steady rise of bond yields. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note, a measure of borrowing costs that influences mortgages, business loans and many other types of debt, jumped above 4.9 percent on Thursday, the highest level since 2023.

Note: Data delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

The effect of rising yields, which move inversely to prices, is apparent in the housing market. The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage, the most common home loan in the United States, hit 6.76 percent this week, the highest level in more than a year, according to the mortgage financing giant Freddie Mac. Sales of existing homes fell 2 percent in August from the month before, the National Association of Realtors said Thursday.

“Americans are hitting the pause button on home buying,” said Heather Long, the chief economist at the Navy Federal Credit Union.

The S&P 500 fell about half a percent at the close of trading on Thursday, the fourth consecutive decline for the benchmark stock index.

How stocks are trading in the United States

Note: Data delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

The latest turmoil on Wall Street was provoked, in part, by reports from Yemeni officials on Thursday that the Iranian-backed Houthi militia had captured a port city, giving it greater control over passage through the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia had been using this route to export its oil and bypass the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman.

The continued disruption to shipping in the Persian Gulf and Red Sea has snarled the global supply of energy, with few signs of an end in sight. President Trump said on Wednesday that the fighting would continue through the November midterm elections in the United States.

Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which carried a fifth of the world’s oil supply and a significant amount of natural gas before the war, is still running at a small fraction of prewar levels. Twelve ships passed through the strait on Wednesday, compared with more than 130 per day before the war, according to Kpler, a maritime information company.

Oil exports from Saudi Arabia, long the world’s biggest oil exporter, fell last month to their lowest levels in at least 13 years, according to Kpler.

With Iran targeting tankers in the Persian Gulf and the Houthis targeting Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, Saudi Arabia is now exporting more oil north through the Red Sea via the Suez Canal. This route is longer and costlier, but Saudi Arabia has few good options.

Fawaz A. Gerges, a professor at the London School of Economics, said the Houthis viewed the war in Iran as their best opportunity to both consolidate power and completely cut off the route that Saudi Arabia just months ago considered a lifeline for its oil exports.

“If this descends into all-out war, this could have catastrophic implications,” he said.

U. S. gasoline prices rose on Thursday to a national average of about $4.28 a gallon, according to the AAA motor club. Drivers are paying 44 percent more on average for gas than when the war began. The average price of diesel also climbed, to $5.98 a gallon, up 59 percent since the start of the war.

The market is still pricing in persistent geopolitical risks, “with Persian Gulf tensions showing no credible path to de‑escalation,” analysts at ING wrote in a research note. “If anything, current signals point to further escalation, keeping upside pressure firmly in place.”

Lisa Friedman contributed reporting from London.

Gregory Schmidt is a senior staff editor who has covered real estate since 2022.

Jenny Gross writes about business and economics for The Times and is based in London.

Some in G. O. P. Balk at Trump’s $5,000 Offer: ‘We’re $40 Trillion in Debt’

The New York Times September 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The president’s call to send a $5,000 “dividend” to every American adult if Republicans win the midterms disturbed some members of his party.

By Reid J. Epstein and Shane Goldmacher

Reid Epstein reported from Washington. Shane Goldmacher reported from the Republican convention in Dallas.

Republicans spent the first five hours of their midterm convention in Dallas warning about socialism on Wednesday before President Trump surprised many of them with an audacious trillion-dollar proposal to redistribute wealth.

Mr. Trump’s call to send $5,000 to every adult American — but only if his party wins in November — was quickly denounced by Democrats, who accused him of trying to buy people’s votes. But it also was panned by some Republican fiscal hawks as a socialist-style giveaway and gimmick that could have harmful economic repercussions.

“We’re $40 trillion in debt,” said Representative Ralph Norman, Republican of South Carolina and the vice chairman of the House Freedom Caucus, who called the idea “far-fetched” in an interview. “To make that dependent on keeping the House, I think is problematic and I don’t know where the money comes from.”

Joe Lonsdale, a co-founder of Palantir and a major Republican donor who was a co-host of a Wednesday night party at the Dallas convention with one of Mr. Trump’s sons, Donald Trump Jr., was unimpressed by the proposal.

“For the record, I am hugely in favor of winning the midterms, and love much about this admin, but am strongly against bread and circus bribes,” he wrote on X when his event, billed as The Great American Midterm Party, was scheduled to be underway.

Mr. Trump’s elect-us-we-pay-you plan dismayed a number of Republicans who were not close to the president.

Marc Short, who served as the White House legislative affairs director in Mr. Trump’s first term and as former Vice President Mike Pence’s chief of staff, called the $5,000 proposal the latest in “a series of policy adjustments that blur the line between us and democratic socialists.”

Mr. Short ticked through a list that included the government taking a stake in private enterprises, implementing price controls, capping credit card fees and a labor-friendly trade agenda.

“He understands the marketing. He understands the moment. I don’t think he prioritizes the economics,” Mr. Short said. “Basically, it’s a redistribution of wealth.”

The potential payments, which were estimated to cost roughly $1.3 trillion, could complicate a number of the administration’s pressing economic goals. With Mr. Trump silent on how he would be pay for the proposal, it threatened to add to a national debt that has exceeded $40 trillion, causing jitters in the bond market that the Trump administration has been struggling to contain.

And at a moment when voters are blaming the Trump administration for not doing enough to tame rising costs, the trillion-dollar payment could act much like the Biden-era stimulus measures that Mr. Trump and other Republicans blamed for spiraling inflation. On Thursday, the European Central Bank raised interest rates to the highest level in a year in an effort to tame inflation, blaming the war in Iran for worsening inflation pressure. Federal Reserve officials will consider raising rates next week.

Representative Chip Roy, a Texas Republican and a prominent fiscal hawk, said in a text message that “A trillion and a half dollars of inflationary deficit spending is not my preferred focus, to say the least.”

Of course, for the last decade, Mr. Trump has defined Republican economic policy and discarded much of the party’s longstanding economic goals. Largely gone are concerns about debts and deficits and strict adherence to free-market and free-trade principles.

Asked by Laura Ingraham during a Fox News interview on Thursday, “if you have the money, why not give it now,” Mr. Trump blamed Democrats, even though Republicans control both chambers of Congress, and went on to talk about tariffs.

It was not immediately clear whether the Republicans who control Congress had any appetite to push for the measure.

Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the Republican majority leader, said on Fox News on Thursday that it was a “good question” whether there would be votes for such a package. “We will cross that bridge when we come to it,” Mr. Thune said.

Speaker Mike Johnson has not commented publicly.

Mr. Trump has a long history of making big promises he has failed to win support for. Earlier this term he promised a DOGE dividend paid for with money Elon Musk’s team cut from the federal budget and a “tariff refund” funded with money the government was collecting in import taxes. Neither happened.

Still, the $5,000 offer tied to the midterms proved Mr. Trump still has the ability to shock.

“The policy community on all sides is aghast,” said Maya MacGuineas, the president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, who was in bed reading a book Wednesday night when she received a flurry of text messages about what Mr. Trump had proposed.

Still she did not discount the possibility of Republicans, should they win the midterms, finding a way to legislate Mr. Trump’s proposal into reality.

“Trump has an incredible power over his party to create support where there wouldn’t have been otherwise,” she said. “It’s really hard to say no to giveaways.”

At least some Republicans were enthusiastic about the proposal. Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio wrote that he would prepare legislation “so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately.”

But a parade of Republicans from the party’s diminished old guard registered their disapproval online. Former Gov. Asa Hutchison of Arkansas warned about the national debt and said that Republicans “should be the adults in the room” and reject Mr. Trump’s proposal. Former Representative Justin Amash of Michigan called it a “ridiculous, unrealizable bribe.” And The National Review condemned the proposal under a headline: “Trump Breaks Glass, Joins Socialists, Embraces Bribery.”

The White House did not respond to requests for more details about the president’s plan or questions about criticisms of his proposal.

The policy-minded defense of Mr. Trump’s proposal was left to allies who were intellectually versatile.

Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, appearing on Fox News right after Mr. Trump finished speaking, called $5,000 a “real incentive” even as he tried to attack the other party.

“The Democrats love offering free money,” Mr. Cruz said, just after Mr. Trump’s offer of free money. He went on to attempt to erect some conservative intellectual scaffolding around Mr. Trump’s thin giveaway proposal.

“One way to conceive this that is also an incentive for work is that it’s a tax rebate,” he said. I’d like to see as many incentives as possible for work.”

Mr. Trump did not frame the $5,000 as a tax rebate.

Vice President JD Vance was asked about the proposal on the same network by the hosts Bret Baier and Sean Hannity.

“You guys don’t need it,” Mr. Vance said. “This is for the American middle class.”

That is not how Mr. Trump described it, either.

He said in his convention address that if Republicans hold on to power in Congress: “I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000.”

Reid J. Epstein is a Times reporter covering campaigns and elections from Washington.

Shane Goldmacher is a Times national political correspondent.

Denver Sues to Block Armed ICE Agents at Voting Sites

The New York Times September 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The City of Denver and civil rights groups argued that sightings of ICE agents at polling places are having a chilling effect.

By Jazmine Ulloa

The City of Denver, Latino civil rights organizations and government watch groups asked a federal judge on Thursday to block the Trump administration from allowing armed federal immigration agents to serve warrants at polling sites.

The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Washington, D. C., asserts that Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, and David Venturella, the acting head of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, are allowing federal agents to enforce civil immigration laws at polling locations as a matter of policy. The plaintiffs argue that the practice violates federal laws protecting free and fair elections.

“The presence of federal force at the polls interferes with the smooth administration of elections at the local level,” the lawsuit states. “It disrupts voting and makes it more difficult for state and local election officials and law enforcement to do their jobs by making polling places spaces of confrontation.”

Their lawsuit is the first against the administration over such actions.

In a statement Thursday afternoon, the Department of Homeland Security said that any arrests near polling sites would be the result of “intelligence-driven targeted enforcement.”

Speaking to reporters last week in New York, Mr. Mullin said that Democrats were fear-mongering and that ICE was not patrolling polling places. “The only reason why we would be at polling places is if there is a threat to that polling place,” he said, “or we’re serving a warrant.”

The groups that brought the suit argue such actions violate federal law, which bans military personnel or other “armed” agents from being “at any place where a general or special election is held, unless such force be necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.”

Civil rights and government watch groups say they have chronicled several encounters at polling sites nationwide since the spring that they said failed to meet that bar. In May, they allege, armed agents “swarmed” the parking lot of an active polling site in San Antonio to detain a person in plain view of voters until the county sheriff ordered them leave.

In June, ICE agents entered a polling site in Syracuse, N. Y., to interrogate an election volunteer over a social media post that she made five months earlier regarding the fatal ICE shooting of a woman in Minneapolis, according to the lawsuit.

The possibility of federal agents at the ballot box has intensified concerns of Election Day chaos in an already volatile campaign season. Ahead of the 2026 midterms in November, the Trump administration has sought to impose restrictions on mail voting, prompted a congressional redistricting race and escalated efforts to identify and deport noncitizens who registered to vote, even with no evidence of widespread voter fraud.

Fears that the Trump administration might send armed federal agents or troops to polling places or election offices have simmered among Democrats, voting rights groups and immigrant rights networks for months. Mr. Trump has long repeated unfounded assertions of electoral fraud and has called for Republican officials to “take over” elections in parts of the country.

Trump administration officials have said there is no plan to deploy armed agents or troops in the upcoming elections. But they have also not ruled out the possibility that armed agents could be present at polling locations or involved in elections.

In the lawsuit filed on Thursday, city and county officials in Denver said the area is home to a large immigrant population, making it a likely target for ICE operations during the midterm election.

The presence of armed officers could deter residents from casting votes or dropping off mail-in ballots and could fuel anxiety among election workers and volunteers, they said in the lawsuit. Election officials in Denver have already scheduled training for election workers on how to identify federal agents in plain clothes, document their presence and de-escalate interactions, according to the lawsuit.

In a statement, Mayor Mike Johnston of Denver, a Democrat who has sparred with the Trump administration over its mass deportation efforts, said his city would “fight tooth and nail” to prevent the stationing of ICE agents near polling sites.

“Our right to vote is powerful and enshrined in the U. S. Constitution and U. S. Code,” Paul López, the Denver clerk and recorder, said in a statement.

The groups involved in the lawsuit — Common Cause; the League of United Latin American Citizens, or LULAC; and UnidosUS — said recent ICE activity at polling locations was already chilling voter registration drives, canvassing efforts and civic participation in the electoral process. The organizations have also diverted funding, staff time and ad space away from standard voter mobilization efforts toward establishing rapid-response safety networks, “Vote Safe from ICE” educational materials and de-escalation training.

In a statement, Janet Murguía, the president and chief executive of UnidosUS, said sending officers into polling locations was “not immigration enforcement” but “voter suppression, plain and simple.”

Juan Proaño, the chief executive of LULAC, called the actions part of the administration’s “attempts to weaken the very institutions it is entrusted to protect.”

Jazmine Ulloa is a national reporter covering immigration for The Times.

Behind the Scenes, Vance Gathered Unvarnished Views of the Iran War

The New York Times September 10, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Times Exclusive

Vice President JD Vance received sobering assessments about the war that did not line up with what he, President Trump and other top administration officials were saying publicly.

By Jonathan SwanAdam Entous and Maggie Haberman

Reporting from Washington

Vice President JD Vance took the unusual step over the spring and summer of calling U. S. military commanders in the Middle East, Europe and Asia directly, seeking their unvarnished assessments of the Iran war, according to current and former officials.

Mr. Vance, who opposed the war from the outset and was charged by President Trump with helping to end the conflict, wanted the commanders’ individual judgments, in their own words, before they were consolidated into a Pentagon view.

The conversations delved into an array of issues related to the war, including its objectives, tactics, casualty estimates, what the Iranians would do in the Strait of Hormuz, how adaptable they had become and how much punishment their government could absorb. Mr. Vance also asked for a detailed accounting of what remained in the commanders’ stockpiles, and how the transfer of weapons to the Middle East would affect their ability to deter China, Russia and North Korea.

On that last point, the commanders were blunt. They were most worried about their depleted stocks of Patriot interceptors, the backbone of their air defenses. By late spring, one theater was down to fewer than 100 of them. The war had also exhausted the theater’s supplies of the Army Tactical Missile Systems, which can reach 190 miles, along with stores of the Precision Strike Missiles, which were meant to replace them. Stocks of critical munitions such as these, they told the vice president, were the lowest they had ever seen.

This account is based on interviews with more than a half-dozen current and former officials, who were granted anonymity to disclose sensitive information.

Mr. Vance came away from some of his conversations with deep concerns about the overall strategy and the prospects for success, according to people who spoke to him. The assessments made clear the extraordinary amount of pain the Iranian government was prepared to endure in its fight for survival, and the limited supply of U. S. defensive weapons available to block Iran’s retaliatory strikes, or to deal with threats elsewhere.

The vice president incorporated these lessons into his private talks with Mr. Trump and their inner circle. At the same time, the president was hearing more in his briefings from Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, about the strain on U. S. stockpiles and the resilience of Iranian forces, which Mr. Trump initially found difficult to believe.

The officials’ accounts, taken together, show how Mr. Vance has sought to surface a greater level of detail and nuance about the war. They also help to flesh out hotly debated questions about what kinds of information about the war Mr. Trump is receiving, and from whom. And for Mr. Vance, who had only limited national security experience before he became vice president, they show how he is now immersed in a costly and inconclusive war that could shadow him in a potential 2028 presidential campaign.

There was a gulf between the sobering private assessments that Mr. Vance received and what top administration officials, including the president and vice president, have said publicly. Mr. Trump has continued to falsely claim that the United States has already won the war, that the Iranian military has been demolished and that there are no problems with U. S. weapons supplies. And Mr. Vance recently downplayed the idea that the United States was even engaged in a war.

Privately, the president has raged about media stories detailing the diminished stockpiles, calling journalists “treasonous” for reporting on the topic. In the wake of the coverage, government investigators subjected dozens of senior military officers at the Pentagon to polygraph tests. Other officials have worried about signaling weakness to China and Russia, who are closely surveilling U. S. stockpiles.

Mr. Vance’s calls to the commanders were made with the knowledge of the president; Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth; General Caine; Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also serves as the national security adviser; and Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, according to officials with direct knowledge.

Sean Parnell, a Pentagon spokesman, said in a statement that “to ensure the president’s team receives all available data points regarding ongoing operations in the Middle East, the secretary has facilitated direct access to combatant commanders for the vice president and other senior White House leaders.”

Joseph Holstead, General Caine’s spokesman, said, “There is no gap in the military advice provided to the president, the vice president, and the secretary of war,” referring to the title Mr. Hegseth uses. Mr. Holstead added: “The chairman, joint staff, and combatant commanders are in direct and continuous communication, and their operational and strategic assessments inform the military options and advice provided to senior leaders.”

Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, said, “President Trump has built the most talented national security team in history. The entire team is laser focused on ensuring that the president has all the information he needs in order to deter America’s enemies. Everybody works in coordination with each other on that mission.”

Mr. Vance, who enlisted in the Marine Corps during the Iraq war, has told colleagues that he considers himself one of the president’s principal advisers on national security.

Luke Schroeder, Mr. Vance’s press secretary, said, “The vice president is thankful for the partnership of Secretary Hegseth and Chairman Caine. He views them as indispensable colleagues in advising the president and executing his decisions.”

Before the start of the war on Feb. 28, Mr. Hegseth and General Caine had restricted planning to an unusually small circle of officers at the Pentagon and in Central Command for operational security reasons, and to prevent potential leaks. Key officials, such as the Treasury and energy secretaries, were excluded from the prewar planning meetings.

That secrecy left commanders around the world largely in the dark until roughly a week before the bombs fell, when secret messages arrived from the Pentagon ordering them to transfer specified munitions, in specified quantities, to Central Command, which directs Middle East operations. No explanation was given, and none was needed.

Mr. Vance’s effort to collect more information on the war began early.

Within days of the start of the war, Mr. Vance told colleagues that he wanted more granular briefings to inform his views and to better advise Mr. Trump. General Caine, for his part, saw his job as providing the president with unbiased military options rather than advocacy. He would interpret Mr. Trump’s intentions and lay out ways for him to achieve them. For each option, he would highlight the secondary considerations, the risks and the potential implications.

But he would not tell the president which option to choose, according to officials with direct knowledge of his presentations. The vice president sought out uniformed military officers who would offer blunt and unfiltered opinions and recommendations, and he would incorporate what he heard into his own counsel to the president.

Mr. Vance’s opposition to the war was no secret inside the White House. In the weeks leading up to Feb. 28, he argued against the operation in meetings in the Oval Office and Situation Room, at times to Mr. Trump’s considerable irritation, according to officials who discussed the matter with the president. But once Mr. Trump made up his mind, Mr. Vance defended the decision in public, including during tense television interviews.

The vice president also became the public face of the peace effort, running a series of talks that yielded a memorandum of understanding in June. Its 60-day window closed in August with no agreement and with the two sides seemingly further apart than when the negotiations started.

Mr. Trump had not seriously contemplated the war lasting long enough to strain U. S. stockpiles. He was fresh off the success of the quick military strike to capture Venezuela’s leader, and was impressed by how the United States and Israel had combined to attack Iranian nuclear sites over 12 days the previous year. Before launching the war in Iran, he had privately expected the government there to collapse within days.

As Mr. Vance was making his calls, the fighting ran well past the roughly six-week window that Pentagon planners had initially budgeted for the campaign. Senior White House advisers beyond the vice president did not believe they had a clear-enough understanding of how much the strikes had changed the calculus of the government in Tehran.

As the war dragged on, commanders were ordered to transfer more of their munitions. They watched with alarm as their stockpiles dwindled.

By April, Mr. Trump could see the war was not going the way he had hoped. He authorized his team — including Mr. Vance, the president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and the special envoy Steve Witkoff — to begin seeking a framework and negotiating a deal with Iran to end the conflict, an agreement that would leave the country’s authoritarians in control. The officials briefed on the calls with the commanders could not say what role, if any, the vice president’s findings played in the president’s shift toward diplomacy.

Mr. Vance is hardly the first vice president to play an active role on national security. President Barack Obama chose Joseph R. Biden Jr. as his No. 2 for his foreign policy experience. And Vice President Dick Cheney was a driving force in launching and directing the Afghanistan and Iraq wars in the George W. Bush administration.

Mr. Vance reached out directly to Admiral Brad Cooper, who commands U. S. forces in the Middle East, and to officers in Europe and Asia — theaters not directly in the Iran fight but whose weapons and equipment have been drawn down to support it.

Chief among his private interlocutors was Admiral Samuel J. Paparo Jr., the head of the U. S. Pacific Command, who is responsible for all American military activity in the region where China is expanding its reach and directly challenging U. S. supremacy. Admiral Paparo brought experience directly relevant to the Iran war: He previously oversaw naval operations across the Middle East, the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. (A spokesperson for Pacific Command declined to comment on the vice president’s communications with Admiral Paparo, referring questions to the White House.)

Mr. Vance has developed a reputation inside the Trump administration for steeping himself in operational detail, a habit that some officials admire and others regard as too much in the weeds. Where Mr. Trump works in a way that leaves even his aides guessing how he arrives at decisions, Mr. Vance obsessively tracks the daily minutiae, including military operations, the internal dynamics of the Iranian political system and the sourcing of intelligence assessments.

John Ratcliffe, the C. I. A. director, has given him direct access to agency analysts; Mr. Vance knows some of them by first name and calls their desks to ask about raw intelligence or items in his morning briefing, intelligence officials said.

To satisfy the vice president’s demands for details, Mr. Hegseth had the Office of Naval Intelligence write Mr. Vance daily reports on the Strait of Hormuz, which Mr. Trump’s other senior aides now receive as well, according to senior Pentagon officials.

These reports describe which ships are transiting the strait, their flags and their cargo. General Caine sends Mr. Vance previews and recaps of U. S. strikes in the detail normally reserved for the officers running them. (General Caine himself is known to reach out directly to senior C. I. A. officers, including station chiefs in conflict zones, in order to solicit their on-the-ground assessments, officials said.)

But such access is the exception. For most senior officials, information about the war remains hard to come by.

Adam Goldman contributed reporting.

Jonathan Swan is a White House reporter for The Times, covering the administration of Donald J. Trump. Contact him securely on Signal: @jonathan.941

Adam Entous is a Washington-based investigative reporter for The Times, focused on national security and intelligence matters.

Maggie Haberman is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

Ancient Tombs, Untouched by Looters, Are Found Under Peru’s Sands

The New York Times September 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

One archaeologist called the tombs “the discovery of the decade” as the first burials from the Chimu kingdom to have escaped centuries of plunder.

By Alan Yuhas

Under a ruined citadel on Peru’s arid northern coast, archaeologists have discovered an ancient mausoleum untouched by centuries of conquest and plunder by the Inca, Spanish colonizers, and generations of looters, officials announced this week.

The site, Chan Chan, whose ruins include giant adobe brick ruins, has been excavated for decades. But researchers had never before found an undisturbed tomb at the city, which was the capital of the Chimu kingdom that ruled much of Peru’s coast before the Inca.

The tombs contained 38 bodies, archaeologists said, adding that the scale of the mausoleum — nearly 55 feet on each side and 16 feet high — and the scores of artifacts within suggest the people buried there were members of the Chimu elite. The team of Peruvian archaeologists said that the tombs were about 600 years old, which would date them to just before or during the Inca conquest of the region, in the mid-1400s.

“This is the discovery of the decade in terms of it’s the very first time that, as archaeologists, we are able to see an elite Chimu burial,” said Gabriel Prieto, a professor of anthropology at the University of Florida, who was not involved in the research.

The Peruvian archaeologists realized only slowly that they had found something different, as they removed sand, soil and debris from the tomb’s entrance one centimeter at a time.

“It was a feeling of anxiety and urgency, to know if we were really in front of a chamber that had never been looted,” said Jorge Meneses, the archaeologist responsible for excavations.

By the time they had cleared about 40 centimeters from the door, he said, the team could peer inside with a flashlight. They saw a series of funerary bundles, still safe from thieves after hundreds of years.

“In that moment we realized that the chamber had not been looted,” he said.

The excavation, near the town of Trujillo, has taken months and is still going on. It has revealed a stairway that descends eight feet into the middle of the mausoleum, where one chamber is flanked on each side by a larger room. One person was buried in the central chamber; the eastern room was nearly empty; and the western room held a trove of artifacts and the remains of about 20 people. Eighteen more have been found elsewhere in the complex.

The skeletal remains in the central chamber had red pigment on the skull and some other bones, Dr. Meneses said, as did two skeletons atop the funeral platform. Archaeologists say the pigment may be cinnabar, another clue suggesting the remains were from the Chimu elite.

Many of the remains had ear ornaments, silver- or copper-plated necklaces, or jewelry made of quartz, shells and semiprecious stones. The researchers also found a large number of metal weapons, heavy beads and a wooden chest containing colorful textiles decorated with images of seabirds and monkeys.

“It’s really like a treasure chest,” Dr. Prieto said.

He said that the design of the tombs and evidence from Chimu art suggests that the mausoleums were “designed to be open.” Chimu people would go in and out, he said, depositing bodies or offerings and taking human remains “out of those burials to be placed on plazas and venerated as ancestors.”

The discovery raises many questions, archaeologists said, and could significantly bolster knowledge about the Chimu. At about nine square miles, Chan Chan was the biggest city of the Americas in its time, with gardens, plazas, pyramids and mausoleums. The tomb could shed light on Chimu practices as well as on their relations with the Inca and other cultures to the north and south.

The Peruvian authorities said the bodies were still being analyzed, and have not yet revealed any details about the dead, including ages, sex, where they were born or how they may have died. (Nearly 140 child skeletons and the remains of 200 llamas were found at another Chimu site in 2019, possibly in an act of mass human sacrifice during a disastrous El Niño.)

“What is clear to us so far is that these people were part of the elite or were associated with the elite,” said Henry Luis Gayoso, the head of the project at Chan Chan and an official in Peru’s Ministry of Culture.

The excavation could provide a wealth of information to archaeologists about a transformative moment in the ancient Americas as one kingdom faced off with a rising empire, said Robyn Cutright, an anthropologist at Centre College who was not involved in the research.

The bodies, the objects and the design of the mausoleum itself could offer clues about how the Chimu and the Inca interacted. While museums and collections around the world hold Chimu objects, including those that appear to be from royal tombs, “this really is a great opportunity to see something we haven’t see before, a royal tomb undisturbed at Chan Chan,” she said.

“You can see something cool in a museum that a looter sold to a collector,” she said, “but this is the real meat of how archaeologists tell stories.”

The Death of Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie’s Child Changed Her View of Nigeria

The New York Times September 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Adichie has moved countless readers with her novels about Nigerians at home and abroad. After the death in Lagos of her toddler son, her homeland no longer feels as much like home.

By Veronica Chambers

The writer Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie and her husband were spending the holidays at their home in Lagos, Nigeria, last December when one of their twin sons came down with what seemed to be a cold. The child, Nkanu, was 21 months old — “precious” and “a funny baby,” in the words of his father, Ivara Esege. He was still playful, but when he developed a fever, Esege, who is a physician, started him on antibiotics.

By New Year’s Day, Nkanu had not improved, so the couple took him to a local children’s hospital. Concerned that he might have atypical Kawasaki disease, a childhood illness that can lead to heart attacks and strokes, Esege also contacted Johns Hopkins Hospital, near the couple’s American home in suburban Maryland. Johns Hopkins agreed to take Nkanu as a patient, but doctors there asked for additional tests to make sure he was safe to travel. Adichie and Esege took Nkanu to Euracare, another hospital in Lagos, for the examination.

The child was sedated with Propofol, a common anesthetic, to keep him still during an M. R. I. of his brain. Adichie was waiting outside when a doctor hurried past her into the cath lab. It was alarming: Why was he rushing to the room where Nkanu was having his test done? She waited in “pure panic,” she said, until the doctor returned. “He was very calm and he said to me, ‘Well, look, they gave him too much Propofol,’” Adichie recalled. “Those were his exact words, which I will never forget until the day I die.”

Nkanu had gone into cardiac arrest. Within 24 hours — it is not clear exactly when — he was dead.

Adichie and Esege told me this story in July, at their home in Maryland. On the table, there was a tray of healthy snacks: bowls of fresh cherries, another bowl of seeds and dried fruit. Adichie, 48, was dressed in a plain, loosefitting dress, her hair combed into two simple braids. Esege, tall with a curly salt-and-pepper Afro, wore a yellow T-shirt and gym shorts. He is 57 and, like his wife, a native of Nigeria.

There was an easy choreography between the couple, but also a palpable weariness. Leading me to the dining room, where we spoke for several hours, they moved slowly, as if bereavement were a kind of arthritis, pain carried in the bones. The house was more than quiet. Their daughter, age 10, was at day camp, and the younger of the twin boys was upstairs, sleeping. (The couple asked The New York Times not to use their children’s names to protect their privacy.)

Adichie and Esege still struggle to understand how their child could have died so suddenly and inexplicably. They have urged a coroner’s court to conduct an inquest — and the court is doing so — in hopes that they can help other Nigerians who have been harmed by the country’s troubled health care system but lack the means and influence to push for change. They stress that they are not suing the hospital or the doctors and just want a better health care system.

“That’s the only thing we can try and do just to help,” Esege told me. “Hopefully someone else will not have to go through this.”

The pain of Nkanu’s death has complicated Adichie’s relationship with Nigeria. The country, with its mix of resilience, vibrancy, corruption and economic desperation, is a vivid milieu in her work, exerting a strong magnetic pull on characters who leave.

In her best-known novel, “Americanah,” the main character, Ifemelu, is a young Nigerian woman who, much like the author, comes to the United States to study and live, only to experience exhaustion and alienation that feels like “cement in her soul.” Nigeria, Adichie writes, was “where she was supposed to be, the only place she could sink her roots in without the constant urge to tug them out and shake off the soil.”

Now Adichie feels uprooted. “My feelings toward Nigeria have changed,” she said. Her son’s death was the first irrevocable loss, her native country the second.

Health care in Nigeria suffers from relatively low government support, limited infrastructure and an exodus of skilled workers. According to a recent estimate from the World Bank, Nigeria has 0.4 doctors for every 1,000 people (the figure is 3.7 in the United States).

But Adichie said she had confidence in Euracare, which she was told was run by international standards. “It was kind of paraded as one of the best hospitals in Lagos,” she explained.

As it happened, she knew the doctor who spoke to her outside the cath lab. His name was Tosin Majekodunmi, and she had met him while accompanying her parents to their annual checkups at Euracare.

“My father liked him very much,” Adichie said. “I did come to consider him a friend. When my father died, he was very kind and called me.”

According to Adichie, Dr. Majekodunmi told her the doctors had saved Nkanu and he was now stable: “He said, ‘But everything is OK now because we got him back.’ And I kind of felt — I felt really confused.”

She shook her head and spoke more slowly, her voice thick with tears. “I trusted him,” she said.

Dr. Majekodunmi did not respond to interview requests from The Times.

The night Nkanu fell ill, she went home to gather the documents and payments necessary to transport him back to the United States the next morning in an air ambulance. She left and Esege stayed at the hospital.

Esege, who retired from his work as a family physician in Baltimore when the twins were born, was still at the hospital when he looked at the report the hospital’s staff had prepared for the air ambulance company. He was shocked to see that it said Nkanu’s pupils were fixed and dilated. And on the Blantyre coma scale the doctors had marked their son at zero in a range of one to five, meaning he had shown no eye movement and didn’t respond to pain.

Egese’s voice cracked as he described his reaction to me: “Nobody said anything to me about this. I mean, this basically means Nkanu is gone.”

Not dead yet, but lacking any meaningful brain function. Esege said he believed, based on the report, that Dr. Majekodunmi knew Nkanu was beyond saving after the first cardiac arrest, but he didn’t want to tell Adichie because of his closeness to her and her family.

Esege said the doctor had urged him not to call Adichie until the hospital could do a CT scan, but he replied that he couldn’t keep the information from her. He texted his wife and asked her to come back, and she returned around midnight. In the next few hours, Nkanu’s heart stopped at least two more times.

“So they basically are doing cardiac resuscitations on this poor boy for more than four hours, until 8 in the morning, when they decided to call it,” Egese said. “Nkanu, our son, was gone.”

It seemed that Esege’s theory about the timing of Nkanu’s death was not one he had shared with his wife. Adichie looked at him, incredulous, and asked, “So, sorry. We don’t actually know when our son died?”

She paused and then said again, in disbelief, “We don’t know when he died.”

Turning to me, Adichie said, “I’m actually hearing this for the first time. Some of it.” She then referred to Esege by his nickname. “I didn’t know about IV’s conversation with the doctor when I went home to try to get the payments for the ambulance. I think IV’s tried to protect me.”

Near us in the dining room, Nkanu’s highchair was still at the table, next to his brother’s. His clothes were still folded upstairs in his room. Adichie mentioned that she now had to buy clothes for one boy, not two, but was still in the habit of adding two of every item — T-shirt, shorts, sweater — to the online shopping cart.

Intermittently, throughout our conversation, she took out her phone and showed me videos of Nkanu. For brief moments, there were echoes of his laughter. On the screen of his mother’s phone, Nkanu sang and danced, played with her jewelry and climbed on Esege’s back while he pretended to be a horse, galloping the child across imaginary fields.

Not long after Nkanu died, Adichie and Esege filed a complaint with the Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria — a separate entity from the one conducting the inquest — and in February the council announced an initial finding of negligence on the part of three physicians: Dr. Majekodunmi; Dr. Titus Ogundare, the anesthesiologist who sedated Nkanu; and a doctor from Atlantis Pediatric Hospital, where Nkanu was first treated. The three were suspended pending a formal hearing; the Atlantis physician has since been cleared.

Dr. Ogundare did not respond to requests for comment.

The coroner’s inquest itself has turned into a battle, with Adichie accusing Euracare of playing a “monstrous cynical game” by creating unnecessary delays. (The inquest has been delayed until the fall.) When Esege joined an inquest hearing remotely in June, Euracare shocked the couple by accusing them of a crime: destroying evidence by having their son cremated. According to local news reports, the hospital’s lawyer, Taiwo Osipitan, said: “What they did is punishable by 15 years imprisonment. The issue is whether somebody who has done something wrong under the law can push for an inquest.”

Sylvester Shih, Euracare’s chief operating officer, did not respond to a request for comment.

“I feel so bad for IV,” Adichie said. “He’s on Zoom. He’s hearing it all. He’s hearing when someone is saying that he destroyed evidence, and by evidence, they mean our child.”

Even before Nkanu’s death, Adichie and Esege were adjusting to the losses of both of her parents and Esege’s brother in recent years. She recalled a conversation she had with her husband on Jan. 7, the day after Nkanu died.

“I just remember looking at IV and saying, ‘Do we have to have another funeral?’ IV said, ‘I cannot.’ And IV said, ‘We’ll cremate him. We’ll take him with us because we can’t leave him behind.’”

Along with her four novels Adichie has given popular TED talks and published short fiction, essays, children’s literature and, after her father’s death in 2020, a book called “Notes on Grief.”

“When my father died, I was struck by the physicality of grief. And this time, even more so,” she told me. “I feel it. It’s in my stomach and it’s in my chest, and you’re just so tired every day. Everything is difficult. Everything. And then you have to pretend. You have to pretend because you have children, and you’re terrified of how they’re doing. Sometimes my son doesn’t want me to hold him because I’m so weepy. He’s 2. So I really try. It feels like the full manifestation of my grief is impossible because of the condition of being a mother.”

About then, the little boy woke up with a wail and Esege went upstairs to get him.

Later, he swept into the room, his sister’s sweater draped over his shoulders like a superhero’s cape. He crawled into the cradle of his mother’s lap until he saw that his father had a soccer ball and went tearing after it. It was the week of the World Cup semifinals and the family found the games to be an engaging distraction.

Then the front door opened and the couple’s daughter bounced in. Tall like her father, she was dressed in all pink, her favorite color. She whispered something to her mother and Adichie smiled. Monday is hamburger day and her daughter wanted to make sure that even though she had eaten a burger over the weekend, she would get to have her favorite American meal because it was still Monday.

When we talked, Adichie had not been back to the country of her birth, the place she has brought to life in novels beloved by millions of readers, in six months. She had mentioned that she and Esege were planning to return there soon, and I asked if they planned to take their son and daughter with them. They have taught their children to love Nigeria even as they learn about its structural and political challenges.

Adichie grimaced and said, “They’re the reason we’re going.”

“Really, we’ve had two homes forever,” she continued. “We were in Nigeria every Christmas, every Easter, every summer. Our daughter said to me recently, ‘Mama, Nigeria is my happy place.’ She’s the one who wants to go.’”

I asked what her little boy understood about all that had happened. She shook her head and said, “He always says his brother is in Lagos.”

Adichie said she had always loved Nigeria and felt grateful to have a home there and one in Maryland. She came to the United States at 19 to study at Drexel University in Philadelphia and went on to earn master’s degrees from Johns Hopkins and Yale.

“I think that America made it possible for me to write, which is my life’s vocation,” she said. “But Nigeria gave me everything I needed to be able to write. And I feel grateful for that.”

But is Nigeria still where she is supposed to be?

She wiped the tears from her face and continued: “I mean, it is so surreal, all of this. I still can’t believe we’re talking about my son who died. You’re going through something, but you also feel like you’re outside of it.”

After a moment she said softly, “I do not want to go back to Nigeria.”

I came to this story with some experience of having a child who needed intensive medical care. When I wrote to Adichie and Esege about an interview, I let them know that I was a journalist but also a mother who spent four months in the NICU with my child. A few weeks later, I traveled to their home in Baltimore where the couple sat together, it turns out for the first time, and went hour by hour through the last night of their son’s life.

Deborah Segun (b. 1994) is a multidisciplinary artist from Lagos, Nigeria, based in London.

Veronica Chambers is the editor of Narrative Projects, a team dedicated to starting up multi-layered series and packages at The Times.

Houthis Seize Strategic Red Sea Port, a Major Victory for Iranian Ally

The New York Times September 10, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The Iran-backed militia routed Yemeni government forces in Mokha, putting the group in a stronger position to attack ships in a crucial waterway for global trade.

By Saeed Al-BatatiShuaib Almosawa and Vivian Nereim

Saeed Al-Batati reported from al-Mukalla, Yemen, Shuaib Almosawa reported from Sanaa, Yemen, and Vivian Nereim reported from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

The Iran-backed Houthi militia captured a strategic Red Sea port city on Thursday, according to two Yemeni officials, in a sweeping ground offensive that could give the group greater control over an important shipping route and further destabilize energy markets.

The Houthis pushed out forces allied with the Yemeni government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, to seize the city of Mokha as well as its port, according to a local official in the city and a senior provincial official. Both spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.

Mokha has been the focus of several days of fierce ground battles between the Houthis and the internationally recognized government.

Sources: Critical Threats Project at the American Enterprise Institute (Houthi-controlled areas).

Samuel Granados/The New York Times

The two sides have been at war since 2014, when the Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa. Soon after, a Saudi-led military coalition began a bombing campaign to try to restore the government to power, plunging the impoverished nation into a devastating war. A fragile truce, reached in 2022, has unraveled in recent months.

A video circulating online and verified by The New York Times shows several pickup trucks with groups of armed men standing in their cargo beds driving through a main road in Mokha. A person behind the camera is heard saying, “Death to America, death to Israel,” part of a Houthi slogan.

For Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies, the capture of Mokha is a major setback, raising questions about their ability to constrain the Houthis.

“It will put the U. S. and the Saudis and their allies in a much tighter situation than they already are,” said Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen specialist at Chatham House, a research institution in London.

For the Houthis, who are increasingly demanding to be treated as the country’s legitimate government — and be granted the power and resources that would come with that — taking Mokha is a significant victory. It also puts an ally of Iran one step closer to controlling a key maritime choke point.

Mokha is less than 50 miles from the narrow Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea. The city’s location made it an important maritime hub hundreds of years ago, and its port was once the main export point for Yemeni coffee beans.

The Houthis have previously attacked ships in the Red Sea from Yemeni territory further north, but control of Mokha gives the militia a foothold closer to the strait, with implications for global trade and oil markets, analysts say. After the Houthis seized the city on Thursday, the price of Brent crude, the global benchmark, rose to more than $105 a barrel, its highest level in months.

“This is potentially one of the more significant turning points, particularly in recent years, of the Yemen conflict,” said Adam Baron, a Yemen-focused fellow at New America, a research organization in Washington.

The Houthis are expected to try to push farther south to try and take territory next to the strait and potentially an island in the waterway. The area is “arguably Yemen’s most strategically valuable real estate,” Mr. Baron said. If the Houthis are able to take that territory, it could leave both of the Arabian Peninsula’s major maritime choke points — Bab al-Mandab and the Strait of Hormuz — under at least the partial control of Iran and its allies, he added.

The Houthi-affiliated foreign ministry said in a statement on Thursday that “maritime navigation is safe” and declared that “skirmishes” in western Yemen, where Mokha lies, “have now been brought to an end,” without elaborating.

Mokha was previously held by Lt. Gen. Tareq Saleh, a commander allied with the Yemeni government. His spokesman did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday, nor did the Saudi government.

Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a Houthi political official, said in an interview that the group’s goal was to “fully restore Yemen’s sovereignty and independence” and to confront “the Saudi enemy,” rather than expand its territory.

“Other factions” in southern Yemen can “retain the areas under their control” until a Yemeni political process is held, Mr. al-Bukhaiti added. He accused General Saleh’s forces of violating Yemen’s truce “on Saudi orders,” and said that this was why the Houthis had fought them.

On Thursday, General Saleh said on social media that he had ordered his troops to “reorganize their ranks and establish an alternative command center in a secure location,” in consultation with the Saudi-led military coalition.

His forces withdrew on Thursday from at least two islands in the Red Sea — Hunaish and Zuqar — according to the senior provincial official and a coast guard official who also spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The fate of Perim island — locally known as Mayyun — an island inside the Bab al-Mandab, remains unclear.

Bab al-Mandab has become increasingly important to energy markets since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest oil exporter, typically ships its oil through the Strait of Hormuz, the waterway connecting the Persian Gulf to the world’s oceans. Iran has effectively closed it since the early days of the war with the United States.

Saudi Arabia pivoted to the Red Sea to export most of its oil, but over the past two months, escalating tensions with the Houthis have disrupted that route.

In July, the militia declared a blockade on Saudi oil tankers passing through the Red Sea, and launched missile and drone attacks at ships and Saudi facilities from their territory in northern Yemen.

The Houthi-affiliated foreign ministry said in a statement on Thursday that the group “will not pose a threat” and that they are “prepared to be part of the regional security framework, particularly with regard to protecting maritime navigation.” The statement did not refer to fighting in Mokha.

The ministry called on the international community “to compel the Saudi regime to stop targeting Yemen.”

In recent days, Houthi officials have accused Saudi Arabia of launching more than 100 airstrikes in Yemen to support its allies in the country. The Saudi government has not commented on those claims.

The Houthis say they have retaliated with multiple missile and drone attacks inside Saudi Arabia. Earlier this week, Saudi authorities said that recent Houthi attacks had injured more than 70 civilians in the kingdom’s southern regions.

Mr. Al-Muslimi said that, going forward, he expected the Yemeni government will try to retake Mokha and “make a comeback,” aided by Saudi airstrikes.

An official familiar with the matter said that Saudi Arabia is working to align its goals with its international partners, and is focused on supporting the Yemeni government as it tries to take back territory across Yemen. The official spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomacy.

The official said that Saudi Arabia views the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia as an attempt to draw Saudi Arabia more deeply and directly into the conflict, which the kingdom would prefer to avoid.

James McManagan contributed reporting from London and Kate Kelly contributed reporting from New York.

Vivian Nereim is the lead reporter for The Times covering the countries of the Arabian Peninsula. She is based in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

Gander Welcomed Americans in 2001. Now, U. S.-Canada Tensions Hit Home.

The New York Times September 10, 2026

Sept. 11

The Newfoundland town welcomed thousands of frightened airline passengers on Sept. 11, but 25 years later, mixed emotions run through anniversary plans amid an escalating trade war.

The Newfoundland town welcomed thousands of frightened airline passengers on Sept. 11, but 25 years later, mixed emotions run through anniversary plans amid an escalating trade war.

A scene from the popular musical “Come From Away,” performed in Gander, Newfoundland, ahead of the 25th anniversary of the attacks. Credit...

Supported by

By Norimitsu Onishi

Photographs by Renaud Philippe

Reporting from Gander, Newfoundland

If any small town ever embodied Canada’s traditionally rock-solid friendship with the United States, Gander was it.

Gander — just inland on the island of Newfoundland — was where generations of U. S. soldiers made their last stop in North America before venturing across the Atlantic to conflicts from World War II to Iran. Where many Canadians and Americans forged friendships and even marriages over the decades.

And where residents took care of thousands of stranded and frightened airline passengers after the Sept. 11 attacks, inspiring the tale of selfless humanity and deep cross-border ties in the hit musical, “Come from Away.”

“We were the best ally they ever had,” said Beulah Cooper, 85, a Gander resident whose real-life bond with Hannah O’Rourke, a New Yorker whose firefighter son was killed in the World Trade Center’s North Tower, forms the musical’s emotional core. She paused, considering current tensions with the United States and added, “It’s — it’s hurtful when you stop and think about it.”

While Gander commemorates the Sept. 11 attacks every year, the event planned for Friday is taking place amid an extraordinary deterioration in relations between Canada and the United States that began with President Trump’s second term and grows more intense by the week. Even as the people in Gander recalled the lifelong friendships with Americans that resulted from the events in 2001, a strong undercurrent of hurt, disappointment and anger has run through the preparations for the 25th commemoration.

“It would be foolish to suggest that stuff is not running in the background,” said Percy Farwell, the mayor of Gander and deputy mayor during the attacks. “But that’s not what we are remembering on Sept. 11. It’s not about the relationship between our two governments or who’s got the biggest trade surplus. We’re talking about humans that we have a lot in common with.”

Still, in an hourlong interview at town hall, Mr. Farwell spoke about his disappointment at the Trump administration’s treatment of Canada.

“We’re polite, and we’re your best friend until you betray us, or threaten us, or insult us, or disrespect us,” he said. “And then we have a pretty strong resolve.”

The deep ambivalence in Gander — ahead of a two-day ceremony involving high-ranking Canadian and U. S. officials, emergency workers, community leaders and passengers from the stranded aircraft — is a microcosm of how the United States’ place in the world and its relations with its closest allies have changed in the past quarter of a century. After the attacks, the United States received an outpouring of sympathy from much of the world.

Last month, after a breakdown in trade talks, Prime Minister Mark Carney described the United States as posing a danger to Canada’s sovereignty and economy. President Trump warned Canadian leaders to “fall in line.”

In his second term, Mr. Trump launched a trade war against Canada, and he threatened to annex Canada and turn it into the 51st state. He has kept up a stream of insults against Canadian leaders and institutions — echoed by members of his cabinet and the U. S. ambassador to Canada, Pete Hoekstra, who is slated to attend the commemoration in Gander.

The breakdown in relations and the escalating trade war have left both Canadians and Americans bewildered.

“I’m angry at our government’s rhetoric and actions — this is not the way you treat your neighbor, period,” Kevin Tuerff, an American whose experience of being stranded in Gander with his partner is told in the musical, said by phone from New York City. “Canadians didn’t just help America on 9-11. They’ve helped us in multiple wars we dragged them into.”

“Honestly, I’m embarrassed,” said Mr. Tuerff, 60, who is scheduled to participate in the upcoming commemoration in Gander.

Moved by the generosity of the people in Gander in the days after the Sept. 11 attacks, Mr. Tuerff founded Pay It Forward 9/11, a charity that encourages acts of kindness on the anniversary. One example has stayed with him a quarter of a century later: He and others sheltered at a college in Gander were allowed to freely make long-distance phone calls.

“So we said, ‘Can we give you some money?’” he recalled. “‘No, no, you would do the same,’ they said. And I thought: Would we?”

Even before 2001, Gander’s airport had played a prominent role in the history of aviation. Canada, the British and Newfoundland built the airport in 1938 in the middle of the wilderness but, critically, along the shortest flight path across the Atlantic on the most eastern landmass in North America, with the exception of Greenland. During World War II, the United States helped expand the facility into one of the largest military air bases in the world. The airport’s largest section was known as the “American Side” — complete with hangars, accommodations, a bowling alley and a movie theater.

A suburban-style, car-friendly town created to service the airport — with large thoroughfares like “Airport Boulevard,” residential crescents named after aviators, few sidewalks and no historic core — grew next to the airport.

The airport itself served as a refueling stop for commercial aircraft after the war. After jets started flying nonstop across the Atlantic in the 1960s, the airport continued to serve as a stop for U. S. military aircraft and an emergency stop for commercial planes.

“Gander has always been a safe haven for anything that happens on the Eastern Seaboard,” said Dion Faulkner, who oversees the operations in Canada for Allied Aviation, a New York-based company that services carriers at airports in North and Central America.

So shortly after the attacks on the morning of Sept. 11 — with U. S. airspace closed — international flights, most en route to the United States, were diverted to Canadian airports. The 38 planes and 6,700 passengers landing at Gander nearly doubled the town’s population.

The planes waited on the tarmac between eight and 24 hours before passengers were allowed to disembark, Mr. Faulkner said.

“We had to go to the local drugstore to get Nicorette, baby formula, diapers, and we started putting that on the planes,” Mr. Faulkner said.

If disembarking passengers were frightened, so, too, were the locals who feared that terrorists could be aboard.

“Who are we letting in here? Who are we going to put in amongst these innocent people?” recalled thinking Betty Moulton, who, as a volunteer with the Red Cross, greeted passengers into the airport’s international terminal.

Nevertheless, countless people in Gander rallied to help.

“We never had to ask for volunteers,” recalled Claude Elliott, the mayor at the time. “People came in, people wanted to help. It was volunteers who stayed there 24 hours around the clock to make sure that passengers were taken care of.”

Passengers were sheltered in schools, churches and many private homes.

Learning that many were staying at her daughter’s school, Dawn Baker took over sanitary pads, sleeping bags and visited repeatedly with salad bowls. A stranded teenage girl stayed in her basement, watching movies for days before she was able to fly out to New York.

Being able to help “was a gift for all of us here,” Ms. Baker said. “We were all watching it on television, and you felt this hopelessness that there’s nothing you can do. But there was something we could do, so we hopped up and did it.”

Raphael Fusco was 17 years old and flying back to New Jersey with his father. Like all other passengers, they had to leave their luggage on the plane.

“We had no idea what was going on, we were distraught,” recalled Mr. Fusco, a composer and pianist, in a phone interview. “And these people, they gave us toothbrushes, toothpaste, they took us bowling. They made us feel like family and gave everything of themselves.”

“So when the whole world was seeing unspeakable acts of violence, the only thing that we saw was how good people could be,” Mr. Fusco said.

Mr. Fusco said he was “embarrassed” by the U. S. government’s current “bullying” of Canada. “It just shows a lack of gratitude, a lack of respect,” he said. “It just bothers me so much to see the opposite of what the Canadians showed us in terms of generosity and hospitality and warmness and brotherhood.”

Tony Toluba, a Virginia resident, is planning to come to Gander for the 25th anniversary on what will be his third visit after being stranded in 2001. He was aware that relations between the two nations are now very different from what they were during his previous visits.

“I don’t know what it will actually be like when I get there, I do have a little bit of trepidation,” Mr. Toluba said in a phone interview. “But the thing that struck me most about Newfoundland is that they’re very friendly, they’re very people oriented. I think on a people level, I think I will have the same kind of experience I’ve had in the past. At least, I certainly hope that I will.”

Norimitsu Onishi reports on life, society and culture in Canada. He is based in Montreal.
