Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

President Trump’s levies on a long, eclectic list of products from Canada have companies scrambling to figure out if their supply chains are affected.

Credit... Kelsey McClellan for The New York Times

Supported by

By Sydney Ember

Rosie Alyea, the chief sprinkle officer at Sweetapolita in Toronto, has had a bitter year.

First, the United States blocked cheap imports from entering the country duty-free, which made a mess of her sales to American customers.

“That was extremely disruptive,” she said.

Then last month, after trade talks between the United States and Canada collapsed, the Trump administration imposed punishing new tariffs on a wide and seemingly arbitrary list of items that included wine, dairy products and hockey sticks. Among them were several ingredients in Ms. Alyea’s sprinkles, like cellulose gum and glucose.

Some 2,500 miles away from Sweetapolita’s headquarters, in Santa Cruz, Calif., Zach Davis suddenly wondered: “Are sprinkles on the list?”

The question was not a trifling one. Mr. Davis is an owner of the Penny Ice Creamery, which buys thousands of dollars’ worth of Sweetapolita’s medleys of colorful sprinkles every year.

“We had to figure it out pretty quickly,” Ms. Alyea said.

In the escalating trade war between the United States and Canada, both countries seem intent on hurting the other just enough to make a point. On Tuesday, President Trump moved to ban a subset of Canadian products after Canada imposed its own retaliatory duties on an array of American exports.

Small companies are caught in the cross hairs. Many businesses are rushing to untangle the byzantine roster of tariffs that both countries have issued to determine whether they are affected.

The tit-for-tat has prompted rebukes from business organizations and disrupted main streets on both sides of the border.

“We cannot allow small-business owners to become cannon fodder in the trade war,” Dan Kelly, the president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, said in a statement last week.

John Arensmeyer, chief executive of Small Business Majority, a nonprofit advocacy group, warned in a statement of “lasting damage to U. S. small businesses.” He added that the group had heard from owners across the country, who said they would have to raise prices in response to the tariffs.

Mr. Davis of the Penny Ice Creamery prides himself on using organic, local ingredients in his ice cream. But a few years ago, he became so enamored with Sweetapolita’s sprinkles, which come in a variety of whimsical shapes and colors, that he decided to make an exception.

“You got to make the kids happy, and they do like rainbow sprinkles,” he said.

Every couple of months, he orders about 100 pounds of sprinkles, at a cost of $1,000 to $3,000, for his seven creamery locations. He recently ordered a batch of Sweetapolita’s birthday party sprinkle medley, which features confetti sequins and edible glitter, to celebrate his company’s 16th anniversary.

When it came to tariffs, Mr. Davis has paid them on refrigerators and freezers from China and Vietnam. Besides that, he did not have much experience with import duties before tensions between the United States and Canada heated up again this summer.

“I didn’t think about it a whole lot in the moment, other than to be kind of annoyed that this was still happening,” he said.

But as the end of August approached and it appeared that Mr. Trump’s 50 percent tariff on some Canadian goods would kick in, he grew nervous. Unable to get answers about whether the Canadian confections would carry the sky-high tariffs, he resolved to ask Sweetapolita directly.

Ms. Alyea knew the tariffs were bewildering for her customers. She was eager for clarity, too, especially since volatile trade policy with the United States had already shaken her business.

Last year, the Trump administration ended a rule that had permitted shipments valued at $800 or less to enter the United States without being subjected to taxes. That threw her direct-to-consumer business in the United States into disarray, pushing up shipping costs and depleting Sweetapolita’s profits.

When the latest round of tariffs on Canadian products went into effect on Aug. 22, she scoured customs forms for any indication of higher duties. To simplify orders for her American customers, who constitute half of her sprinkle business, she had long been registered as an importer of record. That meant she managed all the paperwork on shipments into the United States.

“We had multiple shipments just about to cross, so it was literally, ‘Let’s see what happens,’” she said.

Sprinkles fall under a classification code for confectionary that was not on the Trump administration’s list, she said, even though some ingredients in her sprinkles were. Still, she was relieved when she did not see any evidence that the 50 percent tariffs were being applied. Shipping on orders seemed to be proceeding as normal.

Ms. Alyea said she planned to communicate the good news to her American customers through newsletters and on her website. She also does not want to jinx anything. After all, the trade war has been unpredictable — so much so that it has motivated her to shift her focus to expanding her business in Canada.

“We’re really lucky right now,” she said. “We’re just adjacent to a disaster.”

Sydney Ember covers the U. S. economy for The Times.

U. K. Sanctions on Israeli Settlements in West Bank Divide British Rabbis

The New York Times September 10, 2026

Israel-Hamas Cease-Fire

Advertisement

Supported by

Prominent rabbis reacted with a mix of support, condemnation and concern about the ramifications for Jews in Britain.

By Amelia Nierenberg

Amelia Nierenberg, based in London, has covered the rise of antisemitism and attacks against Jews in Britain and other places.

Britain’s sanctions against Jewish settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank have sparked public division among British rabbis, with many framing their reaction in terms of their own fears about threats against Jews in Britain.

Several rabbis expressed support for the sanctions and spoke about violence they had witnessed or personally experienced from extremist settlers in the West Bank. At the same time, the country’s chief rabbi, the spiritual leader of Britain’s Orthodox Jews, was among several prominent Jews who condemned the move.

Such conflicting statements — coming days before the holiest period in the Jewish calendar — are among the most public signs of the deep divisions among British Jews, who have faced a series of violent attacks in recent months.

“Nobody should ever suggest that they represent the single opinion of any group of Jews anywhere,” said Rabbi Jeremy Gordon, who published a letter on Wednesday supporting the sanctions and detailing his own experiences with settlers.

But while British Jews have varied opinions on both Israeli and British politics, he said, almost none support or condone the violence. “There are very, very few people who would associate themselves with the extreme far right in Israel,” he said.

The sanctions, jointly announced with Canada and France, ban trade in settlement goods, and a dozen countries in all supported them.

In response, Israel’s foreign minister said the sanctions were based on “outrageous lies,” ordered the British Consulate in Jerusalem closed and barred from Israel a dozen British lawmakers and others he deemed anti-Israeli and antisemitic.

The sanctions come at a tense time for Britain, Israel and the West Bank. International attention is focused on Israel’s tightening grip on the enclave and its expansion of settlements there. In recent weeks, settlers have repeatedly attacked Palestinians as the Israeli military has stood by.

Britain, a longtime ally of Israel, has condemned the West Bank settlements, which are considered illegal under international law. The sanctions represent a striking escalation of its criticism. They come after British Jews have faced a recent wave of antisemitic attacks.

In October, two Jews died in Manchester in an attack on their synagogue during Yom Kippur. In March, arsonists destroyed ambulances belonging to a Jewish volunteer service in London. In April, two men were stabbed in a Jewish area of London, in what British officials called a terrorist attack.

In July, the British government accused an arm of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps of almost certainly directing some of those attacks.

Many British Jews have wrestled with how to reconcile the attacks with outrage over Israel’s support of the settlements and its war in Gaza, in which tens of thousands of Palestinians have been killed. The war was set off by the Hamas-led attacks in 2023, which killed about 1,200 people.

Some argue that any anti-Israel statements or actions by the British government can lead to violence against Jews.

“These measures will succeed only in bolstering the very extremism they seek to target,” Britain’s chief rabbi, Ephraim Mirvis, said on social media on Tuesday.

He said Britain’s Jews were “more vulnerable than ever” and argued that the sanctions add to the danger they face.

“Gesture politics of this kind feeds into an increasingly hostile discourse about Israel, and the cumulative effect of such punitive policies is to further embolden those, at home and abroad, who use hatred as a weapon against Jews,” he added.

Some British Jews argue that Israel’s policies have made them less safe, as those angry with the Israeli government could misdirect their rage against Jews and Jewish sites in Britain.

“Part of the reason why this is happening — this isn’t to condone it — is because terrible things are being said by people who are condoning and inflaming the West Bank settlers who are violently attacking Palestinians in the West Bank,” said Rabbi Gordon.

He and several others couched their support for the sanctions in terms of their own experiences in the West Bank.

Rabbi Jonathan Wittenberg, who leads the Masorti Jewish communities in Britain (which is similar to the conservative communities in the United States), said in a letter posted on social media on Wednesday that he had spent time this week in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair in the West Bank.

There, he said, he met a man whose brother had been killed by a settler 13 months ago. The settler violence “is a Chillul HaShem, a violation of God’s name of the worst order,” he wrote.

He described a village “under siege,” saying that he had met families who could not reach their livestock or access the toilet. The Israeli authorities defend the settlers, he said, not the villagers.

“It desecrates the millennia-old good name of the Jewish People,” he continued. “It prepares the way for more and yet more conflict, suffering and grief.”

Britain’s move drew criticism from the U. S. ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, who warned the sanctions could stoke tensions with Washington and, potentially, a U. S. response.

As in Britain, the settlements and Israel have proved intensively divisive among American Jews, and Mr. Huckabee, an evangelical Christian, has himself condemned settler violence.

Amelia Nierenberg is a Times reporter covering international news from London.

A U. S. Open Match Ended at 3:30 a. m. It Wasn’t Over for the Workers.

The New York Times September 10, 2026

U. S. Open

Advertisement

Supported by

After the epic match between Carlos Alcaraz and Ben Shelton was finally done, cashiers, ushers and cleaning crews got to work. Their next shift was only hours away.

By David Waldstein

When Steve Brown checked the time after the last sale of the night was made at the U. S. Open’s flagship souvenir shop, it was 4:11 on Wednesday morning. Mr. Brown, the store’s manager, locked the doors six minutes after that. When he went outside to go home, he was stunned to see so many people still on the grounds of the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, the site of one of the craziest nights in tennis.

“There’s people sitting out there drinking their Honey Deuces or what have you, and I’m like, Don’t you people want to go home?” Mr. Brown said during his next shift, which began less than four hours after his previous one ended.

The fans he saw had just witnessed a historic night in U. S. Open history. It was the fourth straight match in over 16 hours of tennis in Arthur Ashe Stadium. The first one started on Tuesday at 11:30 a. m. and the last of the quadruple marathons ended when the American Ben Shelton beat the defending U. S. Open champion, Carlos Alcaraz of Spain, in a fifth-set tiebreaker.

Their post-match hug was at 3:33 a. m., the latest a U. S. Open match has ever gone. But there was still work to do.

The players had post-match interviews to attend. Ushers had people to shoo out of the stadium. Cleaning crews swept up. Photographers filed their shots of the astounding match, reporters wrote stories and concession workers like Mr. Brown closed up shop. The last two members of the U. S. Open communications department remaining on site, Brendan McIntyre and Patrick Mitsch, exited the grounds at 5:05 a. m.

And despite the late ending, thousands of fans stayed until the exhausting but thrilling conclusion.

“It was at least 40 percent full in the lower bowl of the stadium,” said the veteran sports photographer Geoff Burke of Imagn Images. He recorded the final moments of the match, bundled up his equipment and grabbed one of the last media shuttles. He entered his Midtown Manhattan hotel room by 4:20 a. m. — and was back later the same morning to photograph the day’s first scheduled match in Ashe Stadium.

“Late matches are part of the lore of the U. S. Open,” said Mr. Burke, who has photographed 15 U. S. Opens. “It’s a big deal, and it’s really a privilege to be able to say you were there for the latest finish in history.”

Tennis matches can last several hours — Shelton and Alcaraz played for 4 hours 28 minutes.

The exceptionally late ending, though, was a result of four consecutive long matches at the stadium, so they did not start their match until about 11 p. m.

It is also not uncommon for U. S. Open matches to stretch past midnight. In 2022, Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner played until 2:50 a. m. Some complain that no sporting event should extend so late, and that the U. S. Open could address the issue by moving matches to Louis Armstrong Stadium when there is a backlog. That might not sit well with fans in high-priced luxury boxes in Ashe, who expect to see the top matches of the day.

The burden is more on the workers who must stay to the bleary-eyed ending. But Mr. Brown, a teacher in his regular job, was delighted to accrue the overtime. He worked 74 hours last week and has already clocked 83 this week, he said.

According to David Konecky, the United States Tennis Association’s head of talent acquisition, the workers are entitled to overtime. Because the work is condensed into a tight, three-week window, many are eager to make as much as possible during that time.

On Wednesday, Mr. Konecky said, accommodations were made to allow some workers more time to recover from the night before. “We try to rotate people and have them come in later and be as flexible as possible,” he said. “They work very hard.”

Dean Whylie is a maintenance worker who removes trash from the upper reaches of Ashe Stadium. He, too, was surprised to see how many people had stayed until the end of the last match, and he marveled at the crowds exiting the grounds just a couple of hours before dawn.

“When I got down here after 4, it was off the chain,” he said on Wednesday, after he returned to the grounds for the next shift. “It was totally packed like it was the middle of the day. And the 7 train was so crowded, I thought it was going to tip over.”

Mr. Whylie said that he takes two trains to get to his home at the other end of Queens and that he finally made it there by 5 o’clock. He snoozed for a bit and then came right back in, with no complaints.

“I’ve never seen the U. S. Open like that,” he said, before noting that he was named employee of the year in 2025. “It’s a lot of work but, you know, part of history. Plus, making bank.”

As for Mr. Brown, he made it to his home in Elmont, N. Y., for only about two hours. He walked the dog, watched a show, showered, changed and returned for work at the souvenir shop by 8 a. m.

“I’m on straight-up espresso,” he said.

David Waldstein is a Times reporter who writes about the New York region, with an emphasis on sports.

Supreme Court Again Blocks Republican-Backed Missouri Voting Map

The New York Times September 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The ruling deferred to the state’s Supreme Court, which had invalidated G. O. P.-friendly district lines, saying voters must first have an opportunity to approve the map in a statewide referendum.

By Ann E. Marimow and Mitch Smith

Ann E. Marimow covers the U. S. Supreme Court. Mitch Smith reported from the Missouri Supreme Court in Jefferson City.

The U. S. Supreme Court on Thursday once again prevented Missouri from using a congressional map in November that was redrawn to give Republicans an advantage in the midterm elections.

It was the second time this week that the Supreme Court waded into a dizzying legal fight over Missouri’s congressional map, and it came just two months before a general election in which the state’s voters could determine control of the House.

The court’s brief order did not include any reasoning, as is often the case when the justices respond to emergency requests. There were no noted dissents.

Denny Hoskins, the Missouri secretary of state, said in a statement on Thursday afternoon that his office was “directing local election authorities to use the 2022 congressional map,” not the redrawn one, in compliance with the Supreme Court order. That map would position Democrats to retain a seat in the Kansas City area.

The announcement from Mr. Hoskins amounted to a major win for redistricting opponents, who waged a yearlong fight against the new map. But it did not answer the question of how election officials would conduct a general election based on a map different from the one used in the primary in August.

Holding a general election with a different map than what was used in the primary is rare legal territory, and the courts have so far given no specific guidance on how nominees should be selected.

Before Thursday’s order from Washington, Missouri Republican leaders had been insisting they would stick with their preferred map for the general election.

No matter what, logistical and legal barriers seem likely to keep emerging. The deadline to finalize Missouri’s ballot was Tuesday.

Redistricting opponents have suggested in court filings that candidates who won their primaries under the redrawn map might remain the nominees in the same-numbered districts under the old lines. Alternately, they theorized, state law allowed party nominating committees to select candidates for each district.

In response to the Supreme Court’s order, opponents of the new map said the justices’ decision had definitively settled the question of which map will govern the November election.

“The law is the law, the Missouri Constitution is clear as was the Missouri Supreme Court,” Richard von Glahn, the executive director of People Not Politicians Missouri, said in a statement.

Earlier in the week, Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh had taken a similar action, as Missouri Democrats briefly appeared to have prevailed in a yearlong fight to preserve a House seat they hold in the Kansas City area. In that order, he deferred to Missouri’s Supreme Court, which had determined state officials should not have adopted the new map without a voter referendum. The state court ruling came even though Missouri voters already used the new map to nominate candidates in last month’s primary contests.

Instead, the state court said Missouri should use a map that had been in place since 2022 for the upcoming election.

But minutes after the justice’s order landed on Tuesday evening, Stephen R. Clark, the chief federal judge in St. Louis, ruled in the opposite direction, ordering the state to use the map that Missouri Republicans drew last year at President Trump’s request. That map was intended to help Republicans flip the seat in Kansas City.

Judge Clark’s ruling came in a different legal case, brought by a Republican congressman who is running for re-election and a G. O. P. candidate who won the primary under the new district lines. That ruling was then appealed again to the Supreme Court, resulting in Thursday’s action.

Judge Clark cited concerns in his ruling that using a different map for the general election would “wreak havoc on the fairness and orderliness” of the congressional election. He wrote that he was concerned a new map would lead to widespread voter confusion.

Mr. Hoskins, along with the governor and the attorney general, then quickly announced that they would follow the district judge’s ruling, rather than the State Supreme Court’s decision. That set off another round of court filings — and contempt proceedings against Mr. Hoskins before the State Supreme Court.

The G. O. P. map was drawn outside the usual redistricting cycle at Mr. Trump’s request, as part of an effort to improve the Republican Party’s chances of holding the House in the 2026 midterms.

The redrawn Missouri map, adopted by the State Legislature in September 2025, divided the core of Kansas City, the state’s largest city, into several districts in an attempt to unseat Representative Emanuel Cleaver II, one of two Democrats in the state’s congressional delegation. The new map did not significantly alter the partisan makeup of the other Democratic-held district, which is in the St. Louis area.

Democrats and state residents opposed to the boundaries last year collected hundreds of thousands of signatures seeking a referendum on the issue. But Mr. Hoskins said he did not believe that redistricting could legally be subject to a voter referendum, and he declined to add it to November’s ballot.

Ann E. Marimow covers the Supreme Court for The Times from Washington.

Mitch Smith is a Chicago-based national correspondent for The Times, covering the Midwest and Great Plains.

Foldable Phones Are Unpopular. Why Is Apple Selling One?

The New York Times September 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Tech Fix

The company unveiled a new iPhone that costs $1,999. Here are the economics behind that price tag.

By Brian X. Chen

Brian X. Chen is The Times’s lead consumer technology writer and the author of Tech Fix, a column about the social implications of the tech we use.

Apple this week unveiled an iPhone that unfolds like a book to expand its screen size and closes up to fit in your pocket. It’s the biggest physical change to the iPhone’s design in nearly two decades.

But even though they’ve been around for years, foldable phones aren’t particularly popular. They’re expensive, awkward and not as durable as regular smartphones. So why did Apple build one?

The simple answer is that the novel design of today’s foldable phones could help re-establish the high end of the phone market. They are meant to stand out in a sea of standard-issue, if-you’ve-seen-one-you’ve-seen-them-all smartphones.

The quintessential rectangular smartphones have gotten so good over the years that the most expensive models priced upward of $1,000 have become nearly indistinguishable from their cheaper counterparts. (Carrying a phone with three camera lenses versus two probably won’t impress people at parties.)

Foldable phones, on the other hand, are attention getters. And for their price, they’d better be: Apple’s iPhone Duo will cost $1,999 when it arrives in October to compete with Samsung’s $1,900 Galaxy foldable.

“Whenever something is exclusive, limited and luxurious, automatically consumer psychology wants it,” said Nabila Popal, a director at IDC, a market research firm. “It’s like handbags. Why is someone buying a Chanel versus that? It’s not because of the leathers. It’s to show that they have a Chanel and they can afford it.”

Apple and its competitors are following a path that television makers took about a decade ago. When high-definition TVs became commoditized, anyone could buy a bright TV with a large, sharp screen for as little as $500. To find more ways to increase profits, companies like Panasonic, LG and Sony experimented with quirky new designs, like TVs with curved displays and the ability to play movies in 3-D, and charged $3,000 for them.

Those TV concepts turned out to be flops. But in later years, TV makers found success with a different type of high-end television featuring OLED technology, or organic LED, which had more accurate colors for making movies look better and cost upward of $1,000.

Apple’s foldable handset is arriving at a moment when people will need extra persuading to upgrade to a new phone. The costs of most consumer goods, and especially electronics, have skyrocketed.

In response to an industrywide memory chip shortage driven by the artificial intelligence boom, Apple increased prices this year for many of its popular products, including Macs and iPads, by as much as 29 percent. Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro phones will cost $1,199, a $100 increase from last year’s model. The chip shortage has also forced companies to raise the prices of video game consoles and phones.

Foldable phones, which account for less than 2 percent of the handset market, may be the only part of the phone industry that will grow this year. IDC said it expected the chip-shortage-induced price increases to contribute to a 17 percent drop in worldwide smartphone sales this year — the steepest annual decline in history. However, sales of foldable phones could grow 12 percent to 22.9 million because of the iPhone Duo’s arrival, the research firm said.

Still, a foldable phone could be a tough sell even for a company as influential as Apple. Consumers have generally avoided buying foldable phones not only because of their cost but also because of their trade-offs. Their bendable screens are less durable than normal phone displays, which are protected with hard glass. Folded up, they can feel bulkier and heavier in a pocket.

Dan Frommer, a writer for The New Consumer, a tech research publication, said he had long been skeptical about the usefulness of foldable phones because so much online content, including the vertical videos on TikTok and Instagram, was produced for the small rectangular screens of normal smartphones.

“They’ve been used that way for 19 years now,” Mr. Frommer said. “What would you actually want a square, big screen for?”

Apple’s iPhone Duo appears to be addressing some of the shortcomings of previous foldable phones. The device’s name refers to two screens. Closed up, it has a 5.4-inch outer screen that people use as a normal rectangular phone; it opens up to reveal a 7.6-inch inner screen. The larger inner display shows pictures in the same aspect ratio as traditional phone screens. Apple also said the phone’s foldable inner screen was composed of a tougher material than competitors’.

In my tests, when opened, the iPhone Duo was extremely thin, measuring two-tenths of an inch. I liked that a Netflix video took up the full screen instead of showing black bars on the sides, which has been the case with other foldables. Closed up, the phone felt dainty and was about the size of a passport. It also felt less chunky in my pocket than other foldables I’ve tested, such as the $1,900 Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold. The more compact and lightweight, the better.

The inner screen has a matte texture to reduce glare. Still, I occasionally noticed the crease in the center where the screen folds. I didn’t mind it, but that might bother nit-pickers.

Apple also had to leave out some components to make a phone this thin — the iPhone Duo lacks the advanced camera system featured in the $1,199 iPhone 18 Pro phones. It also doesn’t have a face scanner for unlocking the device, relying instead on a fingerprint sensor on the side of the phone.

Though Mr. Frommer predicted that the Apple foldable wouldn’t be the right fit for him, he admitted he couldn’t resist trying one out in a store.

“When Apple makes something, there’s an allure to it to encourage people to at least check it out,” he said.

Brian X. Chen is the lead consumer technology writer for The Times. He reviews products and writes Tech Fix, a column about the social implications of the tech we use.

An N. Y. U. Mathematician Clashed With OpenAI Over a $1 Million Proof

The New York Times September 10, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

Tristan Buckmaster was on the path toward an important proof when one of the A. I. giants used its staggering resources to get there first.

By Kenneth Chang

Over Labor Day weekend, Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University, felt as if he had been rolled over by one of the biggest and most powerful companies in the world — because of a math problem.

Over the course of August, Dr. Buckmaster and another mathematician had made significant progress on a longstanding puzzle involving the Navier-Stokes equations, which describe the flow of fluids like water and air.

But then OpenAI, the artificial intelligence behemoth, jumped into the fray.

Rumors that their archrival, Anthropic, had solved one or two of math’s “Millennium Prize problems” spurred OpenAI leaders to tackle the same list of problems, which offers $1 million for the first proof that passes a rigorous review.

The list includes the Navier-Stokes puzzle, and in less than a week, OpenAI beat Dr. Buckmaster and all of the world’s other human mathematicians, announcing on Tuesday that it had found the answer.

Over the past couple of days, a firestorm has ignited across the social media universe: perceived threats, dangled prize money and suggestions that OpenAI’s A. I. agents had somehow found and incorporated Dr. Buckmaster’s recent work into the company’s proof.

On Wednesday evening, in response to questions from The Times, OpenAI said in a statement that it was “categorically” impossible for its A. I. system to have been influenced by anything Dr. Buckmaster had done in the past two months.

Dr. Buckmaster said he did not care about the $1 million or even winning the race to come up with the answer. “I love math, and I just wanted to be part of the story,” he said during a two-hour recounting of the events in his N. Y. U. office on Tuesday afternoon.

He is now part of a different story: the acrimonious rivalry between OpenAI and Anthropic, which was founded in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders who said OpenAI had become cavalier about the dangers of artificial intelligence.

“When they are two of the biggest companies in the world, they need to get over it,” Dr. Buckmaster said. “I am just a bystander in these petty games.”

The tension between Dr. Buckmaster and OpenAI also reflects a chasm of distrust between the swashbuckling culture of high-flying, high-tech start-ups and the usually cordial and communal collaboration of mathematicians, who nonetheless increasingly rely on the tools of A. I.

Both Dr. Buckmaster and OpenAI officials largely agree on what the two sides discussed over the weekend.

On Sunday, even though OpenAI had completed a proof of Navier-Stokes and Dr. Buckmaster had not, Sébastien Bubeck, the leader of the OpenAI effort, made what would seem to be enticing offers to Dr. Buckmaster: Dr. Buckmaster could publish his results first. He could also serve as the lead author of an OpenAI paper describing the proof or get ample computing resources from OpenAI to further his work. The company would also suggest that Dr. Buckmaster and his collaborator deserved to collect the $1 million prize.

The snag was that his collaborator is Levent Alpöge, a mathematician who works at Anthropic. Although this was a personal side project of Dr. Alpöge, not an Anthropic initiative, Dr. Bubeck was wary.

Dr. Buckmaster said since he and Dr. Alpöge had used both OpenAI and Anthropic tools, the best resolution would have been for the two companies to collaborate in this instance.

“The big sticking point was that they didn’t want Levent on the paper,” Dr. Buckmaster said as he sat in his spartan university office.

Behind him, on the blackboard, was a chronology of their progress on the problem; several chairs were set out nearby. This had served as what he called his “war room," where he had discussed with N. Y. U. colleagues what he should do.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, which is a major investor in OpenAI, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The two companies have denied the suit’s claims.)

In 2000, the Clay Mathematics Institute set forth the Millennium Prize problems — what it regarded as the seven grandest unsolved problems in the field — and offered $1 million bounties as additional incentive.

One of the Millennium problems involves the Navier-Stokes equations, which are named after the scientists who wrote them down in the 19th century to capture the behavior of fluid flow. These equations are of immense use to weather forecasters and aircraft designers, but to mathematicians, they remain mysterious.

A simple question they could not answer: Could the Navier-Stokes equations sometimes produce nonsensical answers in which the liquid accelerates to infinite speeds?

With help from artificial intelligence models, Dr. Buckmaster and Dr. Alpöge had solved that for simpler equations.

But now OpenAI had the grand prize. For the Navier-Stokes equations, at least in some circumstances, the answer is yes.

And Dr. Bubeck was inviting Dr. Buckmaster to join the winning team.

“They couldn’t understand why I wouldn’t take this bargain — why I wouldn’t throw Levent under the bus,” Dr. Buckmaster said.

He also had a troubling suspicion that OpenAI’s multitude of A. I. agents had, perhaps unintentionally and inadvertently, built their proof based on Dr. Buckmaster’s and Dr. Alpöge’s work. Although they had not yet publicly revealed their work, Dr. Buckmaster used an OpenAI tool called Codex, typically used to write and manage computer code, to help clean up and simplify the often messy mathematical ramblings produced by artificial intelligence.

Since OpenAI, like other A. I. companies, includes user data to help train its models, could the OpenAI agents have constructed their solution based on what Dr. Buckmaster had supplied to Codex?

“There’s no proof that they did that,” he said, but the approach in the OpenAI proof and the timeline of events “is highly suggestive that that’s exactly what happened.”

Dr. Buckmaster felt that OpenAI was trying to buy him off. He said no.

Frustrated, Dr. Buckmaster said he might take the dispute public. He said Dr. Bubeck of OpenAI replied, “Why would you ruin your career?”

Dr. Buckmaster said that when he asked how that would ruin the life of an academic researcher, Dr. Bubeck replied, “If you don’t want me to be nice, then I don’t have to be nice.”

In an interview, Dr. Bubeck disputed the tone and intent of what he had said. The offers, he said, were meant to help Dr. Buckmaster, either providing the computing resources for him to complete his proof or allowing him to take over the writing of the paper describing OpenAI’s proof.

Dr. Bubeck said OpenAI had struck similar deals with other mathematicians after earlier OpenAI math proofs. “So I was a little bit shocked by the reaction on the other side, which was not cooperative,” he said.

He said OpenAI wanted to leave Dr. Alpöge off the final paper, because “from our perspective, how can we have an internal OpenAI project with an Anthropic employee?”

He dismissed Dr. Buckmaster’s concerns that the Codex prompts had been used as part of the training for the OpenAI model.

The Wednesday evening statement from OpenAI was more emphatic: “We can say categorically that it is impossible for Dr. Buckmaster’s Codex prompts over the last two months to have influenced the system in any way, including training.”

The statement added, “After investigating, we can say with full confidence that no user inputs past July 3rd could have influenced this system in any way.”

Dr. Bubeck also said that he had not been threatening Dr. Buckmaster. “Quite the opposite,” he said. “I was trying to say: ‘Let’s try to work together. Let’s make this something good.’”

Peter Sarnak, a mathematician at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, was among those whom Dr. Buckmaster phoned on Sunday. “This kind of bargaining I’ve never heard of,” Dr. Sarnak said. “I admire him for behaving the way mathematicians behave.”

On Monday night, just before midnight, Dr. Buckmaster posted three papers on the internet describing the results he and Dr. Alpöge had completed. He also posted an 1,870-word treatise describing the history of the research and apologizing that he had not had time to polish the manuscripts up to his usual standards. And then he recounted in detail his interactions with OpenAI over the previous few days.

At 2:30 a. m., he finally left his office and went home. On Tuesday afternoon, OpenAI announced it had the Navier-Stokes proof.

Dr. Buckmaster said he was worried about what would happen next. “To go against a trillion-dollar company is super scary and frightening,” he said. “We are all scared of OpenAI.”

What has been lost in the fracas, Dr. Buckmaster says, is recognition and appreciation of what human mathematicians brought to the problem.

He points not to himself and Dr. Alpöge but to Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa, two Spanish mathematicians who a couple of years ago came up with a new strategy for attacking problems related to Navier-Stokes, designing a series of kicks that could knock fluid into flowing at impossibly infinite speeds.

“The main intellectual credit has to go to Luis and Diego,” Dr. Buckmaster said.

Most partial differential equations, which include Navier-Stokes, are notoriously difficult — often impossible — to solve exactly. Mathematicians typically take a step-by-step approach, tackling a series of ever more difficult versions to reach their ultimate goal.

In the era before artificial intelligence, Dr. Córdoba and Dr. Martínez-Zoroa would have had the luxury of years to follow through on their initial ideas. “Other people will come in and contribute ideas, and maybe we solve the Millennium Prize problem in 10 years without A. I.,” Dr. Buckmaster said.

But now A. I. has upended everything. In their collaboration, Dr. Buckmaster set up the problem, and then Dr. Alpöge fed that into an A. I. model at Anthropic. Based on what came out, they provided further input and repeated the steps.

The process worked well, but for Dr. Buckmaster, it became discouraging. “On one side it’s, like, super exciting to be part of this,” he said. “On the other side, this is frightening, because I felt like the A. I. had overtaken me.”

Was he now an interpreter of A. I. slop and no longer the discoverer of new mathematical insights?

“What’s the human part of it?” he said.

The next chapter of A. I.’s ascendancy in cutting-edge mathematics may come soon.

In its Wednesday night statement, OpenAI said: “In addition, since the completion of Navier-Stokes, we have made substantial progress on another Millennium Prize problem. We are working through how to share these results thoughtfully.”

Kenneth Chang, a science reporter at The Times, covers NASA and the solar system, and research closer to Earth.

A. I. Boom Poses Growing Public Health Threat, Former E. P. A. Officials Warn

The New York Times September 10, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Air pollution from gas-fired power plants to run data centers is expected to add at least $20 billion in annual health care costs by 2028, the group warns.

By Hiroko Tabuchi

A group representing more than 800 former employees of the Environmental Protection Agency on Thursday sounded the alarm over the health consequences of data centers. It warned that Trump administration policies to weaken pollution safeguards and speed up approvals of the facilities threatened to exacerbate those health harms.

In a report released Thursday, the nonprofit Environmental Protection Network examined pollution from power plants, gas turbines and diesel generators needed to meet data centers’ surging electricity demand. And it listed 30 federal actions taken by the Trump administration that it warned would increase pollution-related health risks as more data centers open across the country.

The report builds on modeling from academic researchers that projects that air pollution from data centers could contribute to roughly 600,000 asthma symptom cases, 1,300 premature deaths and more than $20 billion in annual public health costs by 2028. But the former E. P. A. employees note that these estimates do not account for the rollback of environmental regulations under the Trump administration, which could further increase emissions and health risks.

“What concerns me now is the role E. P. A. and other government agencies are playing and proudly touting: weakening the very safeguards designed to protect people from the pollution in the name of helping tech and power companies accelerate these data center build outs,” said Dr. Lynn Goldman, a pediatrician and former E. P. A. assistant administrator and a member of the group.

“These are decisions that can affect what Americans breathe, what gets into our water and, ultimately, what can make its way into our soil and food supply,” said Dr. Goldman, who is now dean emerita of the Milken School of Public Health at George Washington University.

The E. P. A. did not respond to a request for comment.

Data centers are the target of a national, bipartisan backlash. Much of the debate has focused on worries about a quickly changing economy and the loss of jobs to machines, along with noise, energy costs and water use.

But concerns about air pollution from the gas-burning plants to power the centers are drawing more attention.

More than 1,300 data centers already operate in the United States, and more than 2,000 more are planned, according to Cleanview, a market intelligence company that tracks U. S. power infrastructure and data center development. Still, polling shows the majority of Americans oppose data centers in their communities, elevating the issue to one that could affect November’s midterm elections.

President Trump has held steadfast in his support of A. I. Last week, the president lashed out at communities that are protesting data centers.

“The only reason that communities throughout the U. S. A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Mr. Trump posted on his Truth Social site. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.”

Mr. Trump has acknowledged, however, that families should not have to bear higher electricity bills and his ratepayer protection pledge seeks to prevent A. I. data centers from driving up electricity costs for millions of Americans.

The former E. P. A. employees argue that protecting families from pollution, illness and medical costs warrants the same urgency.

“If the administration has already said that families shouldn’t have to bear higher costs of electricity because of the A. I. boom, we think the same principle should apply to health,” said Marc Boom, a former senior adviser in the E. P. A.’s policy office.

Under President Trump, the E. P. A. has made establishing the United States as the “A. I. capital of the world” a central goal. It has made it easier for data centers to run certain kinds of emergency generators that burn diesel fuel and emit soot, nitrogen oxides and other harmful air pollution. It has proposed a sweeping rule change that would let developers start building data centers and power plants before their air pollution permits are approved. And it has exempted off-grid gas plants that supply data centers from federal limits on pollution that causes acid rain.

To make more electricity available, the E. P. A. has eased restart rules for long-idled coal and gas-burning power plants, proposed the repeal of power-plant carbon standards, and is moving to make it harder for communities to weigh in on proposed data centers through public comment. At the same time, it has throttled clean energy wind and solar projects.

The former E. P. A. employees group also points to a mismatch between the scale of the A. I. build out and the E. P. A.’s capacity to oversee it. With staffing levels at their lowest in four decades, the E. P. A. lacks the personnel and resources to monitor pollution and enforce limits, said Larry Starfield, a former principal deputy assistant administrator in the E. P. A.’s Office of Enforcement.“They’ve got fewer inspectors to go out there,” Mr. Starfield said. “They’re conducting quick and simple inspections. That’s not going to be effective for data centers.”

Shaolei Ren is a professor of electrical and computer engineering who studies A. I. and society at the University of California, Riverside, and led the analysis used by the Environmental Protection Network. He said because of the Trump administration’s explicit focus on increasing the use of fossil fuels, “the actual impact could be worse than we modeled.”

To protect public health, he said, there also needed to be a focus beyond tech companies’ emissions of planet-warming greenhouse gases, to air pollution that harms local communities.

“Tech companies report their energy use, their carbon emissions, but there’s no mention of local air pollution,” he said. And while tech companies often offset their greenhouse gas emissions with investments in clean energy, he said, it was trickier to offset local health risks.

Hiroko Tabuchi covers pollution and the environment for The Times. She has been a journalist for more than 20 years in Tokyo and New York.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Jacob Campbell was a baby when his mother was killed, and he has struggled to come to terms with the tragedy that shaped him. For the grandmother who raised him, it’s even harder.

Jacob Campbell, right, stands with his grandmother, Jeanne Maurer, in front of a tree he planted when he was a child in memory of his mother, Jill, who died on Sept. 11. Credit...

Supported by

By Katherine Rosman

Visuals by Hiroko Masuike

Jacob Campbell and his grandmother were in a dark movie theater in Sayville, N. Y., waiting for a screening of his film, “Those Left Behind,” about his quest to know his mother, who died in the Sept. 11 attacks.

But before the film was screened, Jake and his grandmother, Jeanne Maurer, 85, would have to white-knuckle it through “9/11: An American Requiem,” a 2011 documentary with harrowing images of towers spewing black smoke and fire and witnesses talking about jumpers.

As pictures of destruction flashed on the screen, Jake, 25, whispered to me. “Tell her she doesn’t need to do this,” he said.

Jeanne was sitting on the other side of me with her eyes squeezed shut. Her fingers plugged her ears.

Over the past quarter-century, Jeanne had done her best to steer clear of such footage. What she could not look at, though, Jake cannot avoid. That is in part because he grew up on the internet, where such images were inescapable.

But it is also because, through the passage of time and a relentless series of challenges, he had come to realize that he had no choice but to look squarely at all that had shaped and haunted him since the very beginning of his life.

The morning Jill died, at age 31, her parents, Jeanne and Joseph Maurer, had come to her Middle Village, Queens, apartment as usual. As their daughter put on her makeup and dashed for the train, Grandma Jeanne and Grandpa Joe waited for 10-month-old Jake to wake, then fed him and drove the few blocks back to their house.

When they arrived, there was a message on the answering machine.

“An airplane hit the World Trade Center, the other tower,” Jill’s voice said.

“We’re all safe,” she said. “I don’t think they’re even evacuating us.”

Jeanne turned on the television. Then she and her husband watched a plane hit the South Tower, exploding through the 78th floor, where their daughter worked as an administrative assistant.

In the following days and weeks, Jeanne vacillated between hysteria and magical thinking, convinced that Jill was roaming Manhattan with amnesia.

Joe, a retired Fire Department captain, knew better.

“My husband, from the very beginning did not think we would ever find her because he said she was at the point of impact,” said Jeanne. “‘She was vaporized,’ he said.”

Jill’s husband, Steve Campbell, was a Police Department officer. He visited his young son at the Maurers’ house, and Jeanne and Joe thought Steve would take Jake home once he had his bearings. When it became apparent to the Maurers that Jake would remain with them, they moved their grandson’s bassinet upstairs from the living room. What had been Jill’s childhood bedroom would become Jake’s.

In many ways, he had a typical and happy upbringing, raised in a middle-class neighborhood. There were Little League games. Visits to Santa’s Village. Catholic school. Church on Sunday — and Mets games, the family’s other religion.

Still, Jake told me recently, “It was sort of unavoidable that something was off.” He felt an emptiness. “The person that brought me into the world — the reason I existed, the anchor to my own existence — just was not there,” he said. “It’s hard to describe the strangeness of the feeling.”

In a nightly bedtime ritual, Jeanne and Joe would hand Jake a framed photograph of his mother for him to kiss. Among his earliest childhood memories is the feel of glass against his lips.

The medical examiner never identified any remains as Jill’s, so ground zero became the cemetery the family visited every Sept. 11 and on Jill’s birthday in June.

Like most curious children, Jake had many questions. But he often was afraid to ask them, not wanting to see his grandparents sad.

One day when he was 4, he summoned his courage and approached his grandparents about the woman in all the pictures: Did my mom talk?

Jake pored over Jill’s scrapbooks and family photo albums. He watched grainy VHS tapes, like the one with Jill swaying with baby Jake in her arms at his baptism, with the Lee Ann Womack song “I Hope You Dance” playing in the background. Jake loved the home movies because he could “see her move and see her being herself in a way that was not someone telling me about her,” he told me.

One of his favorites was a video his father gave him. His mother was pregnant, and “she was kind of annoyed that he kept sticking the camera in her face,” Jake said. “Those moments show the little things that make a person who they are.”

Sometimes information came when he was not prepared. When Jake was 7, he asked his grandfather who the bearded man on the cover of the newspaper was.

“He’s the man who killed your mother,” Joe said.

Jake had not understood until then that she had not simply died. Someone had taken her from him.

Jeanne did not need videos to understand what she had lost.

She had 31 years of memories playing on repeat in her mind. And they were often too difficult to talk about.

While her contemporaries were shifting into carefree grandparenting, spoiling little ones with ice cream and toys, she was starting over, raising a child.

“Jake was a gift from Jill,” Jeanne told me. “He gave us something to live for.”

She resolutely refused to cry in front of her grandson, but Jake still sensed that his family lived under a veil of sadness.

“Never Forget” became something of a family mantra, with banners on walls showing the American flag flying in front of the twin towers and a framed flag sent by U. S. soldiers in Afghanistan with a plaque honoring Jill. Sept. 11 lived among them, and more and more space was made to accommodate that housemate.

By now, Jeanne struggled to believe in God. When she prayed, she prayed to Jill.

“Three long years without your sweet smile,” she wrote on an internet memorial page for her daughter in 2004.

“Wish we could turn back the clock,” she wrote in another message, “and keep you from going to work that day.”

“It breaks my heart to not be able to hold you,” she wrote on one of Jill’s birthdays.

The cloud of Sept. 11 grew darker when Joe, who had helped with recovery efforts after the towers came down, developed esophageal cancer — an illness that has been linked to exposure to toxins at the World Trade Center site.

When he died, just as Jake was starting high school, it hit the family hard.

“Joe was my whole world,” said Jeanne.

“I felt lost,” Jake said.

As Jeanne sunk deeper into sorrow, Jake started to rebel against his sense that his identity was being swallowed by Sept. 11. Was this all he was meant to be? Part of a tragic household of martyrs?

Even before his grandfather died, he said, “I always felt that they were wallowing in the pain and the feeling that they always had to remember the event and remember her.”

“I thought, ‘I have to get away from this in order to be myself,’” he said. “I gave it its place, on the anniversary I went to ground zero, but outside of that, I didn’t want to do anything with it.”

There would be more losses to bear. When Jake was 16, his father, whom he had been estranged from for three months, died from a heart attack at 52.

“It was just unbelievable to me that this was continuing to happen,” Jake said.

Weeks later, on a cruise with his grandmother and aunt, he stepped out on a ledge over the dark water with a plan to jump.

He thought about what his aunt and his grandmother would face once they realized he was missing.

He stepped back. “I didn’t want to disappear like my mom.”

Jake left for the University of Michigan a year later. But starting fresh was not so simple.

Everyone at his high school had known Jake’s story. But in Ann Arbor, there was no way to casually answer questions about his family.

He struggled to make friends and then stopped trying. He was drinking and smoking weed alone, and he continued to think about suicide.

Jake had been determined to reject the life of grief that he believed had engulfed his family, but he did not know how. “I went so full force into putting it in a little box and trying to avoid it,” he said, “that I wound up coming back around the other side like a horseshoe.”

The coronavirus pandemic hit his sophomore year, and he traveled to Georgia to stay with his half brother, Steven Campbell, the son of Jake’s father and his first wife.

Steven, nine years older than Jake, challenged him to stop feeling sorry for himself. “He loved my mother,” Jake said, “but he wasn’t destroyed by her death. I got a different perspective.”

Jake and his brother took walks and watched movies. Jake began to think, maybe this is what happiness is — the simple things.

He started picking classes that excited him — philosophy and history — and weaned himself from alcohol and weed.

“This happened 10 months into my life,” he said. “So, if I stay miserable, that means it will have ruined my entire life. If I let that happen, we would have lost my mother, we would have lost Grandpa and we will have lost me.”

He started weekly sessions with a therapist he found through an app. And he turned back to the Catholicism of his youth.

Jake was particularly taken by a Gospel story in which the disciple Peter denies knowing Jesus amid the furor leading up to the crucifixion. And yet, Peter was forgiven. “There is at no point anyone or any situation that is beyond hope or beyond redemption,” Jake said.

Jake also found himself moved by an interview in which the talk show host Stephen Colbert discussed losing his father and two of his brothers in a plane crash when he was a child.

In the interview with Anderson Cooper, Mr. Colbert said he came to recognize and even appreciate the goodness that has come as a result of the loss — that he had allowed himself to view tragedy through a lens of gratitude. “What punishments of God are not gifts?” Mr. Colbert said, quoting J. R. R. Tolkien.

Jake transcribed Mr. Colbert’s comments into a journal and has returned to them so often he has nearly memorized them.

In 2018, I read an article about Jake in The Wall Street Journal. It ran with a photograph that showed how he had placed a “Michigan Mom” T-shirt over the spot where Jill’s name is cut into the bronze of the Sept. 11 memorial.

My own mother, who died in 2005, was a Michigan mom. I reached out to Jake on Facebook, and my sister and I sent him a care package of Michigan swag. He and I kept in touch. The next summer, over lunch, he told me how he had been reading more history and nonfiction about Sept. 11. I encouraged him to write about trying to learn about his mother by studying the event that ended her life.

When the Opinion desk of The New York Times published his essay “Growing With Grief in the Shadow of Sept. 11,” Jake felt a shift. Maybe he could try to process the impact of Sept. 11 in his life using his brain and his pen.

And so after he graduated with a business degree in hand, Jake applied and was accepted into a graduate creative writing program at Dartmouth. A new start.

Then he looked at the school calendar. The first day of classes would be Sept. 11, 2023. Jake felt caught between his past and his future. He chose the future, skipping the ground zero ceremony for the first time.

On that first day of class, he met a high-energy graduate student named Abby, who would become his girlfriend.

“It’s a day that I have given new meaning to,” he said. “I think my mother would be happy.”

But less than two months into his new beginning, his Aunt Linda, who lived her adult life in the bedroom next to his, grew critically ill. He sat by her bedside for days before she died. “I felt like I was stepping up a little bit instead of buckling,” he said.

As he dug into filmmaking at Dartmouth, Jake began to think more about how to reconcile his desire to reject the culture of mourning he was raised in with his longing to connect with the very subject of that mourning.

Maybe the answer was seeking the woman his mother was when alive, before she became a myth.

She had gone skydiving, so he went skydiving. She went backpacking in Europe, so he did too. She traveled to Australia, and off he went.

While he was there, he spent a few weeks with the family of a woman who had traveled with his mother decades before and later became her pen pal. She shared letters with Jake that Jill had written. About talking to the actor Matt Dillon at a bar at 2 in the morning. About a tour guide who had hit on her. About dating Jake’s father.

“Growing up, I heard stories,” Jake told me. “But it was a hagiography, not necessarily a real person’s story — a saint’s story with some truth sprinkled in.”

“Reading the letters,” he said, “was a tremendous experience for me. They were really funny because she doesn’t hold anything back.”

It was Jill telling her own stories, he said, “and I recognized bits of myself.”

On a visit home to Queens, he started scrounging cabinets for more. He happened upon student videos Jill had made while in college, shot at a fire station where Joe had worked. Then his grandmother told him that Jill once worked as an editor for a video company.

Learning that they shared a love of filmmaking gave Jake what he called “the courage and the clarity” to finally contend with her death in a way that felt authentic.

The result is his film, a 22-minute documentary. In it, he asks a foundational question: “What is it like to miss someone you don’t know?”

Jill is the inspiration. But Jeanne is the star.

The film, “Those Left Behind,” was selected for the Sayville International Film Festival, and Jake returned home for the festivities in August.

With the 25th anniversary of Sept. 11 approaching, I asked Jake and Jeanne if they would consider talking to me, not as a family friend but as a reporter. I had many anguished conversations with each of them.

A few days before the film festival screening on Long Island, I drove out to Queens to see them both.

Over turkey sandwiches, we talked about grief.

I asked Jeanne why she would not let herself cry in front of Jake. “I’m trying to protect him,” Jeanne said. “I’m his grandmother.”

Jake told her she did not have to keep things bottled up. “I don’t want you to have to be a little turtle, sort of hiding everything inside,” he said.

But when she asked him how he would feel to see her cry, he told her he did not know.

At my suggestion, Jake pulled up the clip of Mr. Colbert talking about finding gratitude in personal tragedy — the insight that helped Jake reframe his own attitude about the loss of his mother.

When Mr. Colbert quoted Tolkien — “What punishments of God are not gifts?” — Jeanne looked taken aback.

“It’s hard for me to feel like that, really,” she said afterward. Yes, there were gifts, the closeness of her relationship to Jake foremost among them. “But I’ll never be grateful for the punishment of losing her,” she said.

“I’m not asking you to,” Jake said softly, but Jeanne was not done speaking.

“Why does it have to happen?” she said. “Even if good does come out of it, why does it have to happen?”

“I’ll never have an answer for that,” he said.

She turned to me.

“I want him to be at peace, you know, and to be happy in his life,” she said. “I’m very happy for him that he has gone back to God.”

But she just could not square his equanimity with the losses.

“How many kids his age have gone through what he’s gone through?” she asked. Her lost faith in God, she added, is not just about Jake. “There is too much suffering.”

Jake looked at his grandmother. “You can say there is suffering,” he said, “or you can also say that it’s people like you who, faced with that suffering, decided to raise a baby and give all of yourself to something that was helpless.”

“It’s not that, Jake,” she replied. “When I see these children that are suffering, it breaks my heart.”

He threw his arms up in frustration.

“That was me!” he said. “I was the child!”

He paused and then spoke softly. “There are children out there who are suffering, and they are helped,” he said. “There are people out there who are in the midst of tragedy, and are helped. There is love in the world in equal measure to the suffering.”

Two days later, we all met in Sayville, N. Y., along with some of Jake’s friends and relatives, as well as his girlfriend, Abby, and her parents.

“Those Left Behind” opens in his childhood bedroom — also Jill’s. In voiceover, Jake explains that as a child at night, he felt the presence of his mother — “nondescript and unmistakable” — in the corner.

Later on, he talks about imagining how his mother felt at the very end of her life.

“Part of me believes that if I can conjure that moment as vividly as possible — if I can place myself in it with her, if I can see her — then I can, through some strange transference, let her know that I’m there,” he says. “I become the ghost. I sit down with her, and I tell her that I’ll be OK. That I’m still here, still trying.”

After it ended, the crowd applauded him. When they realized that Jeanne was also in the theater, they applauded her, too.

The next day, at the festival’s wrap-up luncheon, Jake was presented with one of the “best director” awards. Jake, Jeanne and Abby called me from the car ride back to Queens. I asked Jeanne how it felt to see her grandson win an award for something that had brought him closer than ever to his mom.

She answered simply: “We raised an amazing young man.”

What is it like to miss someone you did not know? That is a question asked by Jake Campbell, who was 10 months old when his mother was killed in the south tower of the World Trade Center. I have known Jake for years. This summer, he and his grandmother Jeanne Maurer -- who raised him while mourning her daughter -- agreed to talk to me about never forgetting, not remembering, God, lost faith, suffering and goodness.

Katherine Rosman covers newsmakers, power players and individuals making an imprint on New York City.

Hiroko Masuike is a New York-based photographer and photo editor for The Times.

Dudamel Lands in New York, With Big Ambitions and a Packed Schedule

The New York Times September 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

“This is not a job — it is a mission,” the new conductor of the New York Philharmonic said, starting a month of performances before taking the orchestra on a European tour.

By Adam Nagourney

Visuals by James Estrin

Adam Nagourney reported this story from Los Angeles and New York.

Wearing bright white sneakers and carrying a New York Philharmonic tote bag, Gustavo Dudamel stepped out of a black S. U. V. at Lincoln Center on Labor Day morning and headed for the stage door of David Geffen Hall. This was his first day on the job, no matter that he seemed to be all over New York this past year.

“Here we are,” he said as he walked through the open door, passing musicians arriving for rehearsal. “Let’s go.” Dudamel, the new music and artistic director of the Philharmonic, took an elevator upstairs to inspect his new office, before heading for a day of stop-and-start-and-stop rehearsals of Mahler’s Fifth Symphony and Prokofiev’s Symphony No. 5.

Less than a month ago, Dudamel was at the center of four consecutive nights of farewell celebrations at the Hollywood Bowl that captured the musical influences that shaped his 17 years leading the Los Angeles Philharmonic: classical, but also Latin, rock, pop and movie scores. He performed with the bass-baritone Ryan Speedo Green (opening night) and the founder of Coldplay, Chris Martin (closing night). There were appearances by Los Tigres del Norte, Foo Fighters, Natalia Lafourcade and Beck. One night, nearly the entire concert was sung and spoken in Spanish.

And yes, there were fireworks.

On that deserted Labor Day morning, Dudamel began a no less elaborate arrival on the East Coast. He will lead 14 concerts in three halls over the next three weeks before taking the orchestra on its first European tour in a decade. It is a meticulously choreographed arrival in its programming (more than 30 musical works, including three world premieres) and in its choice of guest performers (a roster that includes Yo-Yo Ma, St. Vincent and Aaron Tveit). And it signals that Dudamel is moving swiftly to put his imprint on the New York Philharmonic and classical music in general.

“This is not a job — it is a mission,” Dudamel said during an interview at his office. “It’s important to open up the doors and begin to connect with people. I know sometimes people panic: Where is Brahms? What is all of this?”

“But look, I’m starting this as a journey,” he continued. “We will have the chance to develop the core repertoire, which is crucial, but also be flexible and open to do these wonderful things with great artists from other fields from other styles. For me, this has not been something uncomfortable. Never.”

Still, for all the interest that has greeted his arrival — it is hard to walk down the street in Midtown without seeing his face on a poster — Dudamel, 45, faces challenges in the city that he didn’t in Los Angeles. With its exacting audiences and critics and its deep bench of artistic institutions, New York is a tougher musical environment. He will compete for patrons and attention, be it with Carnegie Hall or across Lincoln Center’s plaza at the Metropolitan Opera. And he is taking over the Philharmonic at a time when interest in classical music is waning in the city and across the country.

“It’s hard to impress the New York culture community because people think they’ve seen and heard everything,” said Darren Walker, the former head of the Ford Foundation who was also once a member of Lincoln Center’s board of directors. “New York certainly has the most vibrant cultural landscape in America and possibly the world. That is the context he’s coming in to.”

“Having said that, Gustavo Dudamel is a rare treasure: He’s a unicorn,” added Walker, who lives in New York and Los Angeles. “Not since Bernstein has there been so much excitement and anticipation for a season at the Philharmonic.”

It has been a long time since any cultural figure arrived in New York on such a wave of attention and high expectations. No matter how he expands the idea of what a modern orchestra can be, classical music fans are looking to Dudamel to rejuvenate a style of music that was once so ingrained in society that it was regularly featured on Bugs Bunny cartoons and “The Ed Sullivan Show.” It is now often dismissed as elite or dusty.

“This whole mantle is coming down on his shoulders,” Alec Baldwin, the actor who hosts “The New York Philharmonic This Week” on WQXR, said in an interview. “The Dudamel who is arriving here knows how important this is. He knows what people are expecting. He knows what’s riding on this.”

Dudamel already seems to have caught the attention of the ticket-buying public. When he took the orchestra to play with the Spanish Harlem Orchestra at the United Palace theater in May, nearly two-thirds of the audience were first-time Philharmonic ticket buyers. Ticket revenues for this season have jumped 8 percent compared with this time last year; and subscription sales have topped $12 million, a record.

“It’s not just the arrival of a new music director — it’s the extraordinary new music, the new hall,” said Matías Tarnopolsky, the president and chief executive of the Philharmonic, referring to the renovated Geffen Hall. “It is a new world compared to what we had before.”

In Los Angeles, Dudamel proved he was comfortable moving through different social and professional circles, from composers to celebrities to politicians to wealthy donors. He counts among his friends the composer John Adams, whose “On the Transmigration of Souls” will be performed by Dudamel at Geffen Hall this month; and John Williams, the composer behind “Star Wars,” who was honored at the Hollywood Bowl earlier this year. Dudamel regularly stands with some of the biggest names in pop and movies: Tonight at Radio City Music Hall, he will appear with the singer and rapper Lizzo at an event hosted by the actor Liev Schreiber.

Recently, Dudamel went to London to record an album of classical music written by Anthony Hopkins, the 88-year-old actor, with the Philharmonia Orchestra.

Hopkins, who said he was connected to Dudamel through their mutual friend Bradley Cooper, said that Dudamel was eager to help and offered suggestions on ways to improve the piece as they headed into the studio.

“He suggested to me, Let’s slow down the piece,” he said. “To bring out the full melody. He throws his body and soul in it. He’s a lovely man.”

In Los Angeles, Dudamel was credited with taking an acclaimed orchestra and broadening its appeal in a city that, like New York, was undergoing demographic churn. In one sign of this, Latinos made up a vast majority of the audience on the second night at the Bowl.

To that end, Dudamel said he was intent on ending the lingering perception of the classical arts as elitist. He described watching a video of the conductor Bruno Walter from the 1960s, in which he disparaged jazz and 12-tone music. Dudamel argued that it suggested a kind of intellectualism that alienated potential new audiences.

At this first day of rehearsal, Dudamel walked onstage to cheers from players, who had met him with hugs in hallways and the elevator. “I think we are going to have an amazing journey,” he said on the podium. “I’m so excited and so privileged. Let’s start the rehearsal.”

He raised his baton and set off on Mahler’s Fifth, one of Dudamel’s favorite works: For the next hour, he sang, spoke in English and German, recited Mahler history and music theory, and tried to coax the players into performing the music the way he envisioned it.

“To be honest,” he said at one point, smiling, “we are beautiful, but we are not together.” He lifted his baton and had them try it again.

By the first break, Dudamel’s T-shirt was stained with sweat. As he stood in the wings, the players walking past him, he glanced down at his shirt and announced he would change into another one.

Deborah Borda, who has served as chief executive for the New York and Los Angeles Philharmonics, and recruited Dudamel to come to New York, said, “One of the great pleasures in my life has been to see his development, to see him become such a leader.” She added that life would be different for him now: “New York is the center of the world in so many ways, so everything you say is judged and very visible.”

Dudamel faces adjustments in a city defined by its intensity and competitiveness, and filled with big personalities — in the arts and in politics — competing for attention. When he was in Los Angeles, he counted among his friends mayors, including Antonio Villaraigosa, who often attended performances; and Eric Garcetti, who once joined him onstage at a concert to play piano at Walt Disney Concert Hall with Moby.

By contrast, Dudamel, in response to a question, said he had yet to hear from Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City, and another millennial who has burst on to the New York scene this year.

Still, Dudamel said he viewed New York as different, rather than difficult.

“This is the capital of the world in many senses,” he said. “We have here thousands of possibilities. There are thousands of things — thousands of goals — we can achieve, but we have to be very flexible, very open, to create this story. To evolve the tradition. Not to go back.”

Adam Nagourney is the classical music and dance reporter for The Times.

James Estrin is a photographer and writer who has been with The Times since 1992.

Glass Thinner Than a Human Hair: How the New iPhone Bends but Doesn’t Break

The New York Times September 10, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The screens of foldable phones are a triumph of materials science and microengineering.

By William J. Broad

Apple on Wednesday unveiled the iPhone Duo, its first foldable smartphone with a 7.6-inch glass screen that is capable of bending countless times without breaking.

The Duo is not the first foldable phone; Google, Samsung and Motorola have all released devices with displays that bend. But in his pitch for the Duo, Apple’s new chief executive, John Ternus, said the company’s latest offering “will redesign the experience of using a foldable phone.”

The screens of foldable phones are a triumph of materials science and microengineering. No single breakthrough or industrial secret makes them possible; rather, a series of complementary feats makes a display flexible enough to bend many thousands of times without snapping yet strong enough to survive drops and other abuse.

Glass — the brittle, breakable kind — is what scientists call an “amorphous solid.” It looks and acts like a solid, but glass atoms are actually frozen in a liquid-like state. Everyday glass shatters when bent because those atoms lie in a rigid matrix that, when thick, leads to extreme tension on the outer edge of the curved surface.

But glass becomes flexible if it’s thin. The average human hair is between 50 and 100 micrometers thick. The super-thin layer of glass in a foldable iPhone is reportedly less than 30 micrometers thick, or much finer than a human hair. At this step of miniaturization, the strain on the outer edge becomes so low that the glass tends to curve rather than break.

“The thickness of a material determines its stiffness toward bending,” said John A. Rogers, a professor of materials science and engineering at Northwestern University. “If you make something very thin, it becomes easier to bend.”

Dr. Rogers compared breakable and bendable glass to wood and paper. “If you think about a piece of wood, it’s not very bendable,” he said. “But a sheet of paper, which is also wood, is flexible because it’s much thinner. The same applies to glass.”

In addition to making glass thinner, chemists found that alternative glass formulas could enhance the flexibility. Everyday glass is made of silicon dioxide, which comes from melted sand. But boron trioxide, used mainly in laboratory glassware that expands and contracts very little when heated and cooled, has an atomic matrix that’s amorphous rather than rigid and crystalline. Lab testing showed that, when thin, it bent more easily than regular glass.

Another extremely thin layer in a foldable screen is made of ultra-durable, highly transparent plastic that’s engineered to endure hundreds of thousands of fold cycles without clouding or warping.

Finally, the many layers of a foldable screen are bonded together with what the industry calls optically clear adhesives. Viscous and elastic, they act like a gel, holding the layers together firmly but under the stress of a bend still allow the layers to glide past each other.

Stella Raine Chu contributed reporting.

William J. Broad has reported on science at The Times since 1983. He is based in New York.
